title: The Messy Middle: A Time for Action
abstract: A NACFE thought-leadership report, published February 26, 2023, that lays out the 'messy middle' concept NACFE coined in 2019: the multi-decade transition period between today's diesel-dominated Class 8 long-haul trucking and an eventual zero-emission future. Rather than a fleet demonstration, this is a synthesis and decision-framework document. It surveys every major powertrain option available to fleets at the time -- advanced diesel, renewable diesel, renewable natural gas, biodiesel, CNG, LNG, hydrogen internal combustion engines, hybrids, battery-electric vehicles, and hydrogen fuel cells -- describing each one's technical maturity, cost trajectory, infrastructure availability, and regulatory context as of early 2023. It compares the options directly (Section 6), covers sustainability terminology (well-to-wheels vs. tank-to-wheels), technical maturity via a reliability 'bathtub curve,' range and route flexibility, infrastructure, vehicle integration, and regulatory drivers including California's ACT rule and IRA/IIJA incentives. It closes with a suggested sequential decision framework for fleets (start with BEV, fall back to hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, with efficient diesel as a last resort), explicitly flagged as a simplification since most fleets will need multiple technology decisions across their operations over time. An appendix maps North American fueling station counts by fuel type as of January 2023.
key_findings: Battery electric trucks are estimated at 65% to 85% overall energy efficiency from charger to wheels, versus approximately 40% to 50% for internal combustion engine trucks and 30% to 50% for hydrogen fuel cell trucks.
As of December 2022, the U.S. DOE reported only 60 public hydrogen fueling stations in North America for all vehicle types, 53 of them in California, with only 4 designated for heavy-duty trucks.
Estimated diesel engine costs are projected to rise by $2,300 to $42,000 per vehicle to meet NOx and warranty requirements under the EPA Clean Truck Plan announced in December 2022.
Most industry analysis indicates hydrogen must reach approximately $3/kg ($1.36/lb) to achieve TCO parity with diesel.

In December 2022, Tesla demonstrated a Class 8 Semi traveling 500 miles fully loaded at 82,000 lbs, but NACFE cautions this used nearly 100% of battery state of charge (versus the recommended 20-80% range) at California's 55 mph truck speed limit, unlike the 150-250 mile typical single-charge range of other production heavy-duty BEVs from Daimler, Volvo, Kenworth, and Peterbilt at the time.

By early 2019, NACFE had published three Guidance Reports on electric trucks: Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense (May 2018), Medium-Duty Electric Trucks - Cost of Ownership (October 2018), and Amping Up - Charging Infrastructure for Electric Trucks (March 2019).
BEV maintenance costs are estimated at 50% to 60% of diesel maintenance costs due to significantly fewer moving parts.
data_available: Powertrain technology-readiness comparison matrix (Figure 10: sustainability, range, infrastructure, integration, and maturity ratings by powertrain)
Reliability bathtub curve by technology maturity stage (Figure 11)
North American fueling station maps by fuel type as of January 2023 (biofuel, CNG, electric, hydrogen, LNG, renewable diesel)
EPA PM/NOx emissions progress by year, 1988-2025+ (Figure 6)
ICCT heavy-duty truck CO2 emissions progress by vehicle segment, 2010-2027 (Figure 7)

title: Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving: How 10 Fleets Grew Their BEV Populations
abstract: Documents NACFE's Run on Less - Electric DEPOT (RoL-E DEPOT) demonstration, published May 7, 2024. Unlike a single-truck-per-fleet format, this Run tracked 10 fleet depots operating 15 or more battery-electric trucks each, across 22 vehicle models from 11 manufacturers, located in California, New York, and British Columbia. Vehicles spanned Class 3-5 vans and step vans, Class 6 box trucks, Class 8 terminal tractors, and Class 8 regional-haul tractors. The report documents each depot's electrification journey (infrastructure build-out, utility coordination, charger types, funding and incentive programs), per-vehicle specs including battery capacity and estimated range, and real-world telematics data collected via Geotab (GPS, distance, speed, weight, elevation, state of charge, energy in/out while driving/idling/charging). It also covers driver experience, an Electric DEPOT Bootcamp series, and findings on which depot profiles are most electrification-ready today versus which face longer timelines.
key_findings: 10 fleet depots and 22 BEV models from 11 manufacturers were tracked across sites in California, New York, and British Columbia.
A Freightliner eCascadia at OK Produce and Penske, equipped with a 475-kWh battery, had an estimated range of 230 miles.
A Ford E-Transit step van, equipped with a 68-kWh battery, had an estimated range of 108 miles.
PepsiCo's Sacramento depot operated 21 Tesla Semis; the three tracked in the Run saw ranges of 410 miles on a single charge and completed 1,076 miles in a 24-hour period.
A GM BrightDrop ZEVO 600 step van (165-kWh battery) and an International eMV (210-kWh battery) each had an estimated range of 135 miles.
Fast permanent chargers can bring depot BEVs from 0% to 80% state of charge in about 90 minutes.
Across the four Run on Less demonstrations conducted prior to Messy Middle, NACFE had engaged a total of 48 drivers; RoL-E DEPOT followed the most drivers of any single Run to that point, at 18.
data_available: Per-fleet BEV specs: battery capacity (kWh) and estimated range (miles) by vehicle model
Charging infrastructure type, count, and funding/incentive program by depot
Driver participation counts by Run and by this Run specifically
Per-depot estimated total power/energy needs if fully electrified
Electric DEPOT Bootcamp session attendance

title: How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle
abstract: The overview/blueprint report for Run on Less - Messy Middle, NACFE's fifth Run on Less demonstration, published January 28, 2026. Unlike prior Runs that focused on a single powertrain or duty-cycle segment, this Run tracked 13 fleets operating 14 Class 8 tractors across all four current powertrain options simultaneously -- diesel/renewable diesel, CNG/renewable natural gas, battery-electric, and hydrogen fuel cell -- in long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles, over an 18-day demonstration from September 8-25, 2025. The report documents the year-long process of planning the Run (fleet/OEM selection, the nine-session Messy Middle Bootcamp educational series held February-July 2025, site visits, driver participation, promotion), the dashboard methodology (Geotab-based telematics: GPS, distance, speed, weight, elevation, and powertrain-specific metrics like state of charge and fuel level), and initial high-level findings. It explicitly defers deeper analysis to four companion reports NACFE planned to publish later in 2026: an Operations Report, an Emissions Footprint Report, a TCO Ramifications Report, and a Final Findings Report.
key_findings: 13 fleets and 14 vehicles were tracked across four powertrains (4 diesel/renewable diesel, 3 natural gas/RNG, 4 battery electric, 2 hydrogen fuel cell) over an 18-day demonstration, September 8-25, 2025.
Across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date, NACFE has engaged 63 drivers; for Messy Middle specifically, NACFE conducted 105 interviews across its 13 sites between June 3 and July 23, 2025.
The long-haul segment of trucking is 9% of the market but generates 48% of its emissions, per NREL's Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles report.

Recent powertrain advancements cited include a 15L natural gas engine and 400+ mile battery-electric vehicles; Joyride Logistics' Windrose battery-electric sleeper tractor has a reported range of up to 420 miles.
The nine-session Messy Middle Bootcamp drew 7,171 total registrations (1,191 unique) and 1,943 total attendance (720 unique) from February through July 2025.

NACFE's initial finding is that all four powertrain technologies perform well in the long-haul segment with no single winner; powertrain choice depends on duty cycle, haul length, and fueling/charging access.
A 10,000 lb weight difference affects fuel economy by approximately 0.5 MPG, per NACFE's prior Run on Less findings.
data_available: Per-fleet vehicle specs, routes, and driver profiles for all 13 fleets
Bootcamp session-by-session registration and attendance table
Dashboard metrics methodology across all four powertrains
Example dashboard charts: weather, distance vs. state of charge, speed bands, gross vehicle weight, elevation, truck activity breakdown, fuel efficiency

title: Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report
abstract: The deep operational analysis companion to the Run on Less - Messy Middle blueprint report, published March 15, 2026. It compares the same four Class 8 powertrain technologies (diesel/renewable diesel, CNG/RNG, battery-electric, hydrogen fuel cell) operating simultaneously in revenue freight service -- 13 fleets, 14 production tractors, more than 73,000 validated miles over 18 days in September 2025 across long-haul, regional-haul, drayage, and LTL duty cycles in the US and Canada. High-resolution telematics produced more than two million data points; GPS-referenced digital elevation models enabled terrain analysis for every deployment. The report introduces a duty-cycle archetype framework classifying the 14 deployments into five operational categories (Long-Haul OTR, Regional Linehaul, Regional RTB, Urban/Metro P&D, Drayage/Port Shuttles), then applies cross-fleet regression analysis, time-of-day productivity modeling, and infrastructure dependency assessment. Its central finding, echoed throughout: duty cycle and terrain profile predict efficiency variation more strongly than powertrain technology alone, and no single powertrain is universally superior. Includes per-fleet operational profiles for all 13 participating fleets and a Future Outlook section on autonomy, AI optimization, and infrastructure development.
key_findings: 13 fleets operating 14 production tractors logged more than 73,000 validated miles over 18 days in September 2025.
High-resolution telematics produced more than two million data points across the tracked trucks.
A duty-cycle archetype framework classifies the 14 deployments into five operational categories: Long-Haul OTR, Regional Linehaul, Regional RTB, Urban/Metro P&D, and Drayage/Port Shuttles.
Duty cycle and terrain profile are stronger predictors of efficiency variation than powertrain technology alone.
No single powertrain technology is universally superior across duty cycles; fleets must match powertrain capabilities to specific duty cycles, terrain profiles, and infrastructure conditions.
data_available: Per-fleet operational profiles for all 13 participating fleets (Section 3)
Duty-cycle archetype classification and definitions (Section 4)
Cross-fleet regression analysis and time-of-day productivity modeling
GPS-referenced digital elevation/terrain analysis by deployment
Data validation methodology and technology-specific data-quality considerations

title: Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report
abstract: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) companion report to Run on Less - Messy Middle, published April 30, 2026. Provides a comprehensive TCO framework for Class 8 vehicles across four powertrains (diesel, CNG/RNG, battery-electric, hydrogen fuel cell), five duty cycles (Long-Haul OTR, Regional Linehaul, Regional RTB, Urban/Metro P&D, Drayage/Port Shuttles), and three timeframes (2025, 2028, 2035). Rather than a single national-average TCO per powertrain, the analysis is fleet- and duty-cycle-specific, driven by variables such as utility rates, duty cycle, and asset utilization, and explicitly assumes no incentives in order to give fleets a conservative baseline they can adjust with their own numbers. Central findings include a 'diesel escalator' (diesel's long-term TCO advantage erodes as maintenance, insurance, and emissions-compliance costs rise even as fuel cost per mile drops slightly) and BEVs' aggressive cost-reduction curve, projected to achieve the lowest net TCO in every modeled duty cycle by 2035. Not a fleet demonstration in itself -- it models cost trajectories using data and context from the Messy Middle Run rather than reporting new telematics data.
key_findings: By 2035, BEVs are projected to achieve the lowest net TCO of any powertrain in every one of the five modeled duty cycles.
Approximately 80% of all on-road fuel used in natural gas vehicles in 2023 was RNG.
In March 2026, diesel prices jumped nearly $1.00 per gallon in a single week, illustrating diesel's ongoing budgetary volatility risk.
FCEV TCO viability is almost entirely tethered to green hydrogen delivery price, with a sensitivity range of $4.00 to $15.00/kg modeled.

In the Long-Haul OTR duty cycle, diesel's current $0.61/mile cost advantage is projected to flip by 2035, with BEVs undercutting diesel by $0.09/mile, driven partly by the emergence of 500+ mile range BEVs.
In Regional Linehaul, BEVs are projected to go from roughly twice diesel's cost in 2025 to the most cost-effective option by 2035 ($0.94/mile vs. $1.00/mile for diesel).
In Regional Return-to-Base, BEVs are projected to hold a 12% TCO advantage over diesel by 2035 ($1.13/mile vs. $1.29/mile).
In Urban/Metro Pickup & Delivery, BEVs are projected to go from a cost disadvantage in 2025 (often exceeding $4.00/mile at low utilization) to undercutting diesel by 2035 ($1.92/mile vs. $2.43/mile).
In Drayage/Port Shuttles, BEV TCO is projected to drop nearly 50% over the next decade, reaching $0.19/mile cheaper than diesel by 2035.
data_available: TCO by powertrain and duty cycle across 2025, 2028, and 2035 timeframes
Sensitivity analysis by TCO cost component per powertrain
Per-duty-cycle cost-per-mile breakdowns (fuel, maintenance, insurance, capital)
Pre-analysis checklist for fleets computing their own bespoke TCO

title: Charting the Course for Early Truck Electrification
abstract: A joint RMI/NACFE/Geotab analytical report, published in April 2022, that models truck electrification feasibility in California and New York using anonymized 2019 Geotab telematics data from medium- and heavy-duty (Class 3-8) commercial vehicles. It defines an 'electrifiable' truck as one returning to base within 300 miles in 95% of trips, then estimates charging energy demand, infrastructure costs, and grid emissions under three charging scenarios (anytime, overnight, daytime) as both states move through Advanced Clean Trucks (ACT) regulation compliance through 2035.
key_findings: Using anonymized 2019 Geotab telematics data, 65% of medium-duty and 49% of heavy-duty trucks in California and New York are 'electrifiable' today, representing up to 244,000 electrifiable freight vehicles in California and 145,000 in New York.

Daytime charging (9am-2pm, aligned with solar) cut emissions most (80-97% vs. diesel) but required the highest-power chargers (up to 350 kW for HDTs, ~$185,000/truck for hardware+installation); overnight charging cost less (~$79,000/HDT) but only cut emissions 60-74%.
Electrifiable trucks require 50-400 kWh/day of charging energy on average, comparable to the electricity use of 2 to 14 homes.
data_available: County-level daily-mileage percentile tables for CA/NY (MDT/HDT)
Per-vehicle energy demand and charger-cost tables by charging scenario
Charger hardware+install cost assumption table ($10k-$222k by charger type)

title: Electric Trucks Have Arrived: The Use Case for Medium-Duty Box Trucks
abstract: A NACFE Confidence Report published June 28, 2022, the fourth of four Run on Less - Electric (RoL-E) market-segment reports. It profiles the North American medium-duty box truck market -- vehicle configuration, OEMs, upfitters, and charging -- and reports findings from the three battery-electric box trucks (Day & Ross/Lion6, Frito-Lay/Cummins-Peterbilt 220EV, Roush Fenway Racing/ROUSH CleanTech Ford F-650) that completed NACFE's September 2021 RoL-E demonstration, covering duty cycles, charging behavior, benefits, challenges, TCO, and market-segment carbon-avoidance potential for this return-to-base delivery segment.
key_findings: Three BEV box trucks ran RoL-E in Sept 2021 -- Day & Ross Lion6 (252 kWh), Frito-Lay Cummins-Peterbilt 220EV (155 kWh), Roush Fenway/ROUSH CleanTech Ford F-650 (138 kWh) -- logging 387-756 miles each over 6-13 operating days using charging rates from 19.2 kW to 125 kW.
NACFE estimates electrifying all ~385,687 US/Canada medium-duty box trucks would avoid 7,681,707 metric tons of CO2e annually; average purchase price is ~$200,000 electric vs. ~$80,000 diesel.
Modeled annual fuel savings of about $6,269/vehicle (diesel $8,200 vs. electric $1,931 at 2021 prices, 100 mi/day, 250 operating days).
data_available: Per-fleet vehicle spec/duty-cycle table (Figure 24)
OEM battery/range/price comparison table for available electric box trucks
Diesel-vs-electric fuel cost comparison calculator table

title: Electric Trucks Have Arrived: The Use Case for Heavy-Duty Regional Haul Tractors
abstract: A NACFE Confidence Report published May 5, 2022, one of four Run on Less - Electric (RoL-E) market-segment reports. It examines the North American heavy-duty (Class 8) regional haul tractor market -- weight, length of haul, charging, and regulations -- and reports on the four battery-electric tractors -- Anheuser-Busch/BYD, Biagi Bros./Peterbilt-Meritor, NFI/Volvo VNR, and Penske/Freightliner eCascadia -- that ran NACFE's September 2021 RoL-E demonstration, covering duty cycles, weight, charging, TCO/ROI, and NACFE's revised estimate of this segment's electrification potential.
key_findings: Four Class 8 BEV tractors ran RoL-E in Sept 2021: Anheuser-Busch's BYD 8TT (Pomona, CA beverage delivery), Biagi Bros.' Peterbilt 579EV/Meritor (Napa-Sonoma wine), NFI's Volvo VNR Electric (drayage, Chino-Long Beach), and Penske's pre-production Freightliner eCascadia (Temecula-San Diego); only the Anheuser-Busch beverage duty cycle fully matched its diesel incumbent's daily work as of 2021.

NACFE revised its electrifiability estimate for this segment down to 50% (from an initial 70% RoL-E estimate), projecting avoidance of ~29.4 million metric tons of CO2e/year if half of the ~937,563 US/Canada regional haul tractors electrified.
List price for a BEV regional tractor is $250,000+ vs. $123,000 diesel; payback is 8+ years on list price alone but can drop under 5 years factoring in incentives.
data_available: Per-fleet vehicle spec and SOC/speed/distance telemetry tables
OEM production-tractor spec comparison table (battery, range, charge time)
Diesel-vs-electric TCO comparison table

title: Electric Trucks Have Arrived: The Use Case for Terminal Tractors
abstract: A NACFE Confidence Report published March 6, 2022, the first of four Run on Less - Electric (RoL-E) market-segment reports. It profiles the North American terminal (yard) tractor market and reports findings from the three battery-electric terminal tractors -- NFI/Kalmar Ottawa T2E, Ruan/Orange EV T-Series, and Ryder/Lonestar SV S22 -- that ran NACFE's September 2021 RoL-E demonstration, covering duty cycles, charging, benefits, challenges, and TCO for this fully return-to-base, low-speed yard-spotting application NACFE considers 100% electrifiable.
key_findings: NACFE considers terminal tractors 100% electrifiable; full US/Canada electrification (~25,242 units) would need ~726 GWh of charging electricity and avoid 929,687 MT of CO2e annually.

Three fleets ran BEV terminal tractors in RoL-E: NFI (Kalmar Ottawa T2E, Chino CA), Ruan (Orange EV T-Series, Otsego MN), and Ryder (Lonestar SV S22, Kentucky); daily mileage averaged 14-29 miles across fleets, with a single-day high of 73.5 miles.

Maintenance costs are roughly 60-75% lower than for recent (2017+) diesel terminal tractors, but purchase price is $275,000-$350,000 electric vs. $100,000-$125,000 diesel, giving 8+ year payback without incentives.
data_available: Per-fleet vehicle spec/battery/charging table (Figure 22)
SOC/speed/distance dashboard data per fleet
TCO and payback comparison figures

title: Electric Trucks Have Arrived: The Use Case for Vans and Step Vans
abstract: A NACFE Confidence Report published April 12, 2022, the second of four Run on Less - Electric (RoL-E) market-segment reports. It profiles the North American Class 3-6 van and step van market and reports findings from the three battery-electric vehicles -- DHL/Lightning eMotors, Purolator/Motiv EPIC, and Servall Electric/Workhorse C1000 -- that ran NACFE's September 2021 RoL-E demonstration, covering e-commerce-driven market growth, duty cycles, charging, benefits, challenges, and TCO for a segment NACFE considers 100% electrifiable.
key_findings: NACFE considers vans and step vans 100% electrifiable, estimating that electrifying all 4,143,406 US/Canada vans and step vans would avoid 43,476,632 MT of CO2e annually.
Three fleets ran BEVs in RoL-E: DHL (Lightning eMotors Transit HD, Manhattan), Purolator (Motiv EPIC step van, Vancouver), and Servall Electric (Workhorse C1000, Cincinnati).

Modeled fuel savings are about $8,107/vehicle/year (gasoline $10,065 vs. electric $1,958 at 2021 prices, 100 mi/day, 250 operating days); McKinsey projects the segment could reach 8 million vehicles by 2030.
data_available: Gasoline-vs-electric fuel cost comparison table
Per-fleet vehicle spec tables
Lessons-learned infographic (Figure ES6)

title: A Trucking Fleet Primer for Commercial Truck Electrification
abstract: A short NACFE/RMI thought-leadership primer (2 pages, published 2022) aimed at fleets beginning truck electrification conversations with utilities. It explains why utility partnership matters, what fleets should be prepared to discuss (power needs, make-ready infrastructure costs/timelines, site design, rate structures), and how to navigate North America's 3,000+ utilities via facility managers and trade organizations. It closes by pointing readers to NACFE's five electric-truck guidance reports and the Run on Less - Electric Bootcamp's 10 education sessions.
key_findings: Identifies over 3,000 power utilities in North America and recommends fleets engage utilities early on long-term electrification plans, make-ready infrastructure costs/timelines, site design, and rate structures including time-of-use and demand charges.

Points fleets to NACFE's five electric-truck guidance reports (Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense; Medium-Duty Electric Trucks: Cost of Ownership; Charging Infrastructure for Electric Trucks; Viable Class 7 & 8 Electric/Hybrid/Alternative Fuel Tractors; Making Sense of Heavy-Duty Hydrogen Fuel Cell Tractors) and the RoL-E Electric Truck Bootcamp's 10 education sessions.
data_available: No data tables; narrative guidance for engaging utilities and facility managers

title: Amping Up: Charging Infrastructure for Electric Trucks
abstract: A NACFE Guidance Report published March 1, 2019, the third in NACFE's electric truck guidance series after 'Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense' and 'Medium-Duty Electric Trucks: Cost of Ownership.' It provides a comprehensive overview of charging hardware, software/networking, siting, business models, and financial assistance for deploying commercial battery-electric vehicle (CBEV) charging infrastructure, walking through implementation steps from utility engagement through deployment, and concluding that near-term charging will center on private depot/return-to-base charging rather than public fast-charging networks.
key_findings: Concludes that for the foreseeable future, electric truck charging will center on private depot/return-to-base charging rather than public fast-charging corridor networks capable of quickly charging commercial vehicle batteries.

Cites a 2018 UPS/GreenBiz study in which 44% of surveyed fleets identified lack of EV charging infrastructure as a top electrification barrier (second only to purchase price), and The Climate Group's 2019 EV100 report in which over 70% of EV100 companies flagged charging infrastructure as a 'significant' barrier.
Identifies demand charges as a cost factor that can 'make or break the economics' of CBEV charging, and recommends smart/networked charging software to minimize both capital and operating costs.
data_available: Charger power-level comparison tables (Level 1/2/DCFC, US vs. Europe)
Charging business-model and financial-assistance program tables
Appendix directory of charging equipment suppliers and utility programs

title: Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense
abstract: NACFE's first Guidance Report in its electric truck series, published May 1, 2018. It provides a foundational, unbiased assessment of Class 3-8 commercial battery-electric vehicle (CBEV) viability versus diesel across weight, cost, maintenance, range, time, charging, and battery technology, using duty-cycle data from NREL/CALSTART/FHWA/ORNL and NACFE's 2017 Run on Less database to project when CBEV-diesel 'parity' will be reached across five representative duty cycles, from light-duty delivery through long-haul tractors.
key_findings: Concludes light- and medium-duty (Class 3-6) segments have the greatest near-term electrification potential, with Class 7/8 CBEVs still mostly prototypes or pre-production as of 2018, projected to reach production in the 2019-2020 timeframe.

Builds duty-cycle baseline tables (average/max daily miles, drive time, speed, stops) for five segments, ranging from an average daily range of 37 miles for Class 3 delivery trucks up to 457 miles for Class 7/8 long-haul tractors.

Projects CBEV-diesel 'parity' across 10 factors (weight, cost, maintenance, life, range, etc.) will be reached at different times by vehicle class -- some parity achievable now for Class 3-6, later (2020s-2030s) for Class 7/8.
data_available: Duty-cycle baseline comparison table across 5 vehicle/route segments
CBEV-vs-diesel parity timeline matrices for Class 3-6 and Class 7/8
10 fleet-concerns point-counterpoint summary table

title: Charging Forward with Electric Trucks
abstract: A NACFE Guidance Report published June 6, 2023, titled 'Charging Forward with Electric Trucks,' an updated and expanded successor to NACFE's 2019 charging guidance report. It walks fleets through planning, procuring, and installing commercial electric truck charging infrastructure -- utility engagement, charger types and connectors, construction/permitting, charging business models (CaaS/TaaS), managed charging, power-outage planning, financial assistance, and emerging technologies like the Megawatt Charging System (MCS) -- closing with a 10-step implementation roadmap for fleets.
key_findings: As of May 2023, Level 2 AC chargers (7.2-19.2 kW) cost several hundred to a few thousand dollars while DC fast chargers (22 kW-480 kW) cost $15,000-$90,000 per charger.
Covers the emerging Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standard -- up to 3,000 amps at 1,250V (3.75 MW max) -- expected to be finalized in 2024 to enable fast charging for long Class 8 routes.
Recommends fleets engage their utility 'as soon as they begin thinking about electric trucks,' since increasing power delivery to a site can take significant time to plan and build out.
data_available: Level 2 AC vs. DC fast charger comparison table (voltage/power/price/install)
10-step charging implementation checklist
Appendix directory of Level 2 EVSE 19.2kW+ providers

title: Making Sense of Heavy-Duty Hydrogen Fuel Cell Tractors
abstract: A NACFE Guidance Report published December 16, 2020, titled 'Making Sense of Heavy-Duty Hydrogen Fuel Cell Tractors.' It examines the technology maturity, hydrogen production pathways (green/blue/gray), energy efficiency, costs, safety, and duty-cycle fit of Class 8 hydrogen fuel cell trucks versus diesel and battery-electric alternatives, drawing on hydrogen bus experience, early truck prototypes and pilots, and government ZEV mandates, and concludes hydrogen truck adoption depends on regional hydrogen-production scale-up rather than trucking demand alone.
key_findings: As of 2020, only tens of hydrogen fuel cell heavy-duty trucks are in North American operation versus roughly 1.8 million diesel tractors in service; production Class 8 units remain prototypes or aftermarket retrofits from firms like Ballard, US Hybrid, Meritor/TransPower, Toyota, and Cummins, with Nikola targeting production around 2023.

A car needs about 2-5 kg of hydrogen per fill versus 50-80+ kg for a heavy-duty truck at 700 bar (10,000 psi), and NACFE found no production-proven fast-fueling system yet demonstrated at truck-scale volumes.

Frames hydrogen's real competitor as battery-electric trucks rather than diesel, recommending fleets favor hydrogen where zero-tailpipe-emission needs, minimal tare weight, routes over 500 miles, cold climates, and available green/blue hydrogen all converge.
data_available: Energy content and energy-storage-system comparison tables
US hydrogen production capacity map by region (NREL)
Vehicle tare-weight/payload/fill-time comparison tables (diesel vs. BEV vs. FCEV)

title: Hydrogen Trucks: Long Haul's Future?
abstract: NACFE guidance report published April 2023, updating the council's 2019 and 2020 hydrogen assessments. Examines fuel-cell and hydrogen internal-combustion powertrains for Class 8 long-haul van-freight tractors, covering hydrogen production, transportation, storage, fueling infrastructure, and the regulatory/investment landscape (IIJA, IRA, DOE hydrogen hubs) driving adoption. Synthesizes 2022 interviews with fleets, OEMs, and hydrogen suppliers to assess where hydrogen fits relative to battery-electric and other zero-emission alternatives.
key_findings: Daily one-driver long-haul ranges need to be roughly 600-700 miles, beyond current 300- to 500-mile hydrogen fuel-cell prototype ranges and far beyond current 150- to 250-mile battery-electric ranges.

Hyundai is deploying 30 Class 8 XCIENT fuel-cell tractors at the Port of Oakland in 2023 as part of the NorCal ZERO project, described as the largest US commercial deployment of hydrogen fuel-cell Class 8 tractors to date.
The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act provides an $8 billion DOE hydrogen hub program (funding six to ten regional hubs) plus a $40,000 federal tax credit toward zero-emission truck purchases.
data_available: Hydrogen transportation/storage method comparison figures
DOE fuel-cell cost targets ($/kW) by year
Timeline of federal/state ZEV regulations and incentives

title: Intermodal & Drayage: An Opportunity to Reduce Freight Emissions
abstract: NACFE guidance report published December 2023 examining the relationship between intermodal rail and drayage trucking as a lever for reducing freight emissions. Covers the history of containerized/intermodal freight, rail vs. truck economics and emissions, and the case for replacing diesel drayage and terminal tractors with zero-emission equipment. Analyzes public sustainability commitments and intermodal market share strategies from major railroads and trucking companies to frame recommendations for shippers, carriers, and railroads.
key_findings: NACFE concludes intermodal rail combined with zero-emission drayage can reduce freight emissions on specific lanes but is not universally better, given the six Class I railroads' limited trackage and market segmentation.
J.B. Hunt operates the world's largest intermodal fleet (115,000+ containers, 95,500+ chassis, 6,600+ drayage trucks) and targets a 32% carbon-intensity reduction by 2034 from a 2019 baseline.

The report's three core recommendations are shifting market share from long-haul trucking to intermodal rail, and replacing diesel drayage tractors and diesel terminal tractors with zero- and near-zero-emission equipment.
data_available: Freight-ton-miles by mode, 1980-2020 chart
Per-company intermodal container/chassis/tractor counts and emissions goals
Rail vs. truck emissions and market-share comparison figures

title: Medium-Duty Electric Trucks – Cost of Ownership
abstract: NACFE guidance report published October 2018 analyzing total cost of ownership for medium-duty (Class 3-6, 10,001-26,000 lb GVWR) commercial battery-electric vehicles (CBEVs) versus diesel/gasoline baselines. Covers charging infrastructure costs and business models, battery management and degradation, and known/unknown TCO cost drivers such as residual value, maintenance, and e-commerce-driven demand growth. Based on NACFE interviews with fleets, OEMs, and industry experts rather than a fleet demonstration; includes an accompanying TCO calculator spreadsheet tool.
key_findings: Daily, return-to-base urban duty cycles below 100 miles are well suited for battery-electric drivetrains; long-term uptime expectations for CBEVs are 95-98%, on par with diesel.

Maintenance costs on early-generation CBEVs were on par with diesel/gasoline trucks in 2018, but NACFE expects 40-70% lower long-term maintenance costs from reduced complexity and elimination of emissions aftertreatment systems.

Used battery-electric vehicles depreciated faster than ICE equivalents (JD Power found roughly 22-27% three-year retained value for EVs vs. about 50% for ICE), which NACFE attributes largely to higher pre-incentive list prices rather than a fundamental value problem.
data_available: Gross Vehicle Weight Rating class definitions table
Unknown-factors-in-cost-modeling diagram (market/battery/regulatory/power issues)
Charging system connector, cost, and business-model comparisons

title: Viable Class 7/8 Electric, Hybrid and Alternative Fuel Tractors
abstract: NACFE guidance report published December 2019 comparing battery-electric, fuel-cell, hybrid, CNG/LNG, and propane alternatives to diesel for Class 7/8 long-haul and regional tractors. Introduces NACFE's 'messy middle' framework describing the multi-decade, multi-technology transition period before zero-emission powertrains dominate. Assesses each alternative's duty-cycle fit, total-cost-of-ownership trajectory to 2030, and specialization trends, concluding no single technology will win outright though battery-electric will ultimately predominate on a well-to-wheel efficiency basis.
key_findings: NACFE concludes CBEVs and fuel-cell trucks will be capable of lower total cost of ownership than diesel by the 2030 timeframe, while other alternative fuels offer only near-term improvements over diesel.

The report coins/popularizes the 'messy middle' -- a transition period, likely decades long, during which multiple alternative-fuel powertrains will operate side by side, each optimized for specific duty cycles rather than one universal diesel replacement.

Vehicle specifications are expected to become increasingly optimized for each first user's specific duty cycle and technology choice, limiting equipment resale/second-life applicability compared to today's more interchangeable diesel tractors.
data_available: Alternative Fuel Powertrain Parity exhibits for 2020 and 2030
Fleet operational experience / vehicle-count tables by alt-fuel type (fuel cell, CBEV, CNG, LNG, propane, hybrid)
Bridge Technologies to Future roadmap diagram

title: Run on Less
abstract: NACFE Run on Less demonstration report published February 2018, documenting a first-of-its-kind three-week, cross-country fuel-efficiency roadshow conducted in September 2017. Seven experienced Class 8 long-haul fleets -- Albert Transport, Frito-Lay, Hirschbach, Mesilla Valley Transportation, Nussbaum Transportation, Ploger Transportation, and US Xpress -- hauled real freight on real routes while Geotab telematics tracked MPG, weight, speed, wind, and elevation, establishing the diesel-baseline methodology reused in later Run on Less events.
key_findings: The seven trucks averaged 10.1 MPG over 50,107 miles and 17 days (99 truck-days), compared to a 6.4 MPG national average for over-the-road tractor-trailers.

A multiple regression model found each 10 mph above optimal speed cost about 1 MPG (15 mph over cost about 2 MPG), with additional effects from a 10 degree F temperature shift, 10,000 lb weight change, and 250 ft elevation gain each worth roughly 0.5 MPG.

NACFE distilled the results into 10 recommended fleet actions, including buying all available tractor and trailer aerodynamics, downsped powertrains with AMTs, low rolling resistance tires, and driver education/incentives.
data_available: Daily MPG distribution and per-truck/day results tables
Regression model of MPG impact by condition (wind, temperature, weight, elevation)
Tractor/trailer specification summary by fleet

title: Electric Trucks Have Arrived: Documenting A Real-World Electric Trucking Demonstration
abstract: NACFE Run on Less – Electric report published January 2022, documenting a three-week (September 2021) real-world demonstration of production battery-electric commercial vehicles across 13 fleets in four segments: vans/step vans, medium-duty box trucks, terminal tractors, and heavy-duty regional haul tractors. Participating fleets included DHL, Purolator, Frito-Lay, Day & Ross, NFI, Ruan, Ryder, Anheuser-Busch, Biagi Brothers, and Penske. Geotab telematics captured range, charging, state-of-charge, and consumption data; hard total-cost-of-ownership figures were not yet obtainable from most participants.
key_findings: 13 fleets ran production BEVs in four market segments -- vans/step vans, medium-duty box trucks, terminal tractors, and heavy-duty regional haul tractors -- representing more than 5 million Class 3-8 freight vehicles' worth of addressable market.

Early adopters reported validating an acceptable total cost of ownership in urban medium-duty vans/trucks, terminal tractors, and short regional haul, but NACFE could not obtain hard TCO numbers because many fleets had not operated the vehicles long enough or would not disclose figures.

Longer-haul heavy-duty semi-truck BEV adoption remained largely limited to California as of the 2021 demonstration, with range and charging infrastructure identified as the primary operational challenges.
data_available: Per-fleet vehicle spec tables (battery capacity, estimated range, production status)
Daily telematics dashboards (miles, state of charge, charging rate, energy use)
18-episode Stories from the Road video/topic index

title: Run on Less – Electric DEPOT: Scaling BEVs in the Real World
abstract: NACFE Run on Less – Electric DEPOT report published July 2024, following up the 2021 Run on Less – Electric demonstration with a September 2023 run and March 2024 data workshop analyzing 10 depot-charging BEV fleets: Frito-Lay, OK Produce, Penske, PepsiCo, Performance Team, Purolator, Schneider, UPS, US Foods, and WattEV. Focuses on scaling battery-electric vans, box trucks, and Class 8 tractors at depots, covering telematics/geospatial data, charging infrastructure buildout, state-of-charge patterns, and the National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy.
key_findings: Vehicles in the Run averaged a 60% state of charge, indicating most BEVs return to base with substantial charge remaining rather than near-empty, undercutting common 'worst-case' charging-demand assumptions.

NACFE evaluated 121 candidate fleets with at least 15 BEVs on-site or on order (summer 2022-spring 2023) before narrowing to the 10 fleets with charging infrastructure and trucks in commercial operation by September 2023.

Findings emphasize that small depots are ready for electrification now, but heavy-duty tractor OEMs still need cost and weight reductions, and depot/corridor charging infrastructure buildout is proceeding too slowly.
data_available: Per-fleet/truck telematics tables (state-of-charge box plots, energy consumption kWh/mi)
Directory of commercial electric vehicle depot case examples (Forum Mobility, WattEV, TeraWatt, and more)
US National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy phase maps

title: Run on Less Regional
abstract: NACFE Run on Less Regional report published mid-2020, documenting an 18-day, October 2019 cross-country demonstration benchmarking fuel and freight efficiency of current-production diesel and CNG Class 8 tractors in regional-haul operations (within a 300-mile radius of home base). Ten fleets participated -- C&S Wholesale Grocers, Hirschbach, Hogan Transportation, J.B. Hunt, Meijer, PepsiCo, Ploger Transportation, Schneider, Southeastern Freight Lines, and UPS -- instrumented with Geotab telematics and NREL data loggers, following NACFE's 2017 long-haul Run on Less.
key_findings: The 10 trucks traveled more than 58,000 miles over 18 days achieving a cumulative 8.3 MPG (the nine diesels averaged 8.7 MPG), a 38% improvement over NACFE's estimated 6.0 MPG national average for regional haul.
NACFE estimated that if all regional-haul fleets matched this efficiency, the industry would save more than $9 billion in fuel and 30.6 million tons of CO2 annually.
The report identifies seven regional-haul duty cycles (shuttle, dedicated, dedicated fast turn, hub and spoke, city, diminishing load, milk run), refining NACFE's earlier three-category framework.
data_available: Regional haul duty cycle definitions and per-fleet mapping table
Regression model of MPG predictors (weight, speed, stops, terrain, wind)
Daily results dashboard (miles, gallons/dollars saved, deliveries, payload) by fleet

title: A Utility Company Primer on Commercial Truck Electrification
abstract: Short NACFE primer for utility companies, published 2022, explaining the basics of commercial truck electrification: how heavy-duty trucks differ from passenger EVs, how to identify and engage local fleets, and pointers to NACFE's guidance reports (Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense, Medium-Duty Electric Trucks Cost of Ownership, Charging Infrastructure, Viable Class 7/8 Alternative Fuel Tractors, Making Sense of Hydrogen Fuel Cell Tractors) and the Run on Less demonstration series. Intended to open dialogue between utilities and fleets on charging infrastructure planning.
key_findings: There are more than 990,000 for-hire truck fleets in North America and more than 3,000 utilities; the primer recommends state trucking associations plus CCJ's Top 250 and Transport Topics' Top 100 Fleets lists as ways for utilities to identify fleets in their service area.

NACFE had by this point published five guidance reports specifically to help fleets and utilities understand freight electrification, plus the 13-truck, September 2021 Run on Less – Electric demonstration and an associated 10-session Electric Truck Bootcamp.
Electrification was not yet listed among fleets' top industry challenges in ATRI's annual survey, though NACFE had already identified it as a primary emerging concern for future trucks.
data_available: List of NACFE guidance-report titles and topics
Directory-style list of industry partners (NRECA, EPRI, EEI, APPA, SEPA)

title: Confidence Report on Tractor Aerodynamic Devices
abstract: This NACFE Confidence Report, published September 9, 2020, evaluates aerodynamic devices for Class 8 day cab and sleeper tractors pulling 53-foot van trailers. It covers OEM base-model aerodynamics, chassis fairings, wheel covers, vented mud flaps, cab and roof extenders, mirrors and camera systems, and deployable tractor-trailer gap reducers, drawing on wind-tunnel testing, CFD analysis, and NACFE fleet field data. The report rates NACFE confidence and expected payback for adopting aerodynamic tractor packages — full aero sleeper, aero day cab, partial aero sleeper, non-aero day cab, and classic sleeper — via its standard confidence-matrix methodology.
key_findings: Chassis fairings/skirts deliver 2% to 4% fuel economy improvement for aerodynamic tractors pulling 53' van trailers
Cab and roof extenders that close the tractor-trailer gap improve fuel economy by about 1% to 2%; aftermarket deployable gap-closing devices (e.g., XStream TruckWings) claim 4% to 6% fuel savings
Integrated aerodynamic mirror design reduces drag by 2% to 3% (a 2007 TMA/DOE study estimated eliminating mirrors entirely would yield a 6% improvement)
data_available: Confidence matrix (information available vs. payback years) rating Full Aero Sleeper, Aero Day Cab, Partial Aero Sleeper, Non-Aero Day Cab, and Classic Sleeper
EPA/NHTSA GHG Phase II aerodynamic bin tables (CdA by tractor type)
Fuel savings/adoption trend charts from NACFE's Annual Fleet Fuel Study, 2003-2018

title: Confidence Report on Idle-Reduction Technologies
abstract: This NACFE Confidence Report, published July 30, 2019 as an update to the 2014 edition, assesses technologies that reduce sleeper-cab idling for Class 8 tractors, including fuel-operated heaters, diesel and battery-powered auxiliary power units, automatic engine start/stop systems, electronic idle parameters, driver training and incentives, and truck-stop electrification. Drawing on fleet interviews and a NACFE fleet survey, it evaluates each technology's fuel-savings potential, cost, and adoption barriers, and rates NACFE's confidence in the expected payback period for each via its standard confidence-matrix methodology.
key_findings: A fleet investing in idle-reduction technology can save about 1,800 gallons of fuel per truck per year, and sleeper-tractor idling burns over a billion gallons of diesel annually nationwide (~8% of total fuel burned)
A 10% reduction in annualized idle percentage (e.g., 30% to 20%) is worth about 1% in fuel economy, roughly $500-$700/year per truck at $3.00/gallon fuel
Confidence-matrix payback estimates range from about 1.1 years (fuel-operated air heaters, electronic engine idle parameters) to about 3.2 years (diesel APUs)
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. information available) for 10 idle-reduction technologies
NACFE fleet survey results on idle-technology usage, preferred solutions, annual idle percentage, and ROI
Matrix mapping energy sources (diesel, battery, shore power, off-board HVAC) to the idling benefits each addresses

title: NACFE Confidence Report on Lightweighting
abstract: This NACFE Confidence Report, published February 15, 2021 as an update to the 2015 edition, examines weight-reduction options for Class 8 tractors and trailers, segmenting the market into three fleet categories based on how often they reach the 80,000-lb. gross weight limit. It details component-level weight savings — wheels, frame and chassis, cab, axles, tires, and trailer flooring/structure — along with their relative costs, and includes early findings on battery-electric truck weight. NACFE rates its confidence in the lightweighting investment case, and the expected payback, separately for each fleet category via its confidence-matrix methodology.
key_findings: Converting steel duals to wide-base tires and aluminum wheels can save nearly 1,300 lbs. per tractor-trailer combination

Category 1 bulk-hauler fleets (about 2% of the industry, grossing out on nearly 100% of routes) already show high confidence with a 1-2 year lightweighting payback; Category 2 and 3 fleets show medium confidence with 2-3 year paybacks
About 50% of the market already uses aluminum wheels, and both steel and aluminum wheel weights have each dropped 7 lbs./wheel in recent years (steel from 72 to 65 lbs., aluminum from 45 to 38 lbs.)
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. information available) broken out by fleet weight-sensitivity category
Weight Reduction Options tables for tractors (Figures 19a/19b) and trailers (Figure 24) listing lbs. saved per component
Lightweighting price-category breakdown (No Cost/Some Cost/More Cost) for tractors and trailers

title: Confidence Report on Low Rolling Resistance Tires
abstract: This NACFE Confidence Report, published October 15, 2020 as an update to the 2015 edition, evaluates low rolling resistance (LRR) dual and wide-base tires for Class 8 tractor-trailers. It compares non-LRR duals, LRR duals, and LRR wide-base tires on fuel economy, tread life, traction, and total cost of ownership, drawing on interviews with 11 large fleets and 5 tire manufacturers plus a broader fleet survey. The report concludes with a high-confidence, short-payback rating and provides decision tools, including a total-cost-of-ownership calculator, to help fleets choose tires for their duty cycles.
key_findings: Tire rolling resistance accounts for roughly 30-33% of total truck fuel consumption for an aerodynamic long-haul tractor at highway speed, up from about 15-20% before aerodynamic trucks became common

SmartWay-verified LRR tires must cut fuel consumption at least 3% versus best-selling non-LRR tires; wide-base tires originally offered 3-5% fuel economy gains, now reduced to 1-2% as dual-tire rolling resistance has improved
NACFE rates LRR tires (both duals and wide-base) as high confidence with a good case for adoption; wide-base tires also save about 800 lbs. per truck/trailer versus duals
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. information available) for LRR duals and wide-base tires
LRR/wide-base tire adoption-rate trend charts, 2003-2018 (NACFE Annual Fleet Fuel Study)
Total cost of ownership calculator example outputs and SmartWay CRR target/GHG Phase 2 rolling-resistance tables

title: Confidence Report: Tire Pressure Systems
abstract: This NACFE Confidence Report, published May 15, 2020 as an update to the original 2013 edition, surveys tire pressure monitoring systems, dual tire pressure equalizers, automatic tire inflation systems, central tire inflation systems, and passive pressure containment approaches for Class 8 tractor-trailers. It describes each system type, fleet adoption trends, and deployment best practices based on supplier and fleet interviews, and rates NACFE's confidence in the technology's investment case and expected payback via its standard confidence-matrix methodology.
key_findings: Tires underinflated by 10 psi cause about 5-12% degradation in tire wear and a 0.5-1.0% increase in fuel consumption; historical payback for tire pressure systems ranges from under 1 year to about 3 years, with annual savings of $750 to over $1,000 per vehicle

About one in five tractors and one in five trailers operates with at least one tire underinflated by 20+ psi; only 46% of tractor tires and 38% of trailer tires were within +/-5 psi of target pressure (FMCSA 2003 study)

Approximately 70% of new trailers are equipped with automatic tire inflation systems (ATIS), making it the most-specified tire pressure option on trailers; NACFE rates confidence in tire pressure systems as high
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. information available) for TPMS, ATIS, and related technologies
Tire pressure system adoption-rate trend chart, 2003-2018 (NACFE Annual Fleet Fuel Study)
Classification chart of five tire pressure system technology categories and sub-types; federal legislation summary table

title: Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report: Downspeeding
abstract: This Trucking Efficiency (NACFE) Confidence Report, published October 28, 2015 as the eighth in the series, evaluates downspeeding -- pairing a faster (numerically lower) rear-axle ratio with an overdrive transmission to reduce engine RPM at highway cruise -- for Class 8 tractors. It quantifies the fuel-efficiency gain from lower cruise RPM against the resulting increase in driveline torque, covers driver-comfort and drivetrain-durability tradeoffs, and rates the technology via NACFE's standard confidence-matrix methodology (information available vs. expected payback in years).
key_findings: Fuel efficiency improves about 1% for every 100 rpm decrease in engine RPM at cruise; downspeeding increases driveline torque by about 29% comparing a 1,450 rpm cruise engine to a 1,125 rpm downspeed engine

In 2014, diesel fuel cost the industry $0.58 per mile, as much per year as drivers' wages and benefits combined -- a key motivator cited for pursuing downspeeding and other fuel-efficiency technologies

NACFE's confidence matrix rates downspeeding as spanning medium-to-high confidence with an estimated 1.5 to 2.5 year payback; common rear-axle ratios shifted from the 3.21:1-3.9:1 range as of 2011 to the faster 2.47:1-2.64:1 range becoming common by 2015
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. information available) for downspeeding
Meritor tandem axle ratio sales-mix chart (current vs. 2011)
Fuel-economy-vs-RPM-reduction and driveline-torque-vs-axle-ratio charts (source: Dana)

title: Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report: Programmable Engine Parameters
abstract: This Trucking Efficiency (NACFE) Confidence Report evaluates programmable electronic engine parameters — vehicle speed limits, engine speed/torque limits, idle-reduction settings, driver rewards, and miscellaneous MPG features — across Class 8 tractors. Findings draw on interviews with nine NACFE-affiliated large fleets, dealership sales staff, and engine OEMs, plus a 45-fleet Michelin Fleet Forum survey on parameter usage and optimization challenges. The report assesses fuel-economy impact and adoption barriers, and rates programmable parameters as a high-confidence, roughly one-year-payback technology via NACFE's standard confidence-matrix methodology.
key_findings: A fleet using only OEM default engine parameter settings could gain about 5-8% fuel efficiency by fully optimizing parameters, or 3-5% by optimizing just a few key areas like vehicle speed limiting and idle reduction
NACFE's confidence matrix places programmable parameters in the high-confidence, roughly 1-year-payback 'great case for adoption, no testing required' cell
More than half of surveyed Michelin Fleet Forum fleets reported never receiving help from dealerships or OEMs in optimizing their engine parameters
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. information available) for programmable engine parameters
Parameter usage-rate bar chart by fleet type (NACFE-interviewed fleets vs. large vs. small Fleet Forum fleets, Figure 18)
Appendix B: OEM-by-OEM parameter name comparison table (Cummins, Detroit, Mack, Navistar, PACCAR, Volvo) and ordering/service tools contact table

title: Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report: Electronically Controlled Transmissions
abstract: This NACFE/Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report, published December 2014, evaluates automated manual transmissions (AMTs) and fully automatic transmissions for Class 8 tractors. Based on interviews with five transmission manufacturers, five truck OEMs, and 19 fleets running over 12,500 automated transmissions, it assesses fuel-economy gains, cost, resale value, and maintenance implications. The report rates AMTs on NACFE's confidence matrix, which plots payback period against data confidence, and finds fleets should have higher confidence in AMTs' faster payback relative to fully automatic transmissions.
key_findings: AMTs deliver an estimated 1% to 3% fuel-economy improvement over manual transmissions, with reduced driver-to-driver MPG variability.
NACFE's confidence matrix rates AMTs at roughly 1.8 years payback with high confidence, versus about 3.2 years payback with lower confidence for fully automatic transmissions.
AMTs carry an upfront cost premium of $3,000-$5,000 over manual transmissions, with $1,000-$1,500 lower near-term resale value.
data_available: Confidence matrix (payback years vs. data confidence) for AMTs and automatics
Manufacturer/OEM engine-transmission offering comparison table
Route-simulation fuel economy data (Cummins downspeeding test)

title: Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report: Low-Viscosity Engine Lubricants
abstract: This NACFE/Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report, published June 28, 2016 as the thirteenth in the series, evaluates low-viscosity engine oil for Class 8 over-the-road trucks. Drawing on desk research and structured interviews with fleets, OEMs, and oil manufacturers, it assesses fuel-economy gains, cost, and compatibility tied to the shift from 15W-40 oil to 5W/10W-30 and the incoming CK-4/FA-4 categories launching December 2016. NACFE rates the switch a high-confidence, fast-payback move requiring no upfront investment or operational changes.
key_findings: Switching from 15W-40 to 5W/10W-30 (CJ-4 or CK-4) oil yields an estimated 0.5%-1.5% fuel-economy gain; moving further to FA-4 adds another 0.4%-0.7%.
As of 2016, only about 20% of the trucking industry overall had adopted low-viscosity engine oil, versus roughly 40% among the most efficiency-conscious fleets.
NACFE's confidence matrix rates 5/10W-30 CJ-4/CK-4 oil at high confidence with a 1-2 year payback, while newer FA-4 oil is rated low confidence with about a 2-year payback.
data_available: Confidence matrix for lower-viscosity oils
Fuel-savings-by-source bar chart (oil suppliers/engine makers/fleets)
SAE J300 viscosity grade specification table

title: Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report: Maintenance
abstract: This NACFE/Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report, published December 15, 2015 as the ninth in the series, examines how preventive and predictive maintenance practices affect Class 8 fuel economy. Based on interviews with 12 fleets and component/OEM suppliers, it identifies ten vehicle systems (engine oil, intake/exhaust, cooling, air compressors, alignment, tires, fuel filters, aerodynamics, electrical, and A/C) whose maintenance most affects fuel consumption. Rather than a single technology adoption decision, the report rates maintenance strategies for confidence and payback, urging fleets toward telematics-enabled predictive maintenance.
key_findings: Poor maintenance across the ten reviewed vehicle systems can collectively account for 30% to 50% of a truck's potential fuel-consumption loss.
Fleets reported 5% to 10% fuel-economy improvement after implementing rigorous preventive-maintenance practices.
Cummins-supplied data showed wheel misalignment causing 0.6% to 2.2% fuel-economy loss, while fleets that corrected alignment reported 3% to 11% fuel savings.
data_available: Confidence matrix by maintenance strategy (testing, predictive, preventive)
Wheel alignment vs. MPG effect test table
TMC Recommended Practices reference list (Appendix A)

title: Confidence Report on Solar for Trucks and Trailers
abstract: This NACFE Confidence Report, published June 28, 2018 as the sixteenth in the series, evaluates flexible solar panels for Class 8 tractors and trailers. Based on interviews with 13 fleets and eight solar manufacturers plus 2018 truck-show research, it examines applications supporting battery HVAC, hotel loads, liftgates, telematics, and refrigeration units. Because direct fuel savings from solar are minor, the report's confidence matrix centers on payback for each electrical-load use case, recommending solar mainly to extend battery life and avoid roadside-assistance calls rather than for fuel savings.
key_findings: NACFE's confidence matrix rates solar for telematics support at roughly 1-year payback with high confidence, versus about 2.5 years for battery HVAC support and 3.2 years for hotel-load support without HVAC, both medium confidence.
Fuel savings are described as a very small part of the overall benefit; the primary value comes from extended battery life and avoided emergency roadside-assistance calls for dead batteries.
A 300-watt fairing-mounted panel was estimated to produce about 452 kWh/year in Phoenix, AZ versus about 300 kWh/year in Albany, NY, per NREL's PVWatts calculator.
data_available: Confidence matrix by solar application (telematics/liftgate/reefer/HVAC/hotel load)
PVWatts case study output tables (Phoenix vs. Albany)
Solar PV price/installed-capacity trend chart (2009-2017)

title: Confidence Report: Two-Truck Platooning
abstract: This NACFE/Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report, published September 28, 2016, is NACFE's first Confidence Report on an emerging, not-yet-mature technology: two-truck platooning using vehicle-to-vehicle-connected adaptive cruise control. It surveys nine published fuel-savings studies (track and public-road) alongside real-world traffic-interruption data, and addresses driver acceptance, safety, and payback challenges. NACFE finds fleet confidence in the concept's fuel-saving potential high, but confidence that it works reliably in real-world traffic and terrain still low.
key_findings: Controlled test-track studies show roughly 4% fuel savings for the lead truck and 10% for the following truck at 40-50 ft separation and about 60 mph (a 7% two-truck average).
Accounting for real-world traffic interference and estimating platoons operate together only about 75% of the time, NACFE estimates realistic average savings fall to around 4% between the two trucks.

A field study of 169 drivers over 3 million miles found average highway following distances of 2.4-2.8 seconds (194-308 ft at 55-75 mph), well beyond the close-following gaps tested for maximum fuel savings.
data_available: Summary table of 9 published platooning fuel-savings studies (Browand, NREL/Lammert, Daimler, SARTRE, KONVOI, Japan ITS, etc.)
Fuel savings vs. separation-distance scatter plots (lead and follower trucks)
SAE/FHWA levels-of-automation tables

title: Confidence Report: Variable Engine-Driven Accessories
abstract: This NACFE/Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report, published February 26, 2017, evaluates variable-speed and clutched engine-driven accessories -- alternators, water pumps, cooling fans, air compressors, air dryers, and power steering pumps -- for Class 8 tractors. Informed by interviews with all four DOE SuperTruck I teams and component/OEM suppliers, it finds these parasitic-load accessories consume only 3%-5% of a line-haul truck's total fuel, so individual technology gains are modest and paybacks are lengthened by concurrent trends like downspeeding and improved aerodynamics.
key_findings: Engine-driven accessories collectively consume an estimated 3%-5% of total fuel in typical line-haul operation, led by the water pump at 1.1%-1.8%.
Estimated paybacks at $2.50/gallon fuel: 2-speed/modulating cooling fan 1-2 years, smart air dryer 2-2.5 years, variable-speed water pump about 2.5 years, and clutched air compressor about 3 years.

Electrically driving accessories instead of mechanical drive requires roughly 50%+ efficiency gains to break even, since alternator-to-motor conversion is far less efficient than direct mechanical drive (about 95%+).
data_available: SuperTruck team accessory technology comparison table (Cummins/Peterbilt, Freightliner, Volvo, Navistar)
OEM accessory-technology availability matrix by truck builder
Accessory fuel-consumption-by-component range table

title: Fleet Fuel Study
abstract: NACFE's flagship Fleet Fuel Study (FFS), published December 17, 2024, benchmarks Class 8 fuel economy and technology adoption among data-driven North American fleets. Now biennial, this edition draws on 14 named fleets (CR England, Frito-Lay, Hirschbach, Mesilla Valley Transportation, Nussbaum, Paper Transport, PepsiCo, Pilot Flying J, Pitt Ohio, Ryder, Schneider, UPS, Werner, Wilson Logistics) reporting 2022-2023 purchasing and MPG data, and tracks adoption of 86 fuel-efficiency technologies. It finds fleet-wide average MPG rose to 7.77 in 2023 with technology adoption reaching 42%, its highest level ever.
key_findings: Study fleets' average fuel economy rose to 7.62 MPG in 2022 and 7.77 MPG in 2023, versus the FHWA national average of 6.91 MPG in 2022.
Average adoption of the 86 tracked fuel-efficiency technologies reached 42% in 2023, the highest level in the study's history.
Predictive cruise control adoption reached 96.7% (up 42%) and automatic transmission adoption rose 490% to 18.8% between the 2020/2021 and 2022/2023 survey periods.
data_available: 86 individual technology adoption S-curves, 2003-2023 (Appendix A)
Fleet-wide MPG vs. adoption-rate trend charts
Interactive online benchmarking tool screenshots
ATRI/FHWA/EPA SmartWay MPG comparison tables

title: Run on Less – Messy Middle Bootcamp Finale Workshop
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle Bootcamp finale workshop, held August 2025, closing out a five-month, nine-session educational series (February-July 2025) ahead of the September 2025 Run. Moderated by Rachel with NACFE's Mike Roeth, Rick Mihelick, and Kim, plus guest Josh Fisher (Fleet Owner Magazine editor-in-chief), the session recaps top bootcamp takeaways spanning diesel drop-ins, natural gas, battery-electric, and hydrogen, then walks through NACFE site-visit updates with fleet-specific operating data from 11 of the 13 confirmed Run on Less fleets ahead of fleet-profile publication throughout August.
key_findings: As of mid-July 2025, NACFE had visited 11 of the 13 Run on Less fleet sites and conducted 94 interviews for the fleet profiles set to publish three times a week throughout August.

Wegmans reported its 194-truck fleet (150 CNG) was 76% diesel-free with a goal of 100% diesel-free by end of 2026; Frito-Lay's Topeka site, PepsiCo's highest diesel-fuel-use location, had only 10 of 112 trucks still running petroleum diesel.

The bootcamp series drew about 800 registrants per session on average from 35 speakers across nine sponsors; CALSTART data cited in the session showed over 54,000 alternative-fuel Class 2b-8 vehicles deployed across all 50 US states.
data_available: Bootcamp series stats slide (speakers, registrants, resources, quiz participation)
Fleet site-visit recap for Run on Less fleets (Wegmans, Pilot/Hyundai, Saia/Tesla, 4Gen, Nevoya, UPS, Schneider, Henry Albert, Joyride/Windrose, Penske/Hyundai, Frito-Lay, Kleysen)
Top-10 bootcamp-moments recap discussion

title: Run on Less 2017 Panel - TMC 2018
abstract: Panel discussion at TMC 2018 (March) presenting results of NACFE's original Run on Less demonstration, conducted with seven fleets (U.S. Express, Hirschbach, Ploger, Mesilla Valley, Albert Transportation, Frito-Lay, and Nussbaum) over 17 days in September 2017. NACFE staff summarize the run's methodology and headline 10.1 mpg fleet average, then Nussbaum's Tony Morthland, former U.S. Express maintenance/purchasing lead Gerry Mead, and CR England's Ron Hall discuss driver incentive programs, methodical technology adoption such as aerodynamics and downspeeding, and lessons from bringing real trucks and drivers to a public efficiency benchmark.
key_findings: The 2017 Run on Less tracked seven trucks from seven fleets over 17 days in September, covering 50,107 miles across 99 driving days at a fleet average of 10.1 mpg.

Nussbaum reported its full 350-truck fleet averaged 9.7 mpg for July-September, crediting driver training plus a technology progression starting with 6x2 axles and wide-base tires (2010), then aerodynamic skirts and tails (2011).
CR England's Ron Hall described a dedicated fuel-testing program using two trucks and two 80,000-lb mock-load trailers to validate technology payback over roughly 400-mile test runs before adoption.
data_available: Run on Less 2017 summary stats (miles, driving days, average MPG, load weight, speed, wind conditions)
MPG distribution chart across the 99 driving days

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #9 – The Opportunities and Challenges of Selling Hydrogen
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 9, held July 1, 2025, the third and final session of the hydrogen unit. Moderated by Rachel Ellenberger, panelists Tarek Abdel-Baset (Forvia), Hui Xu (Cummins), Ben Happek (Hyundai Motor America), and Derek Rotz (Daimler Truck North America) cover hydrogen storage technologies (compressed, liquid, cryo-compressed), Cummins' hydrogen internal-combustion engine platform, Hyundai's XCIENT fuel cell truck and its North American deployments ahead of Run on Less, and Daimler's SuperTruck III zero-emission long-haul research program.
key_findings: Hyundai reported 49 XCIENT fuel-cell trucks deployed in Europe since 2020 accumulating more than 8.3 million miles, plus 21 trucks in its own Savannah, Georgia logistics operation and 30 trucks planned for the NorCal Zero project at the Port of Oakland.
The Hyundai XCIENT Fuel Cell 6x4 tractor carries 68.6 kg of usable hydrogen at 700 bar for about 450 miles of range (customers have seen up to 510 miles) with a 20-30 minute refuel.

Daimler's SuperTruck III program is targeting a 600-mile-range, 100-kg-liquid-hydrogen Class 8 long-haul demonstrator with a diesel-comparable 223-inch wheelbase, with a first gaseous-hydrogen prototype in 2025 and a final subcooled-liquid-hydrogen demonstrator in 2027.
data_available: Hydrogen storage comparison slides (compressed gas, liquid, cryo-compressed: energy density, boil-off, pressure)
Cummins X15H/B6.7H hydrogen ICE engine spec table (power, torque, emissions level)
Hyundai XCIENT Fuel Cell tractor spec sheet (range, fuel cell power, battery, motor)
Daimler SuperTruck III B-sample vs. final-demonstrator spec comparison

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #8 – The Distribution & Storage of Hydrogen Fuel
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 8, held June 17, 2025, the second of three hydrogen-unit sessions. Moderated by Rachel Ellenberger, panelists Des Carlisle (Southeast Hydrogen Energy Alliance), Paul Sandsted (Transport Project), Charles Sanders (Air Liquide), and Eugene Reyes (Shell) explain how hydrogen is stored (geologic, compressed, liquefied, material) and distributed (pipeline, tube trailer, cryogenic tanker), compare gaseous versus liquid hydrogen economics and infrastructure needs, and describe Air Liquide's and Shell's West Coast heavy-duty hydrogen refueling station buildouts.
key_findings: Charles Sanders (Air Liquide) said that, per their analysis, moving hydrogen under about 200 miles is typically cheaper as compressed gas, while liquid hydrogen is more economical over longer distances because a single liquid trailer can carry 3.6 tons versus needing far more gaseous tube trailers for the same energy.
Air Liquide's North Las Vegas liquefier, running since 2022, produces 30,000 kg (30 metric tons) of liquid hydrogen per day supplying stations across Northern and Southern California.

Shell's three heavy-duty hydrogen stations (Ontario and two in Long Beach, first opened 2020) each have 1 ton/day capacity with 10-30 minute refuels; SHEA said its 10-state Southeast region has 21 Class 8 Hyundai trucks running in Savannah, with a goal of over 100 by year-end.
data_available: Compressed vs. liquid hydrogen storage/transport comparison tables (cost, energy density, carbon intensity)
Typical compressed and liquefied hydrogen distribution system diagrams
Air Liquide North Las Vegas liquefier and West Coast station network overview

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #7 – The Production Processes of Hydrogen Fuel
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 7, held June 3, 2025, opening the hydrogen unit. Moderated by Rachel Ellenberger, NACFE's Rick Mihelick explains hydrogen production pathways, carbon-intensity accounting, and hub/corridor initiatives; Omar Chaudhary of Accelera by Cummins covers electrolyzer technology and applications; and Connor Dolan of the Fuel Cell and Hydrogen Energy Association details current US hydrogen production scale, blue-versus-green hydrogen economics, and the ongoing congressional fight over the Section 45V clean-hydrogen production tax credit.
key_findings: FCHEA reported the current US hydrogen industry consumes about 11.4 million metric tons per year (~$17.6 billion total value), 77% from steam methane reforming and 23% as refinery byproduct, and projects hydrogen could reach 14% of US energy demand by 2050.

Under Section 45V, the clean-hydrogen production tax credit scales from $0.60/kg (4-2.5 kg CO2 per kg H2) up to $3.00/kg for near-zero-carbon hydrogen; FCHEA cited green hydrogen at $5-7/kg today versus about $1/kg for gray hydrogen and $1-2/kg for blue hydrogen with carbon capture.

There are 1,600 miles of dedicated hydrogen pipeline in the US today, mostly along the Gulf Coast, and Connor Dolan said existing natural gas pipelines can reportedly blend up to about 20-25% hydrogen without retrofits.
data_available: Hydrogen production-pathway ('color spectrum') diagram and US hydrogen-hub map
FCHEA US hydrogen industry base and 2030/2050 growth-potential chart
Section 45V tax-credit table (carbon-intensity tiers vs. credit value) and 45V legislative status timeline
Accelera electrolyzer product/project reference slide (HyLYZER 500/1000 installations)

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #6 – Charging Depots, Networks, & the Economics of Fleet Electrification
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 6, held May 6, 2025, the third session of the battery-electric unit. Moderated by Rachel Allenberger with an update from Mike Roeth, panelists Tom Perlin (C.H. Robinson), Allen Nielsen (Greenlane), Andy Manos (Prologis), and Emilia Sibley (Terawatt) cover charging depots, public charging hubs, and fleet-electrification economics: a 3PL's view of integrating EV freight, Greenlane's public charging-corridor buildout, Prologis's charging-as-a-service depot and hub case studies, and Terawatt's off-site charging network for range extension.
key_findings: Greenlane's first public charging hub, opened April 2025 in Colton, California, has 12 pull-through 400 kW lanes plus 29 bobtail 180 kW chargers; the company also won a $15 million DOE grant for a 10 MW hub there and $26 million for megawatt charging in Ontario, CA.

Prologis's 2.5 MW heavy-duty depot built for Performance Team/Maersk in Los Angeles -- its first charging-as-a-service project -- has grown into a five-depot network that has logged over 10 million electrified miles.

Andy Manos (Prologis) and Emilia Sibley (Terawatt) both estimated all-in charging costs of roughly 40-41 cents/kWh (infrastructure plus energy) at behind-the-fence depots and at public hubs in Southern California, suggesting the two models are cost-comparable once utilization is factored in.
data_available: Prologis case-study slides (heavy-duty depot, FedEx last-mile van depot, yard-tractor electrification) with kW capacity, miles, and CO2 saved
Greenlane Colton hub specs and DOE grant details
Terawatt site network map and a worked range-extension example (Volvo VNR route through the Rialto hub)

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #5 – Strategizing Successful HD BEV Adoption
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 5, held April 27, 2025, the second session of the battery-electric unit. Moderated by Rachel Ellenberger with an update from Mike Roeth, fleet panelists Chris Henry (Purolator), Alexa Branco (NFI), and Jeremy Hock (Schneider) describe their heavy-duty BEV deployment journeys, infrastructure builds, and lessons learned, while Dave Mullaney of infrastructure consultancy truCurrent outlines the strategic-planning questions -- feasibility, TCO, regulatory obligation, and other drivers -- fleets face when electrifying.
key_findings: Purolator has deployed over 250 medium-duty electric vehicles toward a 2030 goal of 60% electrified last-mile delivery, but only one heavy-duty EV to date, citing infrastructure cost/lead times and vehicle availability as the main heavy-duty barriers.

NFI has driven over 5.5 million zero-emission battery-electric daycab miles and operates 18 electric yard tractors (after an initial batch of 27 deployed in 2019); its JETSI-funded Ontario, California site pairs 1 MW of solar with 7.7 MWh of battery storage.

Schneider's 92-truck battery-electric drayage fleet in South El Monte, California (a $13.2 million JETSI grant project) has logged over 6 million zero-emission miles on a 4.8 MW, 16-charger depot that charges trucks to 80% in about 90 minutes.
data_available: Purolator terminal-tier fleet map and EV pilot test-plan objectives table
NFI Jetsi microgrid project timeline and deployment stats
Schneider El Monte site infrastructure specs and lessons-learned list (grid delays, permitting, charger obsolescence)

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #4 – The Current State of HD BEV: Technologies and Capabilities
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 4, held April 8, 2025, opening the battery-electric unit. Moderated by Rachel Ellenberger, with Mike Roeth announcing the 13 fleets confirmed for the September 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle demonstration. OEM panelists Jared Ruiz (Volvo Trucks), Dan Priestley (Tesla), and Wen Han (Windrose EV Trucks) cover current heavy-duty BEV technology, range, and operational lessons learned, while Trisha Dello Iacono of CALSTART covers zero-emission truck deployment data and the shifting federal and state policy landscape.
key_findings: Mike Roeth announced the 13 fleets and trucks confirmed for the September 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle: four diesel/renewable-diesel, three natural gas (Kleysen, UPS, Wegmans), four battery-electric (Windrose, Volvo, Tesla, and an eCascadia), and two hydrogen fuel cell tractors.

Volvo's Jared Ruiz cited Polk data showing US heavy-duty BEV sales grew from under 100 trucks industry-wide in 2020 to nearly 1,000 trucks among over 160 customers in 2024, still only about 1% of the regional-haul tractor market; Volvo estimates 15-20% of the regional-haul market is technically electrifiable today.
CALSTART's Trisha Dello Iacono reported more than 42,500 zero-emission trucks deployed on US roads as of June 2024 across 37 OEMs, per its January 2025 'Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks' update.
data_available: Volvo Polk-data heavy-duty BEV adoption trend chart and lessons-learned findings from the Volvo LIGHTS project
Tesla Semi efficiency/uptime stats and Nevada Gigafactory ramp details
Windrose global testing map (chargers tested, extreme-condition trips) and truck spec sheet
CALSTART ZET deployment-by-state map and federal policy (45V/ACT/ACF) timeline

title: Messy Middle Bootcamp #3 – Future Prices & Availability of Existing Infrastructure: What's Next
abstract: NACFE's Run on Less Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 3, held March 11, 2025, closing the diesel/natural-gas unit. Moderated by Rachel Ellenberger with an update from Mike Roeth on NACFE's newly published 'Messy Middle' white paper, ICCT's Nikita Pavlenko explains life-cycle GHG accounting for comparing fuels, Jerome McCarville (Chevron Renewable Energy Group) and Derek Turbide (Clean Energy) cover biodiesel/renewable-diesel and RNG production, pricing, and station infrastructure, and Ryan Bankerd of UPS describes UPS's multi-fuel 'rolling laboratory' fleet strategy and 2050 carbon-neutrality goals.
key_findings: ICCT's Nikita Pavlenko showed hydrogen loses substantial energy converting from grid electricity (roughly 60% by the time it is compressed and used), so a battery-electric truck on the same California grid electricity emits far less life-cycle CO2 per km than a gray-hydrogen fuel-cell truck, and a hydrogen-ICE truck on gray hydrogen can emit more than a diesel truck.

Chevron Renewable Energy Group reported about 420 million gallons of production capacity across nine biorefineries (2023 figures) and said its Geismar, Louisiana renewable diesel plant was expanding from 90 million to 340 million gallons/year, commissioning in Q1 2025; Clean Fuels data cited put US bio-based diesel consumption at a record 5 billion gallons in 2024.

UPS reported 19,000+ alternative-fuel and advanced-technology vehicles globally, a goal of 40% alternative fuel use in ground operations by 2025, and a target of 50% CO2-per-package reduction by 2035 versus a 2020 baseline.
data_available: ICCT life-cycle GHG comparison charts (soybean/UCO renewable diesel, hydrogen pathways, fuel-vehicle-cycle emissions per km)
Chevron REG production/terminal map and biodiesel-consumption growth chart, 2011-2025
