abstract: Profile of Purolator's Motiv-converted electric curbside delivery vehicles in Vancouver, part of the city's climate action plan. Covers driver feedback, Purolator's history with hybrid/electric pilots since 2005, Motiv's Ford F-53 step-van conversions, and plans to scale to 1,800 electric vehicles.
key_findings: Purolator plans to deploy 1,800 electric vehicles over the next 10 years, building on five fully electric curbside vehicles already running in Vancouver plus units in Toronto and Montreal.
Purolator deployed over 200 hybrid-electric vehicles back in 2005, an early step toward its current full-electric rollout.
data_available: Purolator 10-year EV deployment target (1,800 vehicles)
2005 hybrid-electric deployment count (200+)

title: Electric Profiles – Ryder
abstract: Profile of Ryder's Lonestar Specialty Vehicles electric terminal tractor jockeying trailers at a Kentucky automotive plant. Covers Dana's electrification system, vehicle specs (224 kWh battery, high torque/horsepower, CCS1/J1772 charging, 22+ hour runtime), camera-based visibility, and driver/customer feedback on uptime.
key_findings: The Lonestar/Dana electric terminal tractor uses 224 kWh of lithium-ion batteries and can run over 22 hours continuously before needing a charge.
The Dana electric drivetrain (Sumo MD motor) delivers 315 horsepower and over 2,000 lb-ft of torque, higher than the comparable diesel unit.
data_available: battery capacity (224 kWh) and runtime (22+ hrs)
motor output (315 hp, 2,000+ lb-ft torque)

title: Electric Profiles – Day & Ross
abstract: Profile of Day & Ross's two new Lion6 electric trucks in Montreal, Canada's first delivered units of their kind. Covers the fleet's electrification planning since 2018, route targeting under 200 km/day for return-to-base charging, fast DC charging infrastructure, and driver feedback.
key_findings: Day & Ross targeted delivery lanes under 200 kilometers a day suited to return-to-base charging for its Lion6 electric trucks, Canada's first delivered units of the model.
The trucks charge via two ChargePoint 62.5 kW DC chargers, reaching full charge in under a couple of hours.
data_available: route distance target (<200 km/day)
charger spec (ChargePoint 62.5 kW DC, <2 hr charge)

title: Electric Profiles – DHL
abstract: Profile of DHL's Lightning eMotors electric Ford Transit T350 vans delivering packages across Manhattan. Covers vehicle specs, the pilot's scale-up from an initial 9-vehicle order to dozens more for NYC and California, and driver/city-official feedback on the program's success.
key_findings: DHL's Lightning eMotors electric van has a 43 kWh battery with a dynamometer-tested range of 61 miles.
The initial 9-vehicle NYC pilot led to a follow-on order of 55 more vans for Manhattan and 30 for California.
data_available: van battery/range specs (43 kWh, 61 mi)
fleet scale-up order sizes (55 NYC + 30 CA)

title: Electric Profiles – NFI Terminal
abstract: Profile of NFI's Kalmar Ottawa electric terminal tractors shuttling trailers 24/7 across an eight-building Chino, California campus. Covers Kalmar's EV product history, opportunity charging during breaks, and driver/manager feedback on one of Kalmar's most demanding fleet duty cycles.
key_findings: Kalmar introduced its EV terminal tractor generation in 2018, began deliveries mid-2019, and has just over 100 units operating in the field.
NFI's Chino campus runs the tractors 24/7 across eight buildings, using opportunity charging during breaks/lunches with no reported low-battery or dead-battery issues.
data_available: Kalmar EV terminal tractor deployment count (100+ units) and timeline (2018 launch, 2019 first deliveries)

title: Electric Profiles – Penske
abstract: Profile of Penske's Freightliner eCascadia tractor running freight from Temecula to San Diego along I-15. Covers Penske's role providing development feedback ahead of the eCascadia's series-production launch, utility (Southern California Edison) collaboration, and driver feedback on daily delivery operations.
key_findings: Penske provided direct development feedback incorporated into the eCascadia's series-production design, targeted for end-of-2022 production in Portland, Oregon.
Penske's eCascadia driver delivers to 8-15 customers per shift on the Temecula-to-San Diego route before returning to a charging port.
data_available: eCascadia production timeline (end of 2022, Portland OR plant)

title: Electric Profiles – Frito-Lay
abstract: Profile of Frito-Lay's Cummins-powered electric box truck at its near-zero-emissions Modesto, California manufacturing plant. Covers high reported uptime, on-site solar and off-peak utility charging rates, driver feedback, and battery/regenerative-braking optimization tradeoffs with payload.
key_findings: Frito-Lay's electric box truck runs daily routes five days a week with reported uptime around 99%.
The Modesto facility has close to two megawatts of on-site solar and uses off-peak utility rates to charge the electric fleet.
data_available: truck uptime (~99%)
on-site solar capacity (~2 MW)

title: Electric Profiles – Anheuser-Busch
abstract: Profile of Anheuser-Busch's BYD Class 8 electric tractors at its Inland Empire, CA beverage distribution facility. Eight electric trucks run inloader routes delivering beer across the Los Angeles area; drivers and staff highlight quiet operation, curfew-store compatibility, and easy maintenance as part of the company's goal to cut CO2 25% by 2025.
key_findings: Anheuser-Busch runs 8 BYD Class 8 battery-electric tractors as inloader trucks out of its Inland Empire, CA facility, delivering beer across the LA area since April 2020.
Drivers cite quiet operation as beneficial for deliveries to noise-restricted 'curfew' stores and for improved situational awareness on the road.

title: Electric – Finale
abstract: Campaign wrap-up for Run on Less – Electric (Sept 2021), covering NACFE's electric truck bootcamp, 13 fleet profiles, and daily run metrics. An infographic shows U.S. transportation GHG emissions by segment and estimates that fully electrifying vans/step vans, box trucks, terminal tractors, and regional-haul tractors would avoid roughly 100 million MT CO2e annually.
key_findings: 13 fleet-manufacturer pairs (incl. DHL, Purolator, Ruan, Frito-Lay, Anheuser-Busch, Penske, Ryder) operated electric trucks across four market segments: vans/step vans, box trucks, terminal tractors, and regional-haul tractors.

NACFE/RMI estimate that if all 5.2 million US/Canada trucks in these four segments were electric, the industry would avoid over 100 million metric tons of CO2e annually and require about 168,582 GWh of electricity to charge them.
data_available: market segment population/carbon-avoided/electricity table
US transportation GHG emissions by source, 1990-2019

title: Run on Less 2017 – 10 for 10
abstract: Recap of NACFE's original 2017 Run on Less demonstration: seven Class 8 fleets driven by seven drivers over 17 days (99 driving-days), covering 50,107 total miles at an average 10.1 MPG. Concludes 10 MPG is achievable in the real world and outlines '10 actions for 10+ MPG' fleets can adopt.
key_findings: The 2017 Run on Less covered 50,107 total miles across 99 driving-days with 7 fleets, averaging 10.1 MPG.

NACFE's 10 actions for 10+ MPG include disciplined maintenance, right axle configuration, idle reduction, driver training, tractor/trailer aerodynamics, downsped powertrains/AMTs, and low rolling resistance tires.
data_available: average MPG (10.1)
total miles (50,107)
driving days (99)

title: Regional – Recap
abstract: Recap of NACFE's 2019 Run on Less Regional: 10 fleets driven over 18 days (135 driving-days) in regional-haul operations averaged 8.3 MPG versus a 6.0 MPG national average, saving 2,750 gallons of fuel. Also covers Technology Days on hydrogen and connectivity, and the Geotab/NREL/driver-portal data-collection methodology.
key_findings: 10 regional-haul fleets averaged 8.3 MPG over 135 driving-days versus a 6.0 MPG national average, saving 2,750 gallons of fuel during the 18-day run.
NACFE estimates that if North America's 800,000 regional-haul trucks matched this efficiency, the industry would save over $9 billion in fuel and 30.5 million tons of CO2 annually.
data_available: average MPG (8.3 vs. 6.0 national)
fuel saved (2,750 gal)
projected industry savings ($9B, 30.5M tons CO2)

title: Run on Less – Electric Finale – June 2022
abstract: A June 2022 follow-up recap of Run on Less – Electric (Sept 2021), covering NACFE's bootcamp and 13 fleet-site profile visits. Notes the 13 electric trucks operated across four market segments (vans/step vans, box trucks, terminal tractors, regional-haul tractors) representing about 5.2 million vehicles, roughly 60% of US/Canada commercial trucks. Includes driver testimonials.
key_findings: The 13 Run on Less – Electric trucks operated across four market segments -- vans/step vans, medium-duty box trucks, terminal tractors, and short-haul regional tractors -- representing roughly 5.2 million vehicles, about 60% of all US/Canada commercial trucks.
data_available: market segment scope (5.2M trucks, ~60% of commercial vehicles)

title: Electric DEPOT – Initial Findings
abstract: Initial findings from Run on Less – Electric DEPOT: 10 depots operating about 850 total trucks (291 battery-electric) across 11 OEMs, 8 charger companies, and 5 utilities. Key findings: small energy depots are ready now, large energy depots are gaining momentum, and energizing sites still takes too long.
key_findings: The 10 Electric DEPOT sites operated about 850 total trucks (291 battery electric), with an estimated combined power requirement of 214 MWh/day.
One heavy-duty truck completed 410 miles on a single charge and 1,076 miles in a 24-hour day hauling beverages; depots took 9 to 36 months to get energized.
data_available: fleet composition (850 trucks, 291 BEV)
power requirement (214 MWh/day)
single-charge/24-hr mileage record
energization timeline (9-36 months)

title: Electric DEPOT – Summary
abstract: Montage summary of Run on Less – Electric DEPOT featuring all 10 participating fleets (Frito-Lay, OK Produce, Penske, PepsiCo, Performance Team, Purolator, Schneider, UPS, US Foods, WattEV), the 10-episode bootcamp lineup, and a utility grid-upgrade-likelihood chart by charging load size.
key_findings: A utility grid-infrastructure chart shows the likelihood of needing feeder or substation upgrades rises sharply with charging load size: a 20 MW load has 52-63% likelihood of needing substation upgrades versus near-zero for a 1 MW load.

Highlighted site stats include OK Produce's 10 Freightliner eCascadias with 9 Heliox chargers, and Schneider's 16 chargers supporting dual-cord sequential charging for trucks running 80-100 miles per shift.
data_available: utility grid-upgrade likelihood by load size chart
bootcamp episode list
per-fleet equipment counts

title: Electric DEPOT – Action!
abstract: Short teaser/promotional clip for Run on Less – Electric DEPOT, consisting almost entirely of repeated campaign logo cards ending with a 'Coming soon...' announcement. Contains no substantive narration, data, or fleet-specific content beyond branding for the campaign.
key_findings: This clip is a brief promotional teaser announcing the Run on Less – Electric DEPOT campaign; it contains no substantive findings, data, or narration beyond repeated logo cards and a 'Coming soon' announcement.

title: Electric DEPOT – Final Findings
abstract: Final findings wrap-up for Run on Less – Electric DEPOT: a September 2023 3-week run monitoring 22 trucks over 18 days at 10 depots, with November 2023 initial findings, a White House visit, a 15-organization data workshop, and two published reports covering truck/charger improvements and slow site energization.
key_findings: The September 2023 run monitored 22 trucks over 18 days; NACFE released initial findings November 7, 2023, followed by a White House visit and a data workshop where 15 organizations shared analyses.

Final findings cite big improvements in trucks and chargers since 2021, that energizing sites still takes too long, and that manufacturers should prioritize cost and weight improvements; NACFE is planning a fifth Run on Less for 2025.
data_available: run scope (22 trucks, 18 days)
project timeline

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – Penske
abstract: Profile of Penske Truck Leasing's electric charging site in Ontario, CA, which grew from 6 to 12 charging stalls (about 1 MW) and added on-site battery storage yielding roughly 40% savings from managing heavy charging utilization. Uses Shell Sky software for charge/grid management; driver John Leroux praises the electric tractor's quiet, smooth operation.
key_findings: Penske's Ontario, CA charging site expanded from 6 to 12 charging stalls (about 1 MW) and added battery storage, yielding roughly 40% savings under heavy charging utilization.
data_available: charging stall count/power (12 stalls, ~1MW)
battery storage savings (~40%)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – PepsiCo
abstract: Profile of PepsiCo's Sacramento, CA solar-powered facility running 21 Tesla Semis (four 750kW chargers), electric yard tractors, and eTransit vans. Local delivery routes run under 100 miles over 12-hour shifts; three Tesla Semis handle 250-450 mile long-haul routes at under 1.7 kWh/mile efficiency. Utility SMUD built dedicated ~3MW service over a 3-year project.
key_findings: PepsiCo operates 21 Tesla Semis at its Sacramento facility, three dedicated to 250-450 mile long-haul routes, with fleet efficiency staying below 1.7 kWh/mile (1.1 kWh/km).
Utility SMUD built a dedicated ~3MW service over a 3-year project, enabling 0-80% charging in 45 minutes via four 750kW chargers; PepsiCo targets 75% emissions reduction by 2030 and 100% by 2040.

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – Performance Team
abstract: Profile of Performance Team Logistics' Volvo VNR Electric drayage fleet at a Prologis site in Commerce, CA -- 38 trucks operational (136 on order) at filming. Six-battery packs deliver 200-220 mile range without opportunity charging; regenerative braking is expected to sharply extend brake life versus diesel tractors that wore brakes every 2-3 years.
key_findings: Performance Team had 38 of 136 ordered Volvo VNR Electric trucks operational, with six-battery-pack units rated 200-220 miles of range requiring no daytime opportunity charging.

Regenerative braking is expected to greatly extend brake life versus diesel tractors, which the fleet says previously wore out brake pads every 2-3 years in this drayage duty cycle; the charging site draws about 1.5 MW across 180kW chargers.
data_available: fleet size (38 operational / 136 ordered)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – Purolator
abstract: Profile of Purolator's Richmond, BC terminal running 15 electric last-mile delivery vehicles (Motiv Epic stepvans and Ford E-Transits) with in-building Level 2 pull-down chargers shared across vehicle types. Motiv stepvans carry 127kWh batteries for about 105-mile range on 40-60 mile daily routes; Purolator targets electrifying over 60% of its last-mile fleet.
key_findings: Purolator operates 15 electric delivery vehicles (Motiv Epic stepvans, Ford E-Transits) at its Richmond, BC terminal, using shared Level 2 pull-down chargers (max 19.2kW, ~7hr full charge) for both vehicle types.

Motiv stepvans carry 127kWh batteries with ~105-mile range on routes of 40-60 miles/day; Purolator plans to electrify over 60% of its last-mile delivery fleet and expand to 55 vehicles at this site by year-end.
data_available: fleet size (15 EVs, expanding to 55)
battery/range specs (127kWh, ~105mi)
charger specs (19.2kW L2, ~7hr)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – Schneider
abstract: Profile of Schneider's South El Monte, CA intermodal facility, which deployed 92 battery-electric day-cab tractors by September 2023 for port/rail drayage within 80-100 miles of base. Sixteen 350kW dual-cord sequential chargers (Power Electronics/Daimler) can charge 32 trucks simultaneously; part of the JETSI program upgrading 50 trucks from diesel to electric.
key_findings: Schneider deployed 92 battery-electric day-cab tractors at its South El Monte intermodal facility by September 2023, running drayage routes within 80-100 miles of base.
Sixteen 350kW dual-cord sequential chargers allow 32 trucks to charge simultaneously; drivers are assigned to the next available charged truck rather than a dedicated vehicle.
data_available: fleet size (92 electric trucks)
route range (80-100mi)
charger specs (16x350kW, 32 simultaneous)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – UPS
abstract: Profile of UPS's Compton, CA depot running both electric package cars (Freightliner MT50E, ~170-mile full-charge range) for last-mile delivery and 10 eCascadia Class 8 tractors for middle-mile hauls. Permanent Class 8 charging faced permitting/easement delays, so UPS deployed a temporary 120kW charger while 15 DC fast chargers serve the package cars.
key_findings: UPS's Compton depot pairs electric MT50E package cars (~170-mile range) for last-mile delivery with 10 eCascadia Class 8 tractors for middle-mile routes.

Permanent charging infrastructure for the Class 8 tractors was delayed by permit/easement issues between two jurisdictions, so UPS used a temporary 120kW charger serving two eCascadias at once, alongside 15 DC fast chargers (~30kW) for the package cars.
data_available: fleet composition (package cars + 10 eCascadias)
package car range (~170mi)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – WattEV
abstract: Profile of WattEV's Port of Long Beach, CA site, which runs a 'truck-as-a-service' model providing Nikola electric trucks, charging, maintenance, and insurance for a fixed monthly fee. Phase one includes 13 dual-cord 360kW CCS chargers (26 trucks concurrently, ~5MW) plus a 1,200kW megawatt dispenser cutting charge time to 30-45 minutes.
key_findings: WattEV's truck-as-a-service model bundles the electric truck, charging, maintenance, and insurance for a fixed monthly price, targeting shippers/carriers unable to invest in their own EV infrastructure.

Phase one charging at the Long Beach site includes 13 dual-cord 360kW CCS chargers (26 trucks concurrently, ~5MW) and a 1,200kW megawatt dispenser reducing charge time from 2-3 hours to 30-45 minutes.
data_available: charger specs (13x360kW dual-cord, 1200kW megawatt dispenser)
power draw (~5MW)
charge time reduction (2-3hr to 30-45min)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – OK Produce
abstract: Profile of OK Produce, a family-owned Fresno, CA produce distributor completing phase one of its electrification plan: 10 Freightliner eCascadias, 9 Heliox chargers (~600kW), 3 Orange EV yard tractors, and a 12,000-panel, 4.5MW solar array. Routes of 40-120 miles returned 47-73% battery remaining; phase two adds 27 more charging ports.
key_findings: OK Produce's phase-one buildout includes 10 Freightliner eCascadias, 9 Heliox chargers (three 180kW cabinets feeding nine dispensers, ~600kW), and 3 Orange EV yard tractors, backed by a 12,000-panel, 4.5MW solar array producing about 6.5-7 million kWh/year.
On a 40-60 mile route the truck returned with 73% battery remaining; on an ~80-120 mile uphill route to Oakhurst it returned with 47%, aided by regenerative braking on the descent.
data_available: fleet/charger specs (10 eCascadias, 9 chargers ~600kW)
solar array (12,000 panels, 4.5MW, ~6.5-7M kWh/yr)

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – Frito-Lay
abstract: Profile of PepsiCo/Frito-Lay's Queens, NYC depot converting all 66 route trucks to Ford E-Transit EVs in nine months, in partnership with Prologis Mobility and Con Edison. Covers ConEd's PowerReady infrastructure incentives, temporary house-power charging, driver reactions, and the compact urban duty cycle that lowered charger-ratio needs.
key_findings: Frito-Lay is converting all 66 route trucks at its Queens Prologis site to Ford E-Transit EVs by end of 2023, with 6 temporary chargers powering the initial 30 electric cargo vans while permanent utility infrastructure (about 12 months) is installed.
Con Edison's PowerReady program provides incentives to reduce upfront EV charging infrastructure costs for Frito-Lay's electrification.
data_available: fleet size and conversion timeline
temporary charger count and site power details

title: Electric DEPOT Profiles – US Foods
abstract: Profile of US Foods' La Mirada, CA depot deploying 30 Freightliner eCascadia tractors (15 already in service) using portable chargers ahead of permanent infrastructure. Covers Detroit ePowertrain specs, charging rates, maintenance-role shifts, driver and technician reactions, and US Foods' 32.5%-by-2032 GHG reduction goal.
key_findings: US Foods deployed 30 eCascadias (15 in daily service) at La Mirada using 5 portable chargers (60-75kW) ahead of 15 planned 90kW permanent chargers; eCascadias support up to 270kW dual-port charging, reaching 0-80% in as little as 90 minutes.
US Foods set a goal to cut greenhouse gas emissions 32.5% by 2032; driver Richard Rodriguez reports about 55 miles and 11 stops per shift.
data_available: fleet size (30 eCascadias, 15 in service)
charging power specs (kW, charge time)

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Environmental Justice
abstract: Thematic segment on why NACFE's Electric DEPOT sites target disadvantaged, pollution-burdened communities. Speakers from Empire Clean Cities, San Joaquin Valley Air District, and South Coast AQMD link Class 8 truck electrification to reduced particulate emissions, asthma rates, and community health benefits near major freight corridors.
key_findings: The South Bronx sees about 13,000 truck trips a day, contributing to some of the highest asthma and respiratory illness rates in NYC, per Empire Clean Cities' Joy Gardner.

San Joaquin Valley air district director Samir Sheikh cites over a 90% reduction in some key freight-sector pollutants over the past 20-30 years; Terry O'Day cites about 8,700 premature California air-pollution deaths per year.
data_available: regional air pollution and truck-trip statistics

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Drivers
abstract: Montage of driver and fleet-leader reactions across the Electric DEPOT campaign (Frito-Lay, UPS, Purolator, US Foods, and others) describing quiet, smooth, torque-rich EV driving, regenerative-braking habits, and EVs' appeal as a recruiting tool for attracting new drivers and technicians to trucking.
key_findings: Drivers across multiple fleets describe EV trucks as quieter, smoother, and easier to handle than diesel, with regenerative braking (up to six adjustable levels on some trucks) reducing reliance on friction brakes.
Fleet leaders (e.g., Brian Newman) cite EV trucks as a driver and technician recruiting tool amid industry talent shortages.

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Lessons Learned with Utilities
abstract: Thematic segment on utility-fleet collaboration challenges in depot electrification. Utility and fleet representatives describe the roughly 18-month infrastructure timeline, six factors driving project duration, the "power first, powertrain second" mindset, and debate over phased versus one-time ("touch it once") infrastructure build-outs.
key_findings: Charles Burton estimates roughly an 18-month process from deciding to electrify to actually operating an EV, due to utility infrastructure lead times.
Chanel Parson lists six factors driving EV infrastructure project timelines: project type, site characteristics, added capacity needs, permits/easements, equipment/materials, and customer engagement.
data_available: 18-month infrastructure timeline estimate
six-factor project-duration framework

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Extended Range
abstract: Thematic segment on range strategies for depot-charged EVs: opportunity/return-to-base charging within hours-of-service limits, regenerative braking's role in range recovery, and vehicle design (aero, tires, lightweighting). US Foods' Adrian Amaro details a staged route-mileage ramp-up; WattEV and UPS discuss megawatt charging and driver charging habits.
key_findings: US Foods extended eCascadia route distances in stages, from about 75-80 miles up to nearly 200 miles, against a stated approximately 230-mile battery capacity.
Daimler's Rakesh Aneja notes cases where drivers recovered up to 25% of range via regenerative braking.
data_available: US Foods staged route-mileage progression
regenerative braking range-recovery percentage

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Servicing EVs
abstract: Thematic segment on maintaining and servicing electric trucks across the Electric DEPOT campaign: HV3-certified technician training, required PPE (high-voltage gloves, face shields, shepherd's hooks), dedicated EV service bays, expected reductions in brake and engine maintenance, and technician apprehension about the technology shift.
key_findings: Technicians need specialized PPE (high-voltage gloves, face shields, shepherd's hooks, insulated multimeters) and HV3 certification to work on EV high-voltage components; one facility had 6 fully certified and 2 partially certified technicians while preparing to deploy almost 300 EVs.
Reduced brake wear from regenerative braking and fewer engine-related parts are expected to significantly cut maintenance labor hours versus diesel trucks.
data_available: technician certification counts at one facility

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Shippers and Zero Emissions
abstract: Thematic segment on shippers driving EV adoption to meet their own scope 1-3 emissions and ESG goals. Uber Freight, Goodyear, and Schneider representatives describe RFPs now requesting sustainability data and EV-lane bids, with Schneider's Goodyear-tire intermodal drayage cited as an early zero-emission over-the-road partnership.
key_findings: Uber Freight's Chinmay Jaju says about 75% of its top 100 customers have set public sustainability goals, and RFPs increasingly ask carriers to flag lanes with EV bids.
Schneider is running Goodyear's first EV over-the-road/intermodal drayage shipment, moving tires from ports to distribution facilities with zero tailpipe emissions.
data_available: share of top customers with public sustainability goals

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Managed Charging
abstract: Thematic segment on smart/managed charging strategies for depot fleets: charging "low and slow" to avoid demand charges, telematics-based load prioritization, and site-specific approaches at Penske (Shell Sky software) and Purolator (10-12 hour overnight level-2 charging, no fast charging needed).
key_findings: Penske uses Shell Sky software to manage its chargers, while Purolator relies on 10-12 hour overnight level-2 charging with no DC fast charging needed given its route return times.
Managed/smart charging is used to avoid peak demand charges and to prioritize which trucks charge first based on telematics data and dispatch schedules.
data_available: Purolator overnight charging window (10-12 hours)

title: Electric DEPOT Stories – Total Cost of Ownership
abstract: Thematic segment acknowledging that total cost of ownership for battery-electric trucks remains largely unknown, shaped by unclear resale values, maintenance costs, and incentive availability. Speakers discuss California's ACT/ACF sales-and-purchase mandates, funding sources, and driver experience as an underweighted factor in TCO calculations.
key_findings: Under California's rules, next year 11% of new trucks a dealer sells must be electric (ACT), paired with an ACF fleet-purchase mandate, per Debbie Shust.
Bruce Kurtt argues standard TCO calculators omit diesel-truck downtime/uptime costs, understating EVs' relative economics.
data_available: California ACT dealer-sales percentage requirement

title: Messy Middle Powertrain Service & Maintenance
abstract: NACFE Confidence Report examining service and maintenance requirements across the full range of Class 8 powertrains now in the Messy Middle transition: advanced diesel/ICE, renewable diesel, biodiesel, renewable natural gas, battery-electric, hydrogen internal combustion, and hydrogen fuel cell. Developed as a UC Riverside class project, primary author Marcos Alvarez conducted roughly a year of interviews with OEMs, fleet service managers, and subject-matter experts, plus site visits during NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle (September 2025) and ACT Expo 2025. Covers technician training, safety protocols, diagnostic tools, oil/DEF/coolant maintenance, tires/wheels/brakes, and fueling/charging infrastructure upkeep. Published June 25, 2026.
key_findings: Cummins' Oil Guard oil-sampling program allows approved fleets to extend FA-4 oil drain intervals up to 80,000 miles, a 60% increase over the 50,000-mile baseline for conventional CK-4 oil, while PACCAR's MX-13 recommends 75,000-mile intervals under regular duty and 35,000 miles under severe duty.

Fuel cell electric trucks require filter replacement every 30,000 to 40,000 miles, coolant changes every 150,000 miles, and stack replacement at roughly 400,000 to 700,000 miles depending on duty cycle, a maintenance profile very different from hydrogen internal combustion engines, which follow diesel-like service intervals.

Battery-electric truck curb weights exceed diesel equivalents by 8,000 to 12,000 lbs. (e.g., Tesla Semi over 23,000 lbs., Freightliner eCascadia over 21,000 lbs.), increasing tire contact-patch stress by 30% to 50% during acceleration and requiring tire rotation intervals shortened from 6,000-8,000 miles to 4,500-6,000 miles.
data_available: OEM biodiesel/renewable diesel support matrix (Fig. 14)
DPF regeneration intervals by fuel type (Fig. 9)
oil/coolant/DEF maintenance checklist (Appendix B)
CAN bus diagnostic primer (Appendix C)
high-voltage safety check procedures (Appendix D)
list of diesel/EV technician training programs (Appendix A)

title: The Feasibility of Intentional Pairing: Heavy-Duty Tractors and Trailers
abstract: NACFE report commissioned by a major truck manufacturer investigating whether intentionally matching specific tractor models to specific trailer models (e.g., pairing SuperTruck-spec tractors with SuperTruck-spec trailers) can reliably improve fuel economy in North American dry van and refrigerated trucking. Published July 30, 2019, the study draws on roughly 90 references, NACFE's Annual Fleet Fuel Study data, and a limited survey of 14 of 50 fleets contacted, plus consultation with owner-operators. It concludes that most dry van and reefer trailers operate in drop-and-hook pools rather than dedicated pairings, making full intentional pairing statistically improbable outside niche or small-fleet operations.
key_findings: A 5% to 10% net improvement in truck operating costs would be needed to make fleets consider restructuring operations for intentional tractor-trailer pairing.

The national dry van trailer-to-tractor ratio averages about 3:1 (refrigerated vans about 1.2:1 to 2.2:1), meaning a SuperTruck tractor would need roughly three SuperTruck trailers in the pool to realize its full annual efficiency potential.

NACFE's 2018 Annual Fleet Fuel Study of fleets operating over 71,844 tractors and 236,292 trailers found average fleet fuel economy of 7.26 MPG in 2017, versus a national baseline of 6.7 MPG for the entire U.S. van trailer population.
data_available: fleet survey data (14 of 50 fleets)
AFFS technology adoption curves (Figs. 13-16)
trailer-tractor ratio and duty cycle tables
probability tables for trip length, load weight, and pairing scenarios

title: Confidence Report: Determining Efficiency
abstract: NACFE/Trucking Efficiency Confidence Report (published January 28, 2016) explaining the range of methods used to measure and estimate heavy-duty freight efficiency gains, using aerodynamic technologies as the illustrative example. Covers five test categories -- computational fluid dynamics, wind tunnel testing, track testing (coastdown, constant-speed, SAE J1321/J1526), on-road testing, and fleet composite testing -- along with real-world factors (temperature, wind, road grade, driver, traffic drafting) that cause deviation from controlled test results. Draws on NACFE's 2015 Fleet Fuel Study of 14 large fleets and case studies including a 2013 DOE/Lawrence Livermore/Navistar/Frito-Lay field trial and a 2013 NACFE 6x2 axle Confidence Report.
key_findings: NACFE's 2015 Fleet Fuel Study found participating fleets achieving fleet-wide fuel economy of just under 7.0 mpg versus a 5.9 mpg U.S. average for over-the-road tractors, saving about $9,000 per tractor per year compared to a fleet with no efficiency-technology investment.

A DOE/Lawrence Livermore/Navistar field study of aerodynamic devices over 1.4 million Frito-Lay fleet miles and 690,000 Spirit Truck Lines miles found on-road results roughly half of what SAE Type II track tests and wind tunnel evaluations had predicted.

In a 2013 NACFE Confidence Report on 6x2 axles, ten independent tests (fleet and OEM) all showed positive fuel economy gains ranging from 1.6% to 4.6%, despite using different test methods, illustrating that trend consistency matters more than absolute precision.
data_available: EPA GHG Phase I aero drag coefficient comparison across 4 test methods (Fig. 28)
6x2 vs 6x4 fuel economy test summary table (Figs. 29-30)
list of ~25 SAE/EPA/TMC test standards
payback period charts vs. fuel price and device cost

title: Transformational Technologies Reshaping Transportation – An Industry Perspective
abstract: 2020 SAE L. Ray Buckendale Lecture by Mike Roeth (NACFE Executive Director), the third in an SAE series on transformational change in commercial trucking (following 2018 government and 2019 academia perspectives), giving an industry view. Covers electrification (BEV and hydrogen fuel cell), levels of automation/autonomy, platooning, connected vehicles, the DOE SuperTruck I/II programs, and factors driving fleet technology adoption (S-curve dynamics, residual value, regulation, risk, vehicle life expectancy, operating costs, fuel price volatility). Includes 2020 case studies of PepsiCo/Frito-Lay's Transforming Modesto project, UPS's Rolling Laboratory and CNG/RNG fleet, and NFI's Chino, California battery-electric drayage pilot.
key_findings: NACFE's 2017 Run on Less demonstration of 7 Class 8 tractors averaged 10.1 mpg over 17 days and 50,107 miles at an average GVW of 55,498 lbs., more than double the roughly 5.9-6.0 mpg U.S. average for combination trucks at the time.

PepsiCo's Frito-Lay Transforming Modesto project (announced October 2019) planned to deploy 15 Tesla Semi battery-electric tractors, 38 Volvo CNG/RNG tractors, six Peterbilt 220EV battery-electric box trucks, and associated charging/CNG infrastructure at its Modesto, California facility by 2021.

NFI's Chino, California drayage pilot planned 65 tractors for electrification on a roughly 50-mile-each-way route to the ports of Los Angeles/Long Beach, with net energy consumption estimated at 1.6 to 2.4 kWh/mile on the drayage routes.
data_available: FHWA/EPA vehicle weight classification tables (Figs. 1, 3)
SAE J3016 automation levels (Fig. 10)
technology decision-bias chart (Fig. 12)
SuperTruck I/II vehicle photos and specs
NACFE AFFS 85-technology adoption curves (Figs. 21-23)
UPS/PepsiCo/NFI fleet technology deployment lists

title: Costs and Adoption Rates of Fuel-Saving Technologies for Trailers in the North American On-Road Freight Sector
abstract: Joint ICCT/NACFE white paper (Ben Sharpe, Mike Roeth), published February 2014, based on telephone interviews conducted August-December 2013 with 22 companies -- 11 trucking fleets, 3 trailer OEMs, 6 aerodynamic device manufacturers, and 2 tire manufacturers -- to quantify costs, fuel savings, payback periods, and adoption rates of trailer aerodynamic (side skirts, underbody devices, boat tails, gap reducers) and tire (low rolling resistance duals, wide-base singles, tire pressure systems) technologies. Finds costs for side skirts had dropped roughly 54-70% since 2008-2010 estimates, driven mainly by California's tractor-trailer GHG regulation and the EPA SmartWay program.
key_findings: Side skirts were estimated to be installed on about 40% of new box trailers, at a typical cost of $700-$1,100 and average fuel savings of 3% (best performers up to 7%), yielding payback times of 6 months to 2 years.

Roughly one-quarter of all trailers on U.S. roads had at least one aerodynamic technology (side skirt, underbody device, or boat tail) as of the study, expected to rise to about 33% once California's regulation fully phases in by 2020.

About half of all tractor and trailer tires sold were SmartWay-verified low rolling resistance duals (1-3% fuel savings), while wide-base single tire adoption on new trailers was around 10% (2-4% fuel savings).
data_available: Table 6 summary of cost/savings/payback/adoption by technology
side-skirt/boat-tail cost comparison across TIAX 2009, NAS 2010, and this study (Fig. 2)
payback calculation tables for each trailer technology (Tables 2-5)

title: Driving Maximum Efficiency: How Fleets Are Implementing Existing Technologies to Reduce Costs and Improve Efficiency, and a Closer Look at Renewable Natural Gas in Heavy-Duty Applications
abstract: Shell-sponsored NACFE report with no explicit publication date printed in the text; internal references to a March 2024 NACFE Natural Gas Confidence Report, the September 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle event, Shell Starship 3.0's 2025 INDYCAR circuit runs, and a 2026-dated EIA citation confirm publication in 2026 -- not the ~2012 date the filename suggested. Profiles technologies used by high-efficiency fleets to cut fuel costs and carbon intensity: low-viscosity/FA-4 engine oils and synthetic transmission/axle fluids, and renewable natural gas (RNG). Uses NACFE Fleet Fuel Study data and the Shell Starship demonstration vehicle (three generations, 2018-2023) as case studies, alongside results from Run on Less – Messy Middle (18-day event, September 2025).
key_findings: Diesel trucks in Run on Less – Messy Middle averaged 11 mpg over an 18-day period, more than 50% higher than the U.S. average for diesel and a 9% improvement over the 10 mpg average achieved by comparable trucks and drivers in the 2017 Run on Less.

Shell Starship 3.0, powered by a Cummins X15N engine on renewable natural gas, achieved 9 mpg (diesel gallon equivalent) and freight efficiency exceeding 200 ton-miles per gallon on a 2023 California demonstration run near 80,000 lb GVW.

NACFE Fleet Fuel Study fleets with 50%+ technology adoption rates averaged 8.8 mpg by 2023 versus 6.8 mpg for fleets with under 30% adoption; fleets using low-viscosity CK-4 engine oil reported 0.5-1.5% fuel savings, with FA-4 oil adding another 0.4-0.7%.
data_available: FHWA combination-truck fuel economy trend 2007-2023 (Fig. 1)
FFS technology-adoption vs. fuel-economy trend 2003-2023 (Figs. 2-4)
confidence matrix for low-viscosity engine oil adoption (Fig. 5)
Messy Middle powertrain transition decision framework (Fig. 6)

title: A Need to Redefine Class 8 Long-Haul Trucking
abstract: NACFE white paper by Mike Roeth (2025) arguing that the industry's traditional definition of 'long haul' trucking -- synonymous with over-the-road sleeper operations -- should be broadened to include long-distance return-to-base operations using day cab tractors. Defines short/medium/long regional-haul mileage bands, discusses slip seating and team driving, and previews the September 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration featuring roughly 10 fleets and multiple powertrains (diesel, natural gas, battery electric, hydrogen fuel cell) in long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles.
key_findings: NACFE defines short regional haul as under 50 miles out-and-back (100 miles total), medium regional haul as roughly 100 miles out-and-back (200 miles total), and long regional haul as roughly 300 miles out-and-back (600 miles total).
ACT Research data cited by NACFE shows the Class 8 market splitting into roughly 44% sleeper tractors, 25% day cab tractors, 30% day cab work trucks, and 1% sleeper work trucks.

During Run on Less – Electric DEPOT, Tesla Semi trucks deployed by PepsiCo reached ranges up to 410 miles on a single charge, with one truck completing 1,076 miles in a 24-hour period; team driving separately allows a truck to cover about 1,000 miles in 24 hours under hours-of-service rules.
data_available: Class 8 market segmentation by cab/body type (Fig. 1)
regional haul mileage-band definitions (Fig. 3)
long-haul redefinition schematic (Fig. 4)

title: Driver Tips for Increasing Fuel Economy
abstract: Two-page NACFE driver tip sheet listing 12 practical actions truck drivers can take to improve fuel economy: watching speed, maintaining constant speed, finding the engine's efficient RPM range, avoiding harsh braking, smooth acceleration, tire inflation checks, aerodynamic device maintenance, cruise control use, minimizing idling, following distance, route optimization, and minimizing shifting. No formal study methodology; presents commonly cited industry rules of thumb rather than fleet-specific test data. No publication date appears in the document itself; year is carried over from source metadata.
key_findings: Each mile per hour driven over 60 mph is estimated to reduce fuel economy by about 0.1 mpg, so a truck at 65 mph would see roughly 27% better fuel efficiency than the same truck at 75 mph.
A 10% annual reduction in idling is estimated to be worth about 1% in fuel economy, translating to roughly $300-$500 per year at $3.00/gallon fuel and 100,000 miles driven annually.
Tires underinflated by 10 psi are associated with a 0.5-1.0% increase in fuel consumption.

title: From Source to Highway: The Messy Middle Emissions Report
abstract: This report analyzes well-to-wheel emissions and public-health impacts across the 13 fleets that ran diesel/biodiesel/renewable-diesel, natural gas/RNG, battery-electric, and hydrogen fuel-cell Class 8 trucks in NACFE's 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration. Using telematics data, fuel and energy carbon-intensity scores, and health-impact modeling across 31 target counties, the study quantifies CO2, NOx, PM, and health outcomes by powertrain and fuel origin over an 18-day, multi-route real-freight event, concluding that fuel/energy source often matters more than propulsion technology for emissions outcomes.
key_findings: Best-performing diesel fleets achieved 11.77 MPG (Albert Transport) and 11.74 MPG (MVT) against a 6.5 MPG/156.6 metric-ton annual CO2 baseline, while Frito-Lay's B99 biodiesel truck cut estimated annual CO2 emissions by 86% to 21.8 metric tons.

Battery-electric trucks cut CO2 emissions by 62% to over 99% versus diesel depending on grid carbon intensity, ranging from 351 g CO2e/mile for a drayage truck on the SCE grid to 12-13 g CO2e/mile for Saia trucks charging on PG&E's low-carbon grid.

Wegmans' dairy-manure RNG truck achieved an estimated carbon-negative footprint (CI score of -150 gCO2e/MJ, ~-250% net GHG impact vs. diesel), and replacing the oldest 130,000 diesel trucks in 31 target counties with RNG was projected to avoid more than 100 premature deaths and save roughly $2 billion annually in healthcare costs.
data_available: Figures ES2-ES5: fleet-by-fleet MPG/CO2 and well-to-wheel GHG emissions tables and charts
Diesel/CNG/BEV/hydrogen fleet comparison matrices with speed-band and topography data
Health-impact modeling for 31 target counties (avoided mortality, morbidity, cost)
NOx/SOx/PM criteria pollutant analysis by powertrain (Section 9.2)

title: Natural Gas' Role in Decarbonizing Trucking
abstract: This 2024 NACFE Confidence Report evaluates natural gas (CNG/LNG) and renewable natural gas (RNG) as a decarbonization pathway for medium- and heavy-duty trucking, based on interviews with fleets, OEMs, and industry experts. It covers engine suppliers (led by Cummins' new X15N 15-liter engine), fuel carbon-intensity comparisons to diesel, methane-leakage concerns, fueling infrastructure, and driver experience, and profiles fleet adopters including UPS, Waste Management, Frito-Lay, and Paper Transport. The report frames natural gas as a near-zero-NOx bridge fuel with lower well-to-wheel CO2 than diesel but higher fuel consumption per diesel-gallon-equivalent.
key_findings: Natural gas engines deliver a net CO2 benefit of 13% to 18% versus diesel and produce about 27% less CO2 per unit of energy on a fuel basis, but require 15% to 20% more fuel on a diesel-gallon-equivalent (DGE) basis due to lower engine efficiency.

UPS operates more than 4,000 heavy-duty natural gas tractors and about 6,500 medium-duty CNG vehicles across roughly 50 CNG and 12 LNG private stations, while Waste Management runs more than 12,000 natural gas vehicles and 193 natural gas stations with over $4 billion invested in vehicles and infrastructure.

Paper Transport reports a CNG/RNG breakeven point versus diesel at $4.50/gallon diesel (a 6.5% cost penalty at $3/gallon diesel, a 3.5% advantage at $5.25/gallon); as of 2022, about 69% of natural gas dispensed as motor fuel in the US was renewable (RNG).

Figure 44: carbon intensity summary table by fuel (CARB/GREET model)

title: Empowering Future Trucks: SuperTruck 2
abstract: This report reviews the US Department of Energy's SuperTruck 2 program (2016-2024), in which five OEM teams (Cummins/Peterbilt, Daimler Truck North America, Volvo Trucks, Navistar, and PACCAR) each built demonstrator Class 8 tractor-trailers targeting more than 100% freight-ton-efficiency improvement over a Model Year 2009 diesel baseline at 65,000 lbs. GVW, plus a 55% brake thermal efficiency engine target. Drawing on DOE Annual Merit Review data and public team disclosures, NACFE summarizes each team's technology approach (aerodynamics, engine efficiency, hybridization, lightweighting) and results, and assesses which innovations are likely to migrate into production trucks.
key_findings: All five SuperTruck 2 teams exceeded their DOE freight-ton-efficiency (FTE) improvement targets, which ranged from 100% (Navistar, Volvo, PACCAR) to 115% (Daimler) and 125% (Cummins/Peterbilt) versus each team's MY2009 baseline, with stretch goals as high as 170%.

SuperTruck 2 demonstrators reached fuel economy as high as 16 MPG, versus SuperTruck 1 vehicles that achieved 11-13 MPG against a roughly 50% FTE improvement target; all teams also targeted a 55% brake thermal efficiency engine at 65 mph.

NACFE estimates that a 100% scale FTE improvement, as demonstrated by SuperTruck 2 teams, could extend a 300-mile battery-electric truck's range to roughly 600 miles by applying the same efficiency technologies.

title: Defining Production
abstract: This NACFE thought-leadership report examines the ambiguous meaning of the term "production" as used by commercial truck OEMs, drawing on interviews with OEM engineers and analysis of historical vehicle-launch case studies for Class 3 through 8 trucks. It surveys product-development frameworks (stage-gate, PLM, APQP, V-Cycle), tooling and validation timelines, and real-world examples -- including the Stoneridge MirrorEye camera-mirror system and Kenworth/Daimler alternative-energy vehicle roadmaps -- to show that "production" claims can mean anything from a single low-rate prototype to full-rate, fully supported manufacturing. It argues for a shared industry vocabulary to reduce confusion among fleets, regulators, and media.
key_findings: New heavy-truck product-development cycles typically span four to six years from concept to legally certified production, and established OEM programs such as Daimler's cite roughly a decade to develop a new engine or cab.

As presented at the 2018 ACT Expo, Kenworth's roadmap for alternative-energy (battery/hybrid) tractors spanned eight years, from a 2018 concept vehicle to volume production in 2026, with tollgate investments ranging from $5 million in early design phases to $100-200 million for production phases.

By 2018, North American heavy-truck manufacturing capacity was near 300,000 trucks per year against a base of more than 2 million heavy-duty tractors in North American service, with new technology adoption typically following an S-curve that NACFE tracks across 85 technologies and 20 participating fleets in its Annual Fleet Fuel Study.

title: Confidence Report: 6x2 Axles Update
abstract: This 2017 NACFE Confidence Report updates the original January 2013 6x2 Axles Confidence Report, based on interviews with fleets, OEMs (Volvo, Mack, Meritor, Dana, Hendrickson, Daimler), and tire manufacturers. It revisits the 2013 finding of about 2.5% average fuel savings from 6x2 tandem axles, documents lessons learned by early adopters -- notably accelerated drive-tire wear and driver-perception issues -- catalogs new liftable-pusher-axle ("Generation III") products introduced since 2013, and provides updated tire-selection and driver-training recommendations, plus GHG Phase 2 regulatory adoption targets for 6x2/4x2 axle configurations.
key_findings: 6x2 adoption among North American long-haul fleets rose from about 2% in 2013 to only 4-5% by 2016, well below the EPA's original 60%-by-2024 proposal; the final GHG Phase 2 rule instead assumes 30% adoption of 6x2/4x2 axles by 2027.

Early Generation I 6x2 adopters saw a 50-70% reduction in drive-tire life versus 6x4s, but fleets that implemented full Generation II systems (load-shifting, traction control, torque-limiting) cut that penalty to about 20%; at current fuel prices, a 6x2 with a 50% tire-wear penalty needed roughly a 4%+ fuel-economy improvement just to offset the added tire cost, versus the observed ~2.5% average savings.

New liftable Generation III pusher-axle systems (Volvo Adaptive Loading, in production since 2016; Mack Lifting Pusher Axle; Hendrickson OPTIMAAX, expected 2017) claim an additional ~2% fuel savings over standard tag-axle 6x2s and are recommended for fleets running below 60,000 lbs. GCWR at least 30% of the time.

title: Smart Charging for Electric Depots
abstract: This joint NACFE/Ampcontrol report examines grid capacity constraints, energy-cost management, and smart/managed charging strategies for electrifying truck depots, building on findings from NACFE's Run on Less – Electric DEPOT study of electric trucks. It explains time-of-use rate and demand-charge dynamics, compares cloud-based versus on-site smart-charging architectures, and profiles microgrid and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) trends. Two anonymized real-world depot case studies quantify demand-charge and time-of-use savings achievable through smart charging, and the report closes with a look at Megawatt Charging System (MCS) and certification trends.
key_findings: Large fleet depots can require up to 5 MW of power, and utility approval for grid upgrades can take one to five years; at one 20-charger depot, smart charging capped peak demand at about 1 MW (versus over 1.5 MW unmanaged), cutting demand charges by 50% for about $150,000 in annual savings plus $100,000 in avoided time-of-use costs, for $250,000 total annual savings.

At a second 40-DCFC depot facing peak/off-peak/super-off-peak TOU rates of $0.45/$0.25/$0.20 per kWh, shifting charging to super off-peak hours cut monthly energy costs by 15%-55%, worth $60,000 to $217,800 in annual savings.

Ampcontrol reports observing energy-cost savings of up to 45% from smart charging; current DC fast chargers are generally limited to 360 kW with most vehicles charging below 250 kW, while emerging Megawatt Charging Systems (MCS) target up to 1 MW per port.

title: Peloton Technology Platooning Fuel Economy Test
abstract: This is a NACFE third-party validation letter/report on a SAE J1321 fuel-economy test of the Peloton Technology two-truck platooning system, conducted jointly with CR England near Salt Lake City, Utah, during the week of November 18, 2013. Two Peloton-equipped Peterbilt 386 tractors (first-generation system, 36-foot following gap at 64 mph) were tested against a Freightliner Cascadia control truck across six approximately 40-mile segments on Interstate 80. NACFE oversaw test-protocol compliance and validated the resulting fuel-savings data reported by CR England and Peloton engineers.
key_findings: The lead platooning truck (C1) averaged 4.5% fuel savings and the following/tail truck (B1) averaged 10.0% fuel savings versus the control truck, both measured over three valid test runs at a 36-foot following distance and 64 mph.
The platooning system was engaged for a minimum of 99% of the time across the three validated test runs, as logged by Peloton's onboard data collection equipment.

title: Michelin 5,000 Mile Fuel Challenge
abstract: This is a NACFE third-party validation letter for a 5,000-mile real-world fuel-economy test of three Michelin tire configurations, conducted by Jackson Marketing Group for Michelin North America in July 2011. Three identical Freightliner daycab tractors with DD15 engines ran a multi-day route from Greenville, SC toward Los Angeles and back (12 segments, roughly 400 miles per day), rotating drivers, tires, and trailers, with fuel measured at each fueling stop. NACFE's Mike Roeth and a contracted validator (Mike Modrak) witnessed test preparation, key procedures, and a portion of the on-road testing to confirm protocol compliance.
key_findings: Across all 12 test segments, Configuration 2 tires averaged 7.15 MPG, Configuration 3 averaged 6.87 MPG, and baseline Configuration 1 averaged 6.61 MPG, meaning Configuration 2 outperformed the baseline by 8.13% and Configuration 3 by 3.93%.

Excluding an outlier segment (Segment 5, where Configuration 3 hit 8.08 MPG, about 17.5% above its own average), the fuel-economy advantage over baseline changes to 8.83% for Configuration 2 and 3.08% for Configuration 3.
data_available: Figure 1: per-segment MPG line chart for all three tire configurations across 12 segments

title: XStream Trucking On-Highway Fuel Economy Test
abstract: This NACFE third-party validation letter reports on an on-highway fuel-economy test of XStream Trucking's GapGorilla tractor-trailer gap-closing aerodynamic system, conducted with Hobby Lobby in Oklahoma City during the week of May 9, 2016. A single Volvo tractor with a 53-foot dry van trailer ran paired 68-69-mile round-trip test runs at 65 mph on Interstate 44, alternating between GapGorilla deployed and stowed configurations, using a modified SAE J1321/TMC RP1102A/RP1109 protocol with tank-weight fuel measurement. NACFE's Dave Schaller witnessed test preparation and data collection to validate protocol compliance.
key_findings: Across five paired test runs, the GapGorilla system produced a median fuel-consumption decrease of 2.51% and an average (combined) decrease of 2.49% versus the stowed/control configuration.
Individual paired-run savings ranged from 1.17% to 4.13%; discarding the highest and lowest pairs reduced the coefficient of variation from 44% to 19% and left an average savings estimate of 2.38%.
data_available: Full run-by-run fuel-weight-consumed table for all five paired test runs (deployed vs. stowed)

title: The Idle-Reduction Playbook: Operational Strategies for Modern Trucking Fleets
abstract: A NACFE Confidence Report, published December 22, 2025, covering the full landscape of idle-reduction technologies and practices for over-the-road trucking fleets -- diesel and electric APUs, fuel-operated heaters, intelligent engine-management systems, thermal management, and driver behavior programs -- with pricing, adoption rates, and best practices for each. It appears to be a 2025 update and successor to NACFE's earlier Confidence Report on Idle-Reduction Technologies (2019), presenting substantially refreshed cost, adoption, and diesel-price data (as of July 2025) while addressing the same core technology categories. The report draws on NACFE's 2024 Fleet Fuel Study, government idling regulations by state, and a forward-looking outlook tied to vehicle electrification.
key_findings: A typical Class 8 truck idles at around 0.8 gallons of diesel per hour, burning 1,000 to 1,800 gallons annually depending on climate and duty cycle, equating to $3,500 to more than $6,000 in annual idle-related fuel cost at the July 2025 national average diesel price of $3.81/gallon.

NACFE's fleet snapshots show installing a diesel APU or eAPU typically cuts idle percentage from 30-50% down to the low-20% range, avoiding about 480 gallons of diesel and roughly $1,720 in fuel per truck annually at July 2025 diesel prices.

New diesel APU installations typically cost $8,000 to $10,000 for entry-level systems, $11,000 to $13,000 for mainstream systems, and up to $15,000 for high-end models, plus about $300 to $600 per year in maintenance.

In NACFE's 2024 Fleet Fuel Study, Anti-Idle Electronic Engine Controls were adopted by 84% of participating fleets, Diesel-Fired Heaters by 67%, and cab insulation upgrades by 61%, while Diesel APU adoption among study fleets was only 7%.

The 2024 Fleet Fuel Study's 14 participating fleets, representing a combined 75,000 trucks, achieved an average fuel economy of 7.77 MPG in 2023 (a 16% improvement over 10 years) and saved a combined $512,000,000 versus the national average.

title: More Regional Haul: An Opportunity for Trucking?
abstract: A NACFE thought-leadership report, published April 8, 2019, examining ten interacting trends driving growth in regional-haul trucking relative to over-the-road (OTR) operations: driver hiring/retention, e-commerce growth, GPS-based asset tracking, electric/hybrid vehicle advances, vehicle automation, load-matching innovation, long combination vehicles, warehousing build-out, and data mining. Based on interviews with fleets, manufacturers, and industry groups, the report defines regional haul as operations keeping the truck within a 300-mile radius of a home base with predictable driver-home time, and is distinct from NACFE's separate Run on Less Regional (2019) demonstration and later Electric Trucks Have Arrived (2022) reports on the same general topic.
key_findings: NACFE defines regional haul as an operation where the truck stays within a 300-mile radius of a home base, whether returning daily or on a multi-day route.
The American Trucking Associations projected the driver shortage growing from about 51,000 drivers in 2017 to roughly 175,000 by 2026.

DAT data show average length of haul declined from 2012 to 2018 by about 10% for dry van (approximately 640 to 570 miles), 26% for reefer (approximately 1,060 to 790 miles), and 9% for flatbed (approximately 690 to 630 miles).

Driver turnover at large for-hire carriers (revenue above $30 million) was 90% at the end of 2017, versus 85% at smaller carriers, holding at similar levels since 2015; private fleet driver turnover is far lower.

2002 VIUS/DOT data cited in the report show 83% of US truck trips were under 100 miles (67% under 50 miles, 16% between 51-100 miles), which NACFE believes has since shifted further toward shorter trips with e-commerce growth.

title: Barriers to Increased Adoption of Fuel Efficiency Technologies in Freight Trucking
abstract: A joint ICCT/NACFE/Cascade Sierra Solutions report, published July 2013, identifying the primary barriers preventing wider adoption of fuel-saving technologies in North American freight trucking. The study team conducted in-person interviews, conference calls, and a truck-dealer focus group with 29 end-user and supply-chain stakeholders between late 2012 and early 2013, plus online surveys of 1,892 owner-operators via Cascade Sierra Solutions and Let's Truck. The analysis identifies five primary barriers -- uncertain payback time, insufficient access to capital, lack of credible information, inconsistent reliability, and lack of technology availability -- and additional findings on split incentives and the rebound effect.
key_findings: The study drew on 15 one-hour end-user fleet interviews, interviews with 6 large truck/trailer manufacturers and 14 other supply-chain companies, a truck-dealer focus group, and online surveys completed by 1,892 owner-operators between December 2012 and February 2013.

Five primary barriers to fuel-saving technology adoption were identified: uncertain payback time, insufficient access to capital, lack of credible information (both verifying and sharing), inconsistent reliability, and lack of technology availability.

Fuel costs represented on average 35% of a fleet's total operating expense, and new long-haul sleeper tractor costs rose from about $90,000-$100,000 in 2006 to $115,000-$135,000 by 2013, a 20-30% increase.

Large for-hire fleets generally required a payback of 18-24 months (about half their 3-5 year truck ownership cycle), while private fleets accepted longer paybacks of 24-36+ months given 6-10 year ownership cycles.

Owner-operator survey respondents averaged 122,099 miles driven per truck in 2012 and 6.6 miles per gallon; over 80% wanted a payback of 2 years or less, and 92% deemed under-24-month payback reasonable for retrofit technologies.

title: Decarbonizing Truck & Trailer Refrigeration: Zero-Emission Temperature Control in Trucking
abstract: A NACFE guidance report, published October 17, 2024, examining transport refrigeration units (TRUs) used on refrigerated trucks and trailers and the emerging transition to zero-emission electric TRUs (eTRUs). It covers how TRUs work, the environmental impacts of diesel-powered units, the operational and cost barriers to eTRU adoption (battery sizing, weight, charging infrastructure, driver/technician training), and CARB regulations driving the shift, drawing on interviews with suppliers such as PLM and Thermo King. The report closes with findings on the scope of the refrigerated-freight segment and recommendations for coordinating eTRU charging infrastructure with electric-truck charging build-out.
key_findings: Freight requiring temperature-controlled transport accounts for about 15% of straight trucks and trailers in North America.

CARB estimates the weight penalty of an all-electric eTRU trailer at 728 lbs, while industry experts estimate 2,000-2,500 lbs, versus a federal 2,000-lb weight allowance for electric tractor-trailers that does not separately cover the reefer trailer's added weight.

PLM reported that a new diesel 53-foot TRU reefer trailer costs about $110,000-$115,000, a standby-electric eTRU about $130,000-$145,000, and an all-electric eTRU about $170,000-$250,000, depending on manufacturer.
A standard diesel TRU fuel tank holds about 50 gallons and can be quickly refueled anywhere, while eTRUs are constrained by battery run time and require careful sizing to the specific duty cycle.

title: High-Potential Regions for Electric Truck Deployments
abstract: An RMI/NACFE guidance report, published November 2020 and authored by Jessie Lund and Mike Roeth, presenting a framework for identifying and prioritizing North American regions best suited for early electric truck deployment. The framework organizes indicators into three categories -- Technology (range/climate, electricity pricing, regenerative braking), Need (air quality, environmental justice, greenhouse gas emissions, freight flow), and Support (state/city/provincial policies and incentives, utility programs, training) -- and combines them into a heatmap ranking states and provinces as 'High Priority' or 'Consider' for deployment. The report includes an emerging-megaregions map and closes with conclusions and recommendations for fleets, policymakers, and utilities.
key_findings: Regional-haul heavy-duty trucking (short-haul, return-to-base operations) is identified as a strong early candidate for electrification, with early deployments concentrated in California due to supportive state policy, incentives, and mild climate/terrain.

The report's three-part framework -- Technology, Need, and Support -- combines into a North American heatmap classifying states and provinces as 'High Priority' versus 'Consider' for electric truck deployment potential.
An accompanying map identifies eleven emerging US megaregions as defined by the Regional Plan Association, used as an additional lens for regional prioritization.

title: Development of Specifications for Heavy-Duty Tractor Trucks in Canada and the United States
abstract: An ICCT working paper (2018-27), authored by Ben Sharpe (ICCT) and Dave Schaller (NACFE) and published October 2018, examining how Class 7/8 tractor trucks are specified and purchased in Canada and the United States. Based on 15 interviews conducted with trucking fleets and owner-operators in early 2018, the paper contrasts the small-fleet dealership pathway against the large-fleet OEM national-account-manager pathway, documents how fuel-saving technologies are marketed and evaluated via payback calculations, and covers differences between Canadian and US specification practices as well as macro trends including driver shortages, electrification, and automation. An appendix reproduces an example full tractor specification sheet.
key_findings: The study team conducted 15 interviews with trucking fleets and owner-operators in early 2018: 13 based in Canada (7 owner-operators/small fleets with fewer than 5 trucks) and 2 in the United States, with the larger fleets interviewed ranging from 100 to 2,000 trucks.

For-hire fleets averaged about 90% annual driver turnover versus about 10% for private fleets, per American Trucking Association data cited in the report; for-hire fleets typically own trucks 3-5 years versus 6-10 years for private fleets.

In 2017, the 10 largest for-hire fleets in North America ranged from about 36,000 to 106,000 tractor trucks (UPS the largest), while the 10 largest private fleets ranged from about 3,100 to 11,000 trucks (PepsiCo the largest).

A typical fuel-saving technology payback threshold is 1.5 to 2 years, based on a typical 3-5 year fleet ownership cycle; interviewed fleets averaged 5 years of truck ownership with a payback threshold of just over 3 years, and 8 of 15 responses required payback shorter than the ownership cycle.

Engine technologies were rated the highest-value fuel-saving technology category among the six surveyed (average rating about 2.2 of 6, most important), while telematics/IT and weight reduction rated lowest (averages about 4.2-4.3).

Ten largest for-hire and private fleets by tractor ownership, 2017 (Figure 2)
Truck ownership duration vs. maximum acceptable payback scatter plot (Figure 4)
Fuel-saving technology category value rankings (Figure 5)
Full example tractor specification sheet with weight distribution (Appendix B)

title: Fleet Perspectives on Charging-as-a-Service
abstract: A NACFE report, published March 20, 2025 and sponsored by Electrada, presenting results of an industry survey on Charging-as-a-Service (CaaS) and other outside service-provider models for fleet electrification. Respondents included fleets (38), OEM/software providers, consultants, government, and others; fleet respondents self-reported operation size, duty cycle mix, and electrification maturity. The report identifies working with utilities as the top barrier to electrification, examines when fleets find outside CaaS/managed-charging providers valuable, and reports what fleets and industry members consider markers of a successful electrification project.
key_findings: 38 fleet respondents took the survey (25 operating 100+ trucks); their reported duty-cycle mix was 35% Local, 38% Regional, and 27% Long Haul, with 14 fleets operating in multiple duty cycles.

Both fleet and industry-member respondents identified working with utilities as the top barrier to electrification (24% of fleet responses, 29% of industry responses), ranking above TCO/ROI (14%/17%) and vehicle range (14% each).

About 38% of fleets that had implemented or were implementing electrification used a CaaS or managed-charging provider, while 33% used no outside provider -- of those, 50% wanted to learn for themselves and 37% cited cost as the reason.

Fleet respondents rated Operational Effectiveness (about 4.4 of 5) as the most important factor in judging electrification-project success, followed by Total Cost of Ownership and Customer Satisfaction (about 4.1 each).
46% of fleet respondents said internal company goals require emissions reporting, 37% said both internal and customer goals require it, and 18% said neither.
data_available: Respondent breakdown by industry and by fleet size/duty cycle (Figures 1-2)
Barriers to fleet electrification by respondent group (Figure 5)
Benefits of working with a CaaS/service provider by respondent group (Figure 6)
Success-factor importance ratings, Fleet vs. Industry (Figure 7)
Full 25-question survey instrument (Appendix A)

title: Navigating the Messy Middle
abstract: A short NACFE thought-leadership white paper by Executive Director Mike Roeth, published in 2025 ahead of the September 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle demonstration. It is a distinct, condensed companion piece to NACFE's 2023 report The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, briefly surveying diesel, renewable diesel, biodiesel, CNG/RNG, hydrogen ICE, hybrid, battery-electric, and hydrogen fuel cell powertrains, then presenting a decision framework and factors (duty cycle, fleet size, regulatory factors, energy pricing, infrastructure, well-to-wheel impact) fleets should weigh when selecting a powertrain path.
key_findings: NACFE's Run on Less - Messy Middle demonstration, planned for September 2025, will feature about 10 fleets deploying Class 8 sleeper and day cab trucks across long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles evaluating multiple powertrain solutions.
Battery electric trucks are estimated at 65% to 85% overall charger-to-wheels energy efficiency, versus about 40% efficiency for hydrogen internal combustion engines.

NACFE's powertrain decision framework recommends fleets evaluate battery electric first, then hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas, then renewables/hybrids and hydrogen ICE, with efficient diesel as a fallback, while noting most fleets will need multiple technology choices over a decades-long transition.
The 2024 Fleet Fuel Study analyzed data from 14 fleets showing MPG increases tied to investment in fuel-efficiency technologies.
The first Run on Less (2017) featured seven fleets averaging 10 MPG in long-haul routes; Run on Less Regional (2019) featured 10 fleets averaging 8.4 MPG in regional-haul routes.
data_available: Present/Messy-Middle/2050-Future powertrain technology roadmap graphic (Figure 1)
Factors-to-consider decision matrix spanning fleet size, duty cycle, regulation, energy pricing, and infrastructure (Figure 2)
Sequential powertrain decision-framework flowchart (Figure 3)

title: Technology Overview: Speed Limiters
abstract: A Trucking Efficiency (joint NACFE/Carbon War Room) Technology Overview, published August 2014, on speed limiters for Class 8 tractor-trailers. As the first step in NACFE's Confidence Report process, it summarizes readily available information on setting maximum road-speed engine parameters to reduce fuel consumption, covering fuel-economy and tire-wear effects, existing international and Canadian provincial speed-limiter mandates, US real-world fleet adoption, safety considerations, and the regulatory landscape, with a call for sponsorship funding to support a full Confidence Report on the topic.
key_findings: An estimated 90% of new over-the-road tractors were being ordered with speed-limiting capability at the time of publication, though this figure was not independently surveyed.
Four major US fleets reported no significant productivity loss on 98% of freight shipments after limiting truck speeds, with affected shipments differing by only minutes per day.

Per ATA's Technology & Maintenance Council, fuel consumption drops on average 0.1 MPG for every 1 MPH speed increase above 55 MPH, meaning the difference between 55 and 65 MPH can be up to a full 1 MPG.
Tire tread life decreases by about 1% for every 1 MPH driven above 55 MPH on average.

The European Union has limited heavy truck/bus speeds to 62 MPH since 1994 and Australia to 62 MPH since 1990 (56 MPH for road trains); Japan limits trucks to 56 MPH and Quebec/Ontario, Canada limit them to 65 MPH.
data_available: Power required to overcome rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag by speed, 45-65 MPH (bar chart, page 2, Source: USDOE)
List of NACFE technical advisory group/sponsor fleets and companies (page 4)

title: Ep. 127: Mark Willis – Road Dog Trucking News
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Mark Willis, host of Road Dog Trucking News on SiriusXM Channel 146, about his background in hard news radio and how he built the trucking talk show since its 2004 launch under Sirius. Willis discusses the biggest trucking stories heading into 2026, especially a federal crackdown on non-domiciled CDL holders following high-profile fatal crashes, along with the cyclical economics of trucking and the current prolonged freight recession. The conversation also covers what makes a good radio interview and how the industry's public image shifted, briefly, during the COVID pandemic.
key_findings: Willis has hosted Road Dog Trucking News on SiriusXM Channel 146 since 2004 (launched under Sirius before the XM merger), after a prior career as a longtime ABC Radio news director and Kansas City radio general manager.

Willis highlights the Department of Transportation and FMCSA's active enforcement push against non-domiciled CDL holders as one of the most urgent trucking stories heading into 2026, tied to high-profile fatal crashes in Florida and California that drew attention up to the presidential level.
He describes the current freight downturn as an unusually prolonged cyclical recession, noting that trailer manufacturing revenue in particular can swing 30-40% between high and low freight periods.
data_available: Willis's career background in hard news radio prior to trucking talk radio
Discussion of the non-domiciled CDL enforcement issue and other top trucking stories for 2025-26
Willis's perspective on interview craft and storytelling for a driver-focused audience

title: Ep 70: Michelle Buffington – California Air Resources Board
abstract: Michelle Buffington, a vehicle program specialist at the California Air Resources Board, discusses CARB's $25 million Zero and Near-Zero Emission Freight Facilities (ZANZFF) solicitation and its showcase result, the Frito-Lay Modesto project, alongside CARB's dual role funding demonstration projects and writing the regulations that drive the broader zero-emission transition. She explains why California's air quality crisis (linked to car culture and the state's ports handling roughly 70% of US-bound imports) made it a first-mover on vehicle regulation, and closes with advice for fleets to attend ride-and-drive events and start utility conversations early.
key_findings: The CARB-funded Frito-Lay Modesto project deployed six Peterbilt 220 electric trucks, three BYD electric yard trucks, 12 Crown electric forklifts, and 34 Volvo VNL low-NOx CNG tractors, along with a renewable natural gas fueling station and a 1-megawatt solar carport with energy storage; by the time of the interview all 15 Tesla Semis on site were also delivering product
Buffington reports the Modesto site was measured at 91% lower greenhouse gas emissions given the combined fleet and solar deployment

She states roughly 70% of goods entering the United States arrive through California's ports, a factor she cites as central to why California's freight-related air quality and regulatory push emerged earlier and more aggressively than in other states
data_available: Detailed vehicle counts and technology mix for the Frito-Lay Modesto ZANZFF-funded project; CARB program funding figures; California import/port statistics

title: Ep. 7: Dr. Andrew Brown, Jr. – National Academy of Engineering, Delphi Corporation (ret.)
abstract: Dr. Andrew Brown Jr., former VP and Chief Technologist at Delphi Automotive Systems and a National Academy of Engineering member, explains the role of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) in advising Congress and federal agencies, and walks through the two NASEM committees he served on regarding medium- and heavy-duty vehicle fuel efficiency. The 2010 "phase one" report and a subsequent "phase two" report (produced roughly 2014-2018) were mandated by the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007, which for the first time required DOT to set fuel consumption standards for medium- and heavy-duty vehicles. Brown describes having to educate Congress and White House committees on the sheer diversity of truck body types and configurations (since a large share of a vehicle's price often comes from a separate body-builder rather than the chassis OEM), and recommends the government's regulations be re-evaluated using real-world data around 2020-2022, including how they account for electric trucks.
key_findings: Medium- and heavy-duty vehicles account for approximately 22% of US transportation energy consumption, a figure not subject to fuel economy standards until the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 first mandated them.

Brown recounts having to testify before three White House committees to explain that a single 'fuel economy' metric (like light-duty mpg) doesn't work for the highly diverse medium- and heavy-duty truck market, where a large share of a vehicle's price and configuration often comes from a separate body-builder rather than the chassis manufacturer.

The committee's report recommended an interim evaluation of the medium- and heavy-duty vehicle greenhouse gas regulations around 2020-2022 to assess real-world effectiveness ahead of any standards beyond the 'phase two' rule.
Brown notes the EPA and NHTSA's greenhouse gas phase two rule (finalized around 2014-2015) built in provisions for electric trucks and other advanced technologies earlier than many expected.
data_available: Explanation of the NASEM medium/heavy-duty vehicle fuel efficiency report process and legislative mandate
Regulatory history and recommendations from the phase one (2010) and phase two NASEM reports
Background on how medium/heavy-duty vehicle regulations account for diverse body types and technologies

title: Ep. 135: Steve Mignardi – NACFE Board Chairman
abstract: Steve Mignardi, a 37-year Daimler Truck/Freightliner veteran now serving as NACFE's board chairman, recounts his career path from truck technician to Freightliner's first international expatriate in Mexico during the 1990s to national accounts and market development roles managing major fleet customer councils. He reflects on trucking's boom-bust cyclicality and what resilience means in the industry, and discusses his priorities as NACFE board chair, including the cost of new efficiency technology and the fragmented nature of the trucking industry.
key_findings: Mignardi was Freightliner's first international expatriate, sent to Mexico around the signing of NAFTA; he navigated the 1994-95 peso crisis (peso devaluation from roughly 3 to 10 pesos per dollar, inflation around 52%, lending rates near 100%) that forced a roughly 12-month plant shutdown before the plant restarted building trucks for export.

As Freightliner's director of national accounts managing major fleet customers including Schneider National during the 2008-09 Great Recession, his small team generated the highest revenue-per-employee of any Daimler business unit globally.

He identifies NACFE's biggest board-level challenges as the cost of emerging efficiency technology, navigating a shifting regulatory landscape, and the fragmentation of the trucking industry across single operators, small fleets, and mega-fleets.
data_available: Personal career narrative
Historical anecdote about the 1994-95 Mexican peso crisis
