Qualitative reflection on NACFE board priorities; no quantitative fleet or technology performance data

title: Ep. 33: Ade Thomas – green.tv media
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Ade Thomas, founder of green.tv media and organizer of World EV Day, the EV Summit, and the EV Bike Summit, about what he calls building the 'ideas infrastructure' for zero-emission transport through creative storytelling and campaigns. The two discuss the accelerating pace of the EV transition (including the UK's newly announced 2040/2030 zero-emission vehicle targets for trucks/vans and cars), the driver experience of electric trucks emerging from NACFE's Run on Less Electric event, and the rapid growth of investment in charging infrastructure, including smart/managed charging.
key_findings: During the episode, the UK government announced a transport decarbonization strategy targeting zero-emission vans and trucks by 2040 and zero-emission cars by 2030, and Thomas cites roughly one in four new UK vehicle sales already having a plug.

Roeth relays an anecdote from NACFE's Run on Less Electric (13 fleets, 13 truck OEMs) in which an Anheuser-Busch driver in Los Angeles said the quieter electric truck made him feel safer because he could hear an approaching ambulance.
data_available: Description of green.tv media's campaigns (World EV Day, EV Love) and Thomas's 'ideas infrastructure' framing for driving zero-emission transport adoption
UK policy details on 2030/2040 zero-emission vehicle sales targets as of mid-2021
Anecdotal driver feedback from NACFE's Run on Less Electric event

title: Ep. 76: Jason Cannon – CCJ
abstract: Jason Cannon, editor in chief of Commercial Carrier Journal (CCJ), discusses his path from small-town newspaper journalism into trucking media, CCJ's 112-year history (founded 1911, which would make it the industry's second-oldest 'truck manufacturer' if it were one), and a striking historical footnote: CCJ conceived of a fleet efficiency competition in its March 1911 issue that was never executed but presaged NACFE's Run on Less by over a century. He characterizes the industry's current multi-technology period as an early 'realization stage' of transformation rather than a mature one, and describes his approach to objectively vetting OEM and startup performance claims (including through his own CDL-based test drives).
key_findings: CCJ was founded in 1911, making it roughly as old as the commercial trucking industry itself; Cannon notes an idea for an industry efficiency competition appeared in CCJ's March 15, 1911 issue with a $1,000 prize but was never actually run, an idea Mike Roeth says helped inspire Run on Less in 2017

Cannon holds a Class A CDL and personally test-drives new trucks (including autonomous and electric platforms) for CCJ's coverage, citing a real-world electric truck example where he used double a truck's expected range for a given distance and would print the OEM's explanation for readers

He frames the industry as being in an early 'realization stage' of transformation with no dominant winning technology yet -- with renewable diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, battery-electric, and autonomy each fitting different fleets and duty cycles -- and advises the audience to keep an open mind rather than assume there is one universal answer
data_available: Historical/anecdotal company and industry narrative; description of first-hand test-drive methodology; no quantitative data set

title: Ep. 24: Michael Berube – US Department of Energy
abstract: Michael Berube, acting deputy assistant secretary for sustainable transportation at the US Department of Energy, explains DOE's role as the federal government's lead physical-sciences R&D organization for transportation, spanning 17 national labs, and its co-funding model with industry. He discusses the SuperTruck 1 and 2 programs' success in roughly halving long-haul diesel truck fuel use, DOE's decade-long track record of hitting annual battery cost targets, and the agency's priorities for scaling battery electric trucks.
key_findings: DOE's SuperTruck program (spanning roughly 8-9 years across two phases) aimed to cut the fuel used to move long-haul freight in half, and Berube says that goal has essentially been achieved: new trucks today use about half the fuel of trucks from roughly a decade earlier.

DOE has set annual battery cost targets for over 10 years and has hit every one, with current projections pointing to batteries plus other EV components reaching cost parity with internal combustion in light-duty vehicles around 2028-2030.
DOE typically funds early-stage R&D at roughly an 80% government/20% industry cost share, shifting toward roughly 50/50 as projects move toward demonstration and deployment.

SuperTruck-driven lightweighting research hasn't yet widely reached production trucks because most trucks aren't regularly loaded to their weight limit ("grossed out"), though Berube expects weight to matter more as fleets add freight and as electric powertrains add battery weight.

For electric trucks to scale, Berube identifies three priorities: higher battery energy density, batteries capable of high-power fast charging, and building a domestic US battery supply chain from raw materials through manufacturing.
data_available: SuperTruck program fuel-savings outcome (roughly 50% fuel-use reduction)
DOE cost-share funding ratios by project stage
Battery cost-parity timeline projection (2028-2030)
Description of DOE annual merit review process

title: Ep. 105: Ryan Bankerd – UPS and NACFE board member
abstract: Ryan Bankerd, Global Director of Automotive Sustainability at UPS and a NACFE board member, talks with Mike Roeth about UPS's century-long "rolling laboratory" tradition of testing alternative-fuel vehicles, its current renewable natural gas and DOE wireless megawatt-charging projects, and his own path from loading UPS trucks to leading its sustainability engineering work. He argues efficiency "needs a better publicist" than flashier zero-emission technologies.
key_findings: UPS deployed its first electric delivery vehicles in 1934 (10 each in Los Angeles and New York), and Bankerd describes the company's "rolling laboratory" tradition of testing alternative-fuel vehicles as dating back nearly a century, driven by a dedicated in-house automotive engineering department established by founding father Charlie Soderstrom.

UPS is working with the U.S. Department of Energy on a wireless megawatt-charging pilot for a tractor currently operating in Utah, and has moved to its fifth generation of natural gas engines (the Cummins 15-liter), building on roughly 30 years of natural gas engine experimentation through CARB/DOE partnerships.

Bankerd calls renewable natural gas (RNG) one of UPS's most impactful current decarbonization strategies given its "circular economy" sourcing from captured biomass/agricultural methane, and highlights that UPS's CNG tractors now exceed 6 miles per gallon, a figure once considered a major efficiency milestone for diesel trucks generally.
data_available: History of UPS's "rolling laboratory" alternative-fuel program since 1934
Details of UPS's current DOE wireless megawatt-charging pilot and fifth-generation natural gas engine deployment
Bankerd's career path from loading UPS trucks to leading automotive sustainability, and UPS's role on the NACFE board

title: Ep. 15: Kyle Treadway – Kenworth Sales Company
abstract: Kyle Treadway, third-generation dealer principal of Kenworth Sales Company (founded by his grandparents in 1945) and former chairman of the American Truck Dealers (ATD) board, discusses the role truck dealers play as a "hub" connecting manufacturers, fleets, and suppliers -- covering new/used sales, parts, service, finance, insurance, and leasing. He describes his company's growth from 23 locations across seven western states to 31 locations across 10 states after acquiring Mid-Atlantic dealerships, and discusses the industry's technician shortage (roughly $150,000 and five years to fully train a journeyman technician). He gives his frank, dealer's-eye assessment of alternative technologies: natural gas trucks largely collapsed as a long-haul option after the 2009 fuel-price crash; battery electric trucks remain a niche fit for closed-loop, last-mile, or local delivery routes given current battery weight, range, and charging limitations; ADAS features (automated transmissions, lane departure warning, adaptive cruise) are being readily accepted; and hydrogen shows technical promise but isn't yet cost-competitive.
key_findings: Kenworth Sales Company grew from 23 locations in seven western states to 31 locations across 10 states (1,300 employees) after acquiring eight Mid-Atlantic dealerships.
Fully training a journeyman technician to handle modern electronics and alternative powertrains costs the dealership roughly $150,000 and takes about five years.
Treadway says natural gas trucks 'pretty much collapsed' for long-haul use after the 2009 fuel price and economic crash made the up-front cost hard to justify.

Treadway is skeptical that battery electric trucks will fit long-haul applications given current battery weight, range, and charging-time limitations, describing electrification as fitting a closed-loop or last-mile delivery niche rather than being a 'silver bullet.'

About half of the dealership's customer service appointments are not kept by customers on their own, which Treadway says is a key obstacle to realizing the benefits of AI-based predictive maintenance scheduling.
data_available: Kenworth Sales Company footprint and growth figures (locations, states, employee count)
Dealer's perspective and cost data on technician training
Dealer-level assessment of natural gas, battery electric, hydrogen, and automated safety technology adoption

title: Ep 48: Britta Gross –RMI
abstract: Britta Gross, managing director of RMI's carbon-free mobility work and a former GM electric-vehicle and hydrogen fuel-cell program executive, recounts the history of GM's 1990s EV1, the 2006-07 development of the plug-in hybrid Chevy Volt, and the industry's later shift toward pure battery-electric vehicles as batteries improved and consumers struggled to understand plug-in hybrids. She discusses RMI's focus on 2030 as a near-term decision point on the path to 2050 net-zero goals, the charging-infrastructure and grid-readiness barriers to large-scale EV adoption, and how these dynamics extend to trucking, where she sees a role for hydrogen in longer-haul, heavier-duty applications alongside battery-electric for shorter, more localized routes.
key_findings: Gross says GM discontinued the plug-in hybrid Chevy Volt in part because a pure battery-electric powertrain is simpler to design, build, and maintain than a dual gas/electric system, and because consumers struggled to understand what a plug-in hybrid was.

She describes RMI's rationale for focusing on 2030 (rather than more distant 2040/2050 targets) as reflecting that vehicle technology programs and infrastructure investment take multiple years to execute, so emissions-reduction decisions have to be made now to hit later targets.

Gross identifies charging speeds up to 350 kW as the target for public fast-charging of light-duty vehicles (aiming for roughly 15-minute top-offs), and notes trucking is discussing megawatt-scale charging.

She frames electric-vehicle charging load as unusually flexible compared to past grid-load additions (kitchen appliances in the 1950s, air conditioning in the 1960s-70s), since most charging can happen overnight without urgency, which utilities can leverage without over-building generation capacity.

For heavy trucking, Gross suggests hydrogen may suit longer-range, heavier-duty applications given its refueling speed and range advantages, while battery-electric suits shorter, more localized routes, and expects trucking will not settle on 'a homogeneous battery solution' across the sector.
data_available: First-person industry history of GM's EV1 and Chevy Volt programs
Discussion of charging infrastructure barriers (residential/workplace/public, permitting, grid capacity)
High-level comparative framing of battery-electric vs. hydrogen fit across trucking duty cycles

title: Ep 63: Erik Neandross – Gladstein, Neandross & Associates
abstract: Erik Neandross, CEO of Gladstein, Neandross & Associates (GNA) and a co-founder of ACT Expo, traces GNA's history from its 1993 founding (as G&A) focused on stationary-source air quality, through its pivot toward natural gas trucking infrastructure corridors in the late 1990s (including the first-ever commercial natural gas truck deployment, 12 trucks at Harris Ranch in 1999), to its current work advising major fleets and OEMs on the shift to zero-emission transportation. He frames today's market around three drivers -- massive capital investment, corporate sustainability/net-zero commitments, and a regulatory backstop led by California's Advanced Clean Trucks and Advanced Clean Fleets rules -- and argues total cost of ownership remains the ultimate gating factor for adoption.
key_findings: GNA (originally G&A) was founded by Cliff Gladstone in June 1993 focused on stationary-source air quality; Neandross joined in 1999 as the firm pivoted toward natural gas truck infrastructure corridors such as the Interstate Clean Transportation Corridor (I-5/I-80/I-15)
Harris Ranch deployed the first-ever commercial natural gas trucks (12 vehicles) in 1999 with a supporting fueling station in Central California, built largely with government support

Neandross estimates over $500 billion in total investment now flowing into commercial zero-emission trucking from traditional OEMs, startups, and government programs (IIJA and IRA), contrasting it with the $300 million DOE Recovery Act allocation that helped launch ACT Expo in 2011; he cites an estimated $42 billion in California LCFS credit trades in 2020 alone

As of the interview, California utilities PG&E, SDG&E, and SCE had committed over $700 million combined toward electrification infrastructure, with other utilities like Xcel Energy and Duke starting similar commitments

Neandross frames zero-emission truck adoption as gated by three forces: capital investment, corporate net-zero-by-2040-type commitments, and regulatory backstops such as California's Advanced Clean Trucks rule (already adopted by Oregon, Washington, New York, New Jersey, and Massachusetts) and the forthcoming Advanced Clean Fleets rule
data_available: GNA's company history and Neandross's career background in alternative-fuel trucking policy and infrastructure
Detailed investment/regulatory landscape figures for zero-emission trucking circa 2022 (OEM/startup capital, LCFS credit market, utility infrastructure commitments)
History of early natural gas truck corridor deployments (Harris Ranch, ICTC)

title: Ep. 133: Tom Lincoln – Dana
abstract: Tom Lincoln, Dana's national sales and service manager, discusses Dana's 127-year history as inventor of the universal joint (Clarence Spicer, 1904) and the company's Dana Fleet Council program for gathering direct fleet feedback. He covers the downspeeding trend that has pushed rear axle ratios down (increasing driveline torque loads), Dana's extended-drain axle lubricants, why terminal tractors are a strong near-term battery-electric application, and regional-haul axle ratio trends.
key_findings: Dana's namesake technology, the universal joint patented by Clarence Spicer in 1904, replaced exposed chain-and-sprocket drives and established the foundation of the modern driveshaft and drive axle.

Common on-highway final drive ratios have fallen from about 3.55 fourteen years ago to as low as 2.16 with some vertically integrated OEM powertrains today, roughly doubling driveshaft torque and requiring components engineered for both higher peak strength and longer fatigue life.

Dana's XFE 75W-85 synthetic axle lubricant supports a 500,000-mile drain interval; the company is field-testing a next-generation XFE 75W-80 lube that keeps the same interval while adding up to 1 mpg of vehicle-level fuel efficiency.

Terminal tractors are highlighted as a strong current battery-electric use case due to predictable routes, return-to-base operation, and manageable battery weight/packaging, plus the added benefit of being usable inside warehouses without exhaust emissions.
Lincoln estimates that a recent roughly $1.70/gallon jump in diesel price equates to about $20,000 per truck per year in added fuel cost for a 100,000 mile/year, 7 mpg Class 8 truck.
data_available: Historical and current axle ratio figures
Lubricant drain-interval and fuel-economy specifications
Fuel-cost calculation example
Qualitative discussion of BEV terminal tractor fit

title: Ep 41: Rob Ulsh – Great Dane
abstract: Rob Ulsh, VP of dealer and international sales at Great Dane Trailers, discusses the company's 120-year history and product lines (dry van, refrigerated, and flatbed trailers, plus truck bodies), and argues trailers are far more than 'a box on wheels,' citing Great Dane's role delivering the first COVID-19 vaccines. He describes the company's FleetPulse telematics platform (tire pressure monitoring, light-out alerts, weight reporting, GPS), widespread fleet adoption of aerodynamic devices (skirts, tails, tire inflation systems) even after a federal greenhouse gas trailer rule was struck down, and speculates about future roles for trailers in electrification, including adding range to tractors or feeding energy back to the grid.
key_findings: Great Dane's FleetPulse telematics platform, standard on its trailers, provides tire-pressure monitoring, light-out notifications, weight reporting, and GPS tracking to help fleets locate trailers and avoid maintenance issues.

Ulsh says most Great Dane customers had already adopted aerodynamic devices (skirts, tails, inflation systems) to meet prior greenhouse-gas regulations, and continued doing so even after a federal trailer GHG rule was struck down, because fleets recognize the fuel-savings value independent of regulation.

Great Dane partnered with Aurora to expand its aftermarket parts distribution footprint from one to three parts-distribution centers (PDCs), with plans to reach five within a couple of years, to support new trailer technology.

Ulsh describes early-stage internal projects exploring trailer-mounted regenerative braking/battery storage that could add driving range to a tractor or feed energy back to the grid, describing the idea as still 'embryonic.'
data_available: Company/product history for a major trailer manufacturer
Description of the FleetPulse trailer telematics platform
Discussion of aerodynamic device adoption following a GHG-rule reversal
Speculative discussion of trailer-based battery/regenerative technology

title: Ep. 83: Marie Brougham – Sacramento Municipal Utility District
abstract: Marie Brougham, manager of account management and sales at the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD), describes SMUD as a community-owned, not-for-profit utility (the sixth-largest such utility in the US) that has committed to being 100% carbon-free by 2030, ahead of California's statewide 2045 mandate, while serving about 1.5 million people. She discusses SMUD's role serving PepsiCo's 21-Tesla-Semi Sacramento depot, lessons learned about the multi-year infrastructure planning and mid-project routing changes involved, and the broader planning, load-flexibility, and trust-building challenges utilities face as fleets electrify.
key_findings: SMUD's energy mix is about 49% carbon-free, made up of roughly 24% renewables (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal) and about 25% large hydro, with a board-set goal of reaching 100% carbon-free by 2030, five years ahead of California's statewide 2045 requirement.

SMUD served PepsiCo's Sacramento depot with 21 Tesla Semis; the multi-year interconnection project (started around 2018-2019, delayed by the pandemic) required a mid-project change from a north-side to a south-side service feed for better redundancy, illustrating the value of ongoing utility-fleet communication.

Brougham frames electric truck charging as fundamentally requiring 'load flexibility' planning because fleet charging needs vary widely, from a fleet that can slow-charge overnight for 100 daily miles to one needing fast charging within a 45-minute dwell time for 300 daily miles.
data_available: SMUD's energy mix, carbon-free timeline, and governance structure as a community-owned municipal utility
Case study of SMUD's multi-year interconnection project serving PepsiCo's 21-Tesla-Semi Sacramento depot
Discussion of utility load-flexibility planning challenges as fleets electrify

title: Ep. 79: Brady Matoian – OK Produce
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Brady Matoian, CEO of OK Produce, a California wholesale produce company founded by his grandfather in 1950, about the fleet's early and ongoing push into battery electric trucks. Matoian describes a personal, decades-long commitment to sustainability (starting with an early large-scale solar installation around 2000-2001) and walks through OK Produce's staged rollout of electric trucks: starting with short, low-risk growing-region runs and progressively extending routes as confidence grew, including a successful stretch run to Stockton using an opportunity charge. He also discusses fleet-side observations that electric trucks handle stop-and-start routes better than diesel due to regenerative braking, and that OK Produce (a Run on Less Electric Depot participant) plans to keep scaling its electric fleet despite real cost and range challenges.
key_findings: OK Produce operates 10 Freightliner eCascadias and 3 Orange EVs on site, with 7 additional Volvo electric trucks expected in fall 2023.
Trucks are plugged in around 9:00-9:10 p.m. and charge in roughly 3 to 5 hours, then depart on routes around 3-4 a.m.
On a stretch run to Stockton, a truck used a 20-30 minute opportunity charge in Turlock and arrived home with 20% state of charge remaining.
OK Produce's sustainability program dates to around 2000-2001, starting with a solar installation the company was told was the largest in the western 13 states at the time.
Drivers and fleet leadership observed that electric trucks handle stop-heavy routes better than diesel because of regenerative braking, extending effective range when driven conservatively.
data_available: Fleet composition and charging schedule details for a produce-hauling battery electric deployment
First-hand account of progressively extending electric truck routes and using opportunity charging
Driver behavior and regenerative-braking observations specific to a stop-heavy regional duty cycle

title: Ep. 71: Eric Starks – FTR
abstract: Eric Starks, chairman and senior consultant at FTR (Freight Transportation Research), explains FTR's freight-forecasting business, built around a 'freightcast' model covering roughly 209 commodity groups and more than 80,000 forecasted variables, and how the firm blends model output with subject-matter-expert judgment. He discusses how the pandemic-driven e-commerce/omnichannel shift permanently altered fleets' tractor-to-trailer ratio, and gives FTR's outlook for Class 8 and trailer production through 2023-2026, including then-record order backlogs.
key_findings: FTR's freightcast model forecasts roughly 209 commodity groups with data history back to 1992, using more than 80,000 forecasted variables updated monthly

Starks says the pandemic-driven shift to e-commerce/omnichannel retail caused a lasting change in the tractor-to-trailer ratio, as fleets added preloaded trailers to keep drivers moving rather than waiting on loads

As of early 2023, Class 8 and trailer order backlogs stood at roughly nine months versus a normal four-to-six-month range, with production expected to stay strong through the first half of 2023 before easing, 2024 softening toward replacement-demand levels, and growth resuming around 2025-2026
data_available: FTR's freight/truck-production forecasting methodology
Data-grounded 2023-2026 outlook for Class 8 tractor and trailer production and order backlogs

title: Ep. 27: Greg Hintler – The Mobility House
abstract: Greg Hintler, managing director of The Mobility House USA, discusses his path from climate-driven early career work (including noticing that US transportation emissions had surpassed power-sector emissions by 2016-2017) into EV charging infrastructure, and describes the company's ChargePilot software for cost-efficient fleet charging management. He explains the distinction between V1G (unidirectional managed charging) and V2G (bidirectional vehicle-to-grid) technology, citing a real-world V2G deployment, and offers five recommendations for fleets planning charging infrastructure.
key_findings: Hintler traces part of his path into EV charging work to noticing that, by 2016-2017, US transportation-sector greenhouse gas emissions had surpassed power-sector emissions.
The Mobility House's ChargePilot software manages cost-efficient EV charging at over 300 sites globally, including the largest transit fleet in the St. Louis metro area.

He distinguishes V1G (unidirectional managed/time-of-use charging, which Mobility House deploys today) from V2G (bidirectional vehicle-to-grid discharge), citing a real-world V2G deployment on the island of Porto Santo that discharges vehicle batteries to help stabilize the local grid when renewable generation dips.

His five-point advice for fleets: plan charging infrastructure early, choose interoperable technology, keep optimizing charging after initial deployment, consider alternative ownership models if upfront cost is a barrier, and build infrastructure decisions with future scale and potential V2G participation in mind.
data_available: ChargePilot deployment scale (300+ sites, largest St. Louis transit fleet)
Porto Santo island V2G case example
Five-point fleet planning recommendation list

title: Ep. 92: John Hroncich – BAE Systems
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews John Hroncich, director of North American transit sales at BAE Systems, about how the transit bus market has served as an early proving ground for electrification and alternative fuels ahead of trucking. Hroncich traces transit's progression from CNG through hybrids (including geofenced part-time-electric buses) to full battery electric and, more recently, hydrogen fuel cell buses, aided by federal funding programs like the FTA's Low-No Emission program. He also discusses BAE's modular, powertrain-agnostic propulsion architecture and the company's formal and continuous voice-of-customer process, including a NACFE/BAE Systems/Eaton voice-of-customer event on a simplified battery-electric truck held in Marshall, Michigan.
key_findings: BAE Systems has delivered over 18,000 electric propulsion systems into service, primarily in transit buses, and is expanding into truck, military, and maritime applications.

Transit CNG adoption took hold in pockets (Southern California, Pennsylvania, Texas) roughly 15-20 years ago but has since flattened out, followed by hybrid and now battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell buses.

BAE reports fuel cell transit bus numbers have doubled year-over-year for the past three years, aided by FTA Low-No Emission program funding and new hydrogen hub investments including a California hydrogen hub announcement.
BAE's geofencing capability lets a hybrid bus operate as a part-time electric bus, shutting off its engine within fleet-designated zero-emission zones.
NACFE partnered with BAE Systems and Eaton on a voice-of-customer study for a simplified battery-electric truck, convening fleets, OEMs, and media over three separate days in Marshall, Michigan.
data_available: Chronology of transit bus alternative-fuel adoption (CNG, hybrid, battery electric, hydrogen fuel cell) over roughly two decades
Description of BAE's modular, powertrain-agnostic propulsion architecture
Discussion of formal voice-of-customer product development practices, including the NACFE/BAE/Eaton battery-electric truck study

title: Ep. 3: Jennifer Rumsey – Cummins Inc.
abstract: Jennifer Rumsey, President of Components at Cummins Inc. (and later Cummins CEO), discusses her 21-year career at Cummins -- including four years as Chief Technical Officer -- and the company's evolution from "Cummins Engine Company" to "Cummins Inc." as it expanded beyond diesel into electrified and hydrogen powertrains, including Cummins' 2017 demonstration of the industry's first fully electric semi truck and its New Power business unit. The bulk of the conversation centers on a Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM) high school math modeling competition on the topic of converting a diesel truck to electric, which NACFE helped design; Rumsey's own daughter's team from Columbus North High School (Columbus, Indiana, Cummins' headquarters city) was one of six national finalists among over 760 teams. Rumsey also discusses Cummins' Planet 2050 sustainability plan and the broadening mix of engineering disciplines (electrical, chemical, materials) the company now needs.
key_findings: Cummins demonstrated the industry's first fully electric semi truck in August 2017 and later formed its New Power business unit to commercialize battery, hybrid, and fuel cell technologies.

Cummins partnered with NACFE and SIAM on a national high school math modeling competition themed around converting a diesel truck to electric; over 760 teams participated, and a team from Columbus North High School (including Rumsey's daughter) was one of six national finalists.
Cummins' Planet 2050 environmental sustainability plan incorporates science-based targets covering product CO2 emissions as well as facility water, waste, and energy use.
data_available: Cummins' 2017 electric semi truck demonstration and New Power business unit formation
Details of the NACFE/SIAM/Cummins high school math modeling competition on electric truck conversion
Overview of Cummins' Planet 2050 sustainability plan

title: Ep. 53: Jennifer Wheeler – NACFE
abstract: Jennifer Wheeler, senior program manager at NACFE and an 18-year veteran of Walmart's private fleet (in dispatch operations, delivery-scheduling analytics, and later sustainable transportation/electrification), discusses her Walmart career, including work on demand planning for peak events like Black Friday and Walmart's push, announced by CEO Lee Scott in 2005, to double private-fleet efficiency over 10 years. She then discusses leading NACFE's 2022 report on Class 3-6 electric vans and step vans, noting that segment's roughly 4.1-4.2 million vehicles represent about half of on-road commercial vehicles in the US and Canada, and describes the patience, duty-cycle analysis, and fleet-to-fleet collaboration she sees as necessary to scale electrification into heavier-duty, longer-haul segments.
key_findings: Wheeler says Walmart's private fleet doubled its overall efficiency over roughly a decade after CEO Lee Scott set the goal in 2005, achieved through a combination of dispatching optimization, on-truck technology, and new-technology investment rather than any single solution.

NACFE's Class 3-6 electric van/step van report found there are about 4.1-4.2 million vans and step vans on the road in the US and Canada (roughly half of all commercial vehicles), and that electrifying the segment would avoid an estimated 43.5 million metric tons of CO2 per year.

Wheeler notes vans and step vans are a strong near-term electrification fit because typical duty cycles and range requirements match current battery technology without complex charging-infrastructure needs.

She recommends fleets identify a specific 'lane' or location with predictable return-to-base routing to pilot electric vehicles without the 'dispatching gymnastics' of a broader network rollout, then expand from those pilot findings into fleet-wide strategy.

Wheeler argues that scaling electrification into heavy-duty long-haul Class 8 will require more patience and creative solutions given over-the-road charging and weight constraints, and encourages fleets to share 'behind the fence' charging infrastructure with each other in lieu of relying solely on public charging.
data_available: NACFE Class 3-6 electric van/step van market-sizing and emissions-avoidance figures
Practitioner's account of Walmart's private-fleet efficiency-doubling program
Practical guidance for piloting electric vehicles via lane-level duty-cycle analysis

title: Ep. 132: Derek Turbide – Greenlane
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Derek Turbide, newly appointed Senior Vice President of Sales at Greenlane, about his move after nearly 20 years at Clean Energy Fuels into heavy-duty battery-electric truck charging. Turbide describes Greenlane's flagship Colton, California charging hub on the I-10/215 corridor and the company's near-term expansion plans along major freight corridors, and discusses how lessons from two decades in natural gas fueling infrastructure apply to building out electric charging networks. The two also discuss driver reception of battery-electric trucks based on NACFE's Run on Less driver interviews.
key_findings: Greenlane's Colton, California site, located on the I-10/215 freight corridor between Los Angeles, Arizona, and Las Vegas, has a dozen tractor-trailer-accessible fast-charging lanes at 400 kilowatts and nearly 30 bobtail/tractor-only parking stalls with 240-kilowatt chargers.

Greenlane's near-term (roughly five-year) expansion plans include a Phoenix and Blythe lane, routes up the I-5 over the Grapevine and up the I-15, and a Texas Triangle corridor connecting Dallas, Houston, and eventually San Antonio, targeting about 10 new Greenlane sites.

NACFE has interviewed 60-70 electric truck drivers across its last three Run on Less demonstrations over roughly five years, and both Turbide and Roeth note drivers have generally been enthusiastic advocates for the trucks rather than resistant to the technology.
data_available: Turbide's nearly 20-year career at Clean Energy Fuels in natural gas/RNG trucking before joining Greenlane
Specifications and location of Greenlane's Colton, California charging hub
Greenlane's near-term site expansion roadmap along major freight corridors

title: Ep. 123: Don Baldwin – Retired from Michelin
abstract: Don Baldwin, retired from Michelin and one of NACFE's founding participants, recounts NACFE's origin at an April 2009 Rocky Mountain Institute "charrette," convened as diesel prices were spiking past $4-5 a gallon, and discusses how Michelin's earlier Challenge Bibendum clean-transportation demonstration event shaped NACFE's technology-agnostic, non-promotional model. He and Roeth reflect on NACFE's early fundraising principles (declining sponsorship deals that required logo placement), the difficulty of getting engineers to prioritize weight/fuel savings versus cost, and Baldwin's advice on maintaining passion and guiding principles through a career and into retirement.
key_findings: NACFE originated from an April 2009 charrette (workshop) convened by Rocky Mountain Institute with Amory Lovins; diesel fuel prices crossing $5/gallon in late 2008 was cited as a key catalyst for the effort.

Michelin's earlier Challenge Bibendum program (2001 and 2003), which Baldwin helped run, was a technology-agnostic clean-transportation demonstration event featuring over 100 vehicles across hydrogen fuel cell, electric, and other technologies, and directly influenced NACFE's own non-promotional, technology-agnostic structure.
NACFE deliberately declined sponsorship funding that required donor logo placement on its materials in its early years, prioritizing independence and credibility over fundraising ease.

Of three original goals set at the 2009 charrette (create a technology information clearinghouse, demonstrate technologies are real-world viable, and a third unspecified goal), NACFE substantially achieved the first two through its confidence reports and Run on Less program.
data_available: Oral history interview on NACFE's founding and Michelin's Challenge Bibendum program
Discussion of NACFE's founding principles around independence and non-promotion
No quantitative study or report data presented

title: Ep. 87: Coralie Cooper – NESCAUM
abstract: Coralie Cooper, Deputy Director of NESCAUM (Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use Management, founded in 1967, predating the EPA), discusses the organization's role coordinating state air-pollution regulators across the Northeast on truck-related climate, ozone/particulate, and environmental-justice goals, including a DOE-funded study with National Grid on siting electric truck charging infrastructure along Northeast freight corridors. She also discusses her father, Nobel laureate physicist Leon Cooper (1972 Physics Prize for superconductivity theory), and her own path from witnessing air pollution's health effects in 1980s New York City into environmental advocacy, including early work on NRDC's 'Dump Dirty Diesel' bus advertising campaign.
key_findings: NESCAUM was founded in 1967, before the EPA existed, originally as a New England-states consortium on stationary air-pollution sources, later expanding in the 1970s to include New York and New Jersey and to cover mobile sources.

Cooper describes a NACFE-organized November White House roundtable on electric trucks that brought together representatives from 7 of the 10 Run on Less fleets, which she characterized as showing surprising breadth of understanding among fleets already navigating the electrification transition.

NESCAUM is working under a DOE grant with National Grid and other partners to project electricity demand and identify optimal siting locations for truck charging infrastructure along Northeast freight corridors.
data_available: NESCAUM's history and role coordinating state air-quality regulators on truck policy across the Northeast
Cooper's account of her father Leon Cooper's 1972 Nobel Prize in Physics and its influence on her analytical approach
Description of a DOE-funded Northeast Corridor truck-charging-infrastructure siting study

title: Ep. 90: Amory Lovins – RMI
abstract: Amory Lovins, co-founder and chairman emeritus of RMI, discusses the 15-year-old NACFE-founding charrette, his career-long focus on energy efficiency as a 'master key' for energy, security, environment, and economic puzzles (dating to before the 1973 Arab oil embargo), and RMI's 'integrative design' approach to whole-system optimization. He argues the efficiency resource available to trucking remains far larger and cheaper than commonly assumed, illustrates the point with examples from his own off-grid mountain house and his carbon-fiber BMW i3, and recounts a story of a large fleet operator reluctant to slow trucks down despite a doubling in diesel price, even though the potential savings were, by his calculation, substantial.
key_findings: RMI's 2008 paper argued Class 8 truck efficiency could be doubled or tripled without compromise; from 2005-2015 RMI helped Walmart roughly double the efficiency of its truck fleet.

Lovins estimates current best-in-class diesel powertrains can achieve a factor of 3-4 efficiency improvement versus an average fleet, and that the best electric powertrains achieve a factor of 3-6 improvement, aided by lighter weight and roughly 40% better aerodynamics, depending on test conditions.

He cites that the US now uses about 64% less total energy per dollar of GDP than it would have if efficiency had stayed at 1975 levels, and argues the efficiency resource has grown roughly twofold and become about a third cheaper than his 2011 'Reinventing Fire' estimates, due in part to 'integrative design' (optimizing whole systems, not individual components).
data_available: RMI's historical fuel-efficiency research on Class 8 trucks and its Walmart fleet-efficiency engagement (2005-2015)
Lovins' framework of 'integrative design' with illustrative examples (his passive-solar house, his carbon-fiber BMW i3, and fat/short/straight pipe design for pumps and fans)
Anecdote about a large fleet operator's reluctance to reduce truck speeds despite a calculated large fuel-cost saving during a diesel price spike

title: Ep. 44: Paul Rosa – Penske
abstract: Paul Rosa, senior VP of procurement and fleet planning at Penske, discusses how Penske's role spanning logistics, contract leasing, rental, and consumer businesses across Class 3-8 vehicles gives it a broad view of emerging powertrain and regulatory issues (CARB, ACF, ACT rules), and how customer conversations have shifted from 'should I buy diesel' to detailed total-cost-of-ownership and electrification planning. He describes Penske's participation in NACFE's Run on Less – Electric with a Daimler eCascadia tractor, driver enthusiasm for electric trucks, and the unresolved question of electric-truck residual values as a major unknown in current TCO models.
key_findings: Rosa says California's ACF and ACT rules are now driving detailed fleet-planning conversations at Penske because multi-year lease commitments must account for coming zero-emission-fleet percentage requirements.

Penske co-created and ran a Daimler eCascadia heavy-duty tractor in NACFE's Run on Less – Electric in Southern California, and Rosa says the event was 'perfect timing' for demonstrating that electric trucks could work in real-world applications across vehicle classes.

Rosa identifies electric-vehicle residual value three to six years out as a major unresolved variable in the ROI calculation, since battery/range technology is expected to change quickly and there is uncertainty around future replacement-battery availability for early-generation vehicles.

Interviews with drivers trialing Class 3-8 electric vehicles at Penske consistently surface power, cab quiet/comfort, reduced fatigue, and the absence of diesel smell as top-cited benefits, and drivers routinely ask when they can get a production unit instead of returning the prototype.
data_available: Executive perspective on how CARB/ACF/ACT regulations are reshaping fleet-planning conversations
Run on Less – Electric case study details for a Penske/Daimler eCascadia tractor
Discussion of residual-value uncertainty as an EV total-cost-of-ownership risk factor
Driver feedback themes from Penske's electric vehicle trials

title: Ep. 86: Amanda Devoe – PepsiCo
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Amanda Devoe, fleet strategy and transformation director at PepsiCo, about the company's large-scale, multi-pronged fleet decarbonization program spanning Frito-Lay snacks and Pepsi Beverages. Devoe details PepsiCo's four-part decarbonization framework (miles not driven, efficiency/aerodynamics, alternative fuels, then zero-emission assets), walks through specific electric deployments including E-Transit vans in Queens, NY and medium-duty box trucks in Modesto, CA, and gives an extensive update on PepsiCo's fleet of 36 Tesla Semis operating in Modesto and Sacramento, including charging infrastructure and real-world performance data from NACFE's Run on Less Electric Depot.
key_findings: PepsiCo operates one of North America's largest private fleets, with over 80,000 owned assets, roughly 36,000 of which are powered on-road fleet equipment.
PepsiCo deployed roughly 66 Ford E-Transit electric vans at its Queens, NY facility, operating 10-12 hours a day but under about 50 miles round trip per route.

PepsiCo runs a fleet of 36 Tesla Semis: 15 in Modesto for Frito-Lay regional long-haul work and 21 in Sacramento (18 for local Pepsi Beverages delivery, 3 for regional/long-haul), using 750-kilowatt chargers at the Sacramento site.
During NACFE's Run on Less Electric Depot, one PepsiCo Tesla Semi logged 1,076 miles in 24 hours with three to four charging events.
PepsiCo is the only fleet to have participated in all four of NACFE's Run on Less programs (2017, 2019, and the 2021 and 2023 battery electric runs).
data_available: PepsiCo's four-pronged decarbonization framework and how it maps to specific technology deployments
Detailed electric vehicle deployment data across Frito-Lay (medium-duty, Modesto/Queens) and Pepsi Beverages (Tesla Semi, Sacramento) operations
Charging infrastructure specifications (750 kW chargers) and real-world Tesla Semi mileage/charging-event data from Run on Less

title: Ep. 54: Sean Larkin – Amply Power
abstract: Sean Larkin, director of sales and business development at Amply Power, discusses charge management software (Omega platform) built to lower fleet electricity costs given how commercial electricity rates can swing 100-300% in a day due to demand and time-of-use charges. He explains Amply's move from transit into medium- and heavy-duty and eventually light-duty fleet electrification, the shift from a 'chicken or the egg' to a 'chicken and waffles' mindset where vehicle and infrastructure planning must happen simultaneously, and the importance of bringing all stakeholders (OEMs, utilities, dealerships, port authorities, drivers) to the table early.
key_findings: Commercial electricity rates can fluctuate 100-300% in a single day depending on demand charges and time-of-use periods, unlike diesel pricing which is comparatively stable hour-to-hour
Amply recommends fleets plan charging infrastructure at a 3x to 5x multiplier over near-term needs (e.g., build for 25 stations if you need 5 today) so utilities can plan for future load

Amply's core operational commitment to fleet customers is 99% uptime on charging equipment, framing service and maintenance of infrastructure -- not just the trucks -- as critical to successful deployments
data_available: Qualitative discussion of charge management strategy and utility rate structures; anecdotal industry observations; no quantitative fleet performance data

title: Ep 40: Randy Cornell – CFI
abstract: Randy Cornell, VP of maintenance and asset management at truckload carrier CFI, describes the company's diversification from a pure irregular-route, long-haul truckload carrier (drivers gone two to three weeks at a time across 48 states, Canada, and into Mexico) into dedicated, temperature-controlled, and logistics divisions. He discusses CFI's roughly three-to-five-year tractor trade cycle, its approach to piloting new fuel-saving technologies against a baseline fleet before scaling them, and why he sees electrification and other alternative powertrains as still 'quite a ways down the road' for CFI's irregular-route truckload business, though more feasible in newer, smaller-scale dedicated operations.
key_findings: CFI's core truckload division runs about 1,850-1,870 tractors on irregular routes, with drivers away two to three weeks at a time and typically home about one day per week they're out; CFI also has roughly 850 dedicated and 350 temperature-controlled trucks.
CFI guarantees drivers home on a requested day and hits that target about 95% of the time, which it uses as a driver-retention tool.

CFI trades tractors on roughly a three-to-five-year cycle rather than running them 8-11+ years, citing driver safety/satisfaction with newer equipment, lower breakdown rates, better residual value at trade, and fuel-efficiency gains from newer model-year technology.

CFI pilots new fuel-saving technologies (e.g., automated manual transmissions, aerodynamic devices) on a subset of trucks against a same-sized baseline group before scaling fleet-wide, and Cornell describes deliberately delaying adoption of some new components (e.g., a new 12-speed transmission) by a year to let the OEM work out early bugs.

Cornell says CFI views alternative powertrains (electric, hydrogen) as a longer-term proposition for its irregular-route truckload business, but sees potential nearer-term testing opportunities in smaller-scale applications like sprinter vans or yard goats within its newer dedicated division.
data_available: Fleet composition and operating model details for a large irregular-route truckload carrier
Driver home-time guarantee/retention program description
Tractor trade-cycle rationale and technology piloting methodology

title: Ep. 100: Mike Roeth – NACFE
abstract: For the podcast's 100th episode, Mike Roeth's granddaughter McKenzie flips the script and interviews him about starting the podcast, his career path into trucking, NACFE's founding, and what's coming next. Roeth recounts driving his first (diesel) pickup truck on the family farm at age 13, his first electric truck ride around 2020, and previews the 2025 "Run on Less Messy Middle" event.
key_findings: NACFE originated from an April 2009 Rocky Mountain Institute workshop that generated three core ideas, two of which became reality: NACFE itself and what later became the Run on Less series.
By this 100th episode, the podcast had accumulated roughly 18,000 downloads across its first approximately 90 episodes.

NACFE operates with roughly 12-13 people on its core team at the time of recording, with about 40 total people having contributed to its work over the organization's 15-year history, plus an extended network of RMI collaborators and in-kind industry contributors.

Roeth announces "Run on Less Messy Middle" for 2025, combining diesel-efficiency/aerodynamics, renewable diesel, biodiesel, natural gas/RNG, fast-charging battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cell/hydrogen engine technologies, alongside follow-up visits to the 2023 Run on Less Electric Depot sites.
data_available: Origin story of NACFE and the Run on Less series, traced to an April 2009 RMI workshop
Podcast download/listenership statistics through episode 100
Preview of the 2025 "Run on Less Messy Middle" event scope
Roeth's personal and career biography, including his first diesel and first electric truck experiences

title: Ep. 66: Kenny Vieth – ACT Research
abstract: Kenny Vieth, president of ACT Research (a commercial vehicle market analysis firm founded by his father in 1986), walks through the boom-bust cyclicality of North American Class 8 truck production over the last several decades and explains how housing, industrial production, and carrier profitability drive freight and truck-order cycles. He also discusses how the rise of e-commerce has changed freight density and time-sensitivity, and closes with ACT's near-term Class 8 production forecast, noting ACT now also produces multi-client electrification, hydrogen, and autonomous vehicle industry reports.
key_findings: North American Class 8 production swung from 376,400 units in 2006 to just 118,400 in 2009 (roughly a 70% drop) during the Great Recession, illustrating the extreme cyclicality of the industry; more recent years ranged from 345,000 units (2019) down to 214,000 (2020, pandemic-affected)

ACT's forecast at the time of the interview: about 310,000 Class 8 units for 2022 (versus an estimated 360,000 the industry could have built absent supply constraints), 296,000 for 2023, and a cyclical trough of about 254,000-255,000 units in 2024 -- a notably high trough by historical standards

Vieth explains e-commerce shifted freight toward lower-density, higher-time-sensitivity shipments (e.g., 100 shirts split into 100 separate boxes shipped individually rather than palletized to a store), which increases truck-miles without proportionally increasing weight hauled
data_available: Historical and forecast Class 8 production figures by year; discussion of freight-cycle drivers; references to ACT's separate electrification/hydrogen/autonomous vehicle multi-client reports (not detailed in this episode)

title: Ep. 114: Jason Morgan – Fleet Equipment
abstract: Jason Morgan, content director at Fleet Equipment, discusses how the pandemic accelerated Fleet Equipment's shift from print magazine to digital/video content, his transition from magazine editor to digital content producer, and what has kept him in the trucking industry. He and Roeth reflect on ACT Expo 2025, where diesel trucks were featured alongside alternative fuels, as a sign the industry has moved past hype-driven promotion/opposition into pragmatic, business-focused evaluation of multiple decarbonization pathways amid regulatory and tariff uncertainty.
key_findings: Fleet Equipment ended its print publication in December 2020, moving to an all-digital, video-heavy format starting in 2021.

At ACT Expo 2025, Morgan and Roeth observed diesel trucks featured on the show floor alongside alternative-fuel technologies, which they interpreted as evidence the industry has moved past hype/opposition framing into pragmatic business evaluation.

NACFE is described as having roughly 15 consultants on staff; Morgan attributes NACFE's credibility to focusing conversations on early-adopter fleets and credible technical sources rather than broad industry surveys.
data_available: Interview reflecting on trucking trade media's shift to digital/video and impressions of ACT Expo 2025
General commentary on industry uncertainty (tariffs, regulation) with no quantitative data presented

title: Ep. 78: Ed Chipalowsky – NACFE
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Ed Chipalowsky, NACFE's vehicle service and support manager, about his career as a Ryder technician, district trainer, and later diesel-technology educator (Johnson College and a high school program) before retiring and joining NACFE. Chipalowsky argues the industry's shift from mechanical to electronic systems was the single biggest evolution technicians have faced, recounts the rocky rollout of ABS in the 1970s, and describes what makes a great technician (curiosity about root cause, tenacity, customer focus toward drivers). He closes by arguing the industry is not yet ready for high-voltage electric and hydrogen powertrains and calls for technician licensing on high-voltage systems and greater use of augmented-reality training tools.
key_findings: Chipalowsky identifies the transition from mechanical to electronic truck systems as the single biggest evolution he witnessed in his career, citing troubled early ABS rollouts in the 1970s as an example of technology arriving faster than technician training could keep pace.

He advocates for mandatory licensing of technicians who work on 'ultra high voltage' systems (up to roughly 1,000 volts), comparable to electrician licensing, arguing 12-volt systems are forgiving but higher-voltage mistakes can be fatal.

He believes OEMs are ready for the shift to electric/hydrogen/autonomous trucks but that the technician workforce is not yet ready, and calls for greater urgency on training and augmented-reality tools.
data_available: First-person account of technician career progression from Ryder technician to district trainer to community-college and high-school diesel technology instructor
Discussion of the TMC SuperTech technician competition and its evolution over the years
Advice for technicians and fleets on adapting to new powertrain technologies

title: Ep 4: Elizabeth Fretheim – Nikola Motor Co.
abstract: Elizabeth Fretheim, Head of Business Development and National Accounts at Nikola Motor Co. (and formerly of Walmart, where she first crossed paths with Mike Roeth around 2009), discusses her first year at Nikola following the company's SPAC merger and public listing, and Nikola's manufacturing plans. She details Nikola's partnership with Iveco (part of CNH/Case New Holland) -- describing the arrangement as "Iveco is the bones and we're the guts" -- under which Nikola's first battery electric production trucks will be built at Iveco's plant in Ulm, Germany, while Nikola's US plant in Coolidge, Arizona (about 430 acres, up to 1 million square feet, roughly a 12-month build) targets trucks coming off the assembly line in 2023. She also names other Nikola partners/investors including Bosch, ConMet, and Meritor, and discusses the company's view that trucks operating under roughly 300 miles per day are better suited to battery electric power while longer routes favor hydrogen fuel cell power. Note: a large portion of this episode's source transcript is corrupted by a repeated-text transcription failure, limiting the amount of additional content that could be reliably extracted.
key_findings: Nikola's first battery electric production trucks will be built at Iveco's plant in Ulm, Germany, under a partnership Fretheim describes as 'Iveco is the bones and we're the guts.'

Nikola's planned US manufacturing plant in Coolidge, Arizona covers about 430 acres, will be up to 1 million square feet, and was targeting roughly a 12-month build with trucks coming off the assembly line in 2023.
Fretheim cites other Nikola partners and investors including Bosch, ConMet, and Meritor.
Nikola's internal framing at the time was that trucks operating under roughly 300 miles per day are better suited to battery electric power, while longer routes favor hydrogen fuel cell trucks.
data_available: Details of Nikola's manufacturing partnership with Iveco and plant locations (Ulm, Germany and Coolidge, Arizona)
Nikola's stated battery-electric-vs-fuel-cell range crossover reasoning
List of named Nikola supplier/investor partners

title: Ep 62: Glen Kedzie – American Trucking Associations
abstract: Glen Kedzie, senior executive at the American Trucking Associations, explains ATA's structure (a national association plus 50 affiliated state trucking associations) and why California's unique Clean Air Act carve-out makes it the 'petri dish for innovation' that other states can then opt into. He walks through the decades-long evolution of NOx and particulate matter regulation, arguing the next NOx rule (finalized in 2022 for 2027 implementation, 26 years after the prior 2001 rule) will likely be the last of its kind as the industry shifts toward zero-emission mandates, and discusses how a multi-powertrain future will make fleet manager and first-responder jobs more complex.
key_findings: Under the Clean Air Act, California can develop its own vehicle emissions regulations pending EPA approval, and once approved, other states may 'opt in' and adopt California's regulation as written -- a mechanism Kedzie says is spreading rapidly, especially among West Coast and Northeastern states

The most recent heavy-duty NOx rule (developed circa 2022, effective 2027) follows the prior rule from 2001 -- a 26-year gap -- and Kedzie predicts it will be the last NOx rule the industry needs given the shift toward zero-emission vehicles

Kedzie relays that first responders can face battery fires in electric vehicles that reignite up to two days later, illustrating new safety and fire-code complexities the industry has not previously had to manage; his closing advice is that fleets must speak up early in the regulatory comment process, ideally before a rule is even proposed
data_available: Regulatory history and policy-process commentary; no quantitative emissions or fleet data presented

title: Ep. 102: Jim Park – Journalist and NACFE
abstract: Jim Park, an award-winning trucking journalist and NACFE technologies consultant, talks with Mike Roeth about his two-decade driving career (including hauling hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen for Air Products and Chemicals) before transitioning into journalism, and the editorial philosophy of always writing for a hypothetical small-fleet reader in Brandon, Manitoba. They also debate whether battery-electric trucks' biggest barriers are technological or external (cost, charging infrastructure, grid capacity, and increasingly expensive diesel aftertreatment).
key_findings: Park frames all his trucking journalism around a hypothetical reader: a small, 25-truck fleet operator in Brandon, Manitoba who lacks dedicated technology or safety staff and has limited time to parse industry jargon.

He drove tractor-trailers for about two decades, including hauling hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen for Air Products and Chemicals in Nanticoke, Ontario, before retiring from driving in 1998 to write full time; his journalism career began through years of writing "letters to the editor" and a spot on Ontario's first Road Knights driver team in 1995.

He argues the trucking industry's biggest barriers to battery-electric adoption are external (charging infrastructure, grid capacity, and rate competition from cheaper diesel-hauled freight) rather than the vehicle technology itself, and predicts diesel-electric cost parity could arrive because increasingly complex, expensive diesel aftertreatment systems (for 2027 NOx rules) make diesel pricier -- not because batteries get cheaper.
data_available: Detailed personal driving career history spanning straight trucks, tractor-trailers, and tanker hauling
Editorial philosophy for writing trucking journalism aimed at a small-fleet-operator audience
Perspective on external versus technological barriers to battery-electric truck adoption

title: Ep. 120: Dan Gage – The Transport Project
abstract: Dan Gage, president of The Transport Project (formerly NGV America), discusses the organization's 2024 rebrand to reflect its members' expanding work in hydrogen alongside natural gas, and makes the case for renewable natural gas (RNG) as a scalable, affordable near-term decarbonization solution for trucking. He walks through how carbon intensity varies by feedstock (landfill, wastewater, food waste, dairy manure, swine, poultry), cites national and California-specific RNG adoption statistics, and addresses common misconceptions about RNG supply and distribution.
key_findings: In 2024, 86% of all natural gas motor fuel dispensed for on-road use in the US was renewable natural gas (RNG), not conventional/geologic natural gas.

California's blended bio-CNG carbon intensity score was -194 in 2024, meaning fleets fueling on California natural gas were effectively running carbon-negative with a standard internal combustion engine; dairy-manure-derived RNG can score as low as roughly -400 to -600 CI depending on the specific pathway, while landfill gas is typically a positive 50-60 CI and food/wastewater-derived RNG is closer to zero.
Waste Management, one of the largest natural gas fleets in the US, runs trucks on RNG produced from the trash those same trucks collect, described as a circular-economy example.
Three natural gas fleets participated in NACFE's 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle event.
data_available: Interview with specific cited statistics on national/California RNG fuel-share and carbon intensity by feedstock type
Discussion of RNG production economics, pipeline distribution challenges, and feedstock supply constraints
No original NACFE-generated dataset in this episode itself

title: Ep. 115:Cliff Campbell–Center for Freight & Logistics Efficiency w/ Electrified & Automated Trucking
abstract: Cliff Campbell, managing director and industry liaison officer for the Center for Freight & Logistics Efficiency with Electrified and Automated Trucking (the FLEET Center), explains this NSF Industry-University Cooperative Research Center to Mike Roeth: how it pools industry membership fees to fund pre-competitive research bridging the "valley of death" between academic research and commercial adoption, its current member companies and projects, and how electrification and automation may interact in future trucks.
key_findings: The FLEET Center is an NSF Industry-University Cooperative Research Center founded in 2019 as a Purdue/IUPUI/University of Memphis collaboration, officially launched in August 2024, with five industry member companies and three active research projects underway at the time of the interview.

One active project is a fleet electrification case study developed with Shelby County Schools in Memphis, Tennessee, which is in the early stages of converting its entire bus fleet to electric; another develops a "transverse homopolar AC machine," a new electric motor design that reduces reliance on rare-earth magnets and enables direct stator cooling.

Campbell cites NACFE research finding that removing the driver from a truck saves roughly a third or more of cost per mile in driver wages and direct labor costs, and that roughly 40% of a highway tractor's cost and weight is attributable to accommodating a driver (cab, seats, HVAC, sleeper).
data_available: Explanation of the FLEET Center's structure, funding model, and membership as an NSF IUCRC
Description of current FLEET Center research projects, including a Shelby County Schools electrification case study and a novel electric motor design
Discussion of how electrification and automation might combine in future truck design, including a staged-automation concept for highway convoys

title: Ep. 109: Ken North – NACFE
abstract: Ken North, one of NACFE's Emerging Technologies consultants, talks with Mike Roeth about his roughly four-decade dealership/OEM career (Paccar/Kenworth, Daimler/Freightliner, and Mack/Volvo), a health scare in his 20s that redirected him from a commercial pilot career into trucking, and his work pioneering telematics-based predictive maintenance. He also reflects on trucking's role in economic prosperity and the tension between efficient freight movement and decarbonization.
key_findings: North helped pioneer predictive maintenance using vehicle telematics data during his dealership career, enabling advance warning -- sometimes a week or two ahead -- of component failures so trucks could be serviced proactively rather than break down unexpectedly.

He spent roughly four decades in trucking dealership/OEM roles: many years with Paccar/Kenworth, then about a decade with Daimler/Freightliner (including part ownership of a dealership), then 13 years with Mack/Volvo, before retiring and joining NACFE as an Emerging Technologies consultant.

He quotes former colleague and Volvo Group president Martin Lundstedt describing the industry as having "already climbed to the peak of the mountain of unrealistic expectations" about new technology and now being "down in the valley of developing practical solutions."
data_available: Career history of a four-decade truck dealership/OEM executive who pioneered telematics-based predictive maintenance
Personal story connecting a health scare to a career pivot from aviation to trucking
Perspective on the trucking industry's role in economic prosperity versus its decarbonization imperative

title: Ep. 137: Emily Long – NACFE
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Emily Long, NACFE's Events and Partnerships Manager, about her career path from programming the Mountain Film festival in Telluride for a decade, through a communications role connecting RMI's mobility team with NACFE, to her current work designing NACFE's convenings. The centerpiece of the conversation is a 'data potluck' workshop Long organized, built on NACFE's Messy Middle demonstration dataset, which required every attendee to bring their own analysis rather than passively observe. She also discusses her approach to event facilitation and her outlook on incremental, collaborative change in the industry.
key_findings: Long organized a NACFE 'data potluck' workshop built on the Messy Middle demonstration's dataset (reported in the episode as over 2 million miles of trucking data), where every attendee -- including participants from large fleets such as Amazon and JB Hunt as well as data scientists and industry newcomers -- was required to bring and present their own analysis of the dataset rather than just attend.
The workshop deliberately mixed people across diverse roles and technology focus areas rather than grouping attendees by a single propulsion technology or seniority level.
data_available: Long's career background in events and communications, including a decade programming the Mountain Film festival in Telluride and prior work at RMI
Description of the NACFE data potluck workshop format and the fleets that participated
Long's philosophy on event facilitation and stakeholder engagement

title: Ep. 12: Jeff Baer – LinkeDrive
abstract: Jeff Baer, founder and CEO of LinkeDrive, discusses the company's PedalCoach driver-coaching product, which uses live CAN bus data to give truck drivers a real-time fuel economy target, and MyDrive, a daily driver report distributed during NACFE's 2019 Run on Less – Regional. Baer explains the quantitative impact drivers have on fuel economy, describes LinkeDrive's philosophy of fairness, positivity, and automation in driver coaching, and discusses how the product's underlying math is powertrain-agnostic across diesel, natural gas, and electric trucks.
key_findings: LinkeDrive's data shows driver behavior accounts for roughly 30-35% of a truck's fuel economy outcome.
Following PedalCoach's real-time fuel economy guidance can save drivers roughly 5-12% in fuel, depending on their baseline driving behavior.
In partnership with NACFE's 2019 Run on Less – Regional, LinkeDrive distributed about 140 daily MyDrive reports to drivers, showing route maps, speed profile pie charts, and weather conditions.

PedalCoach's underlying algorithm is fuel/powertrain agnostic, working across conventional diesel, compressed natural gas, spark-ignition, and electric trucks, though EV regenerative braking behaves differently from coasting in a conventional powertrain.
data_available: Interview with company-reported statistics on driver impact on fuel economy and PedalCoach fuel savings
Description of the MyDrive daily driver report distributed during NACFE's Run on Less – Regional 2019
Qualitative product description; no independent third-party validation data in this episode

title: Ep. 38: Avra Brahma – Locomation
abstract: Avra Brahma, principal engineer at Locomation, explains the company's 'human-guided autonomy' approach to truck automation, marketed as the Autonomous Relay Convoy (ARC): two trucks platoon together, and once the convoy is formed, the following driver takes their required rest while the truck keeps moving, mimicking team-driving and slip-seating practices to roughly double runtime without violating hours-of-service rules. He discusses an independent environmental/ESG study on Locomation's technology, the technical and regulatory reliability challenges facing autonomous trucking generally, and why the ARC system is designed to be powertrain-agnostic across diesel, electric, and hydrogen fuel cell trucks.
key_findings: In Locomation's ARC (Autonomous Relay Convoy) concept, once two trucks are platooned, the rear/following driver takes their mandated rest period while the truck continues moving under automation, which Brahma says yields about 22 hours of runtime per truck-pair versus about 11 hours for a conventional solo truck.

Locomation commissioned an independent, science-based ESG impact study (performed by Boundless Analytics) that Brahma says confirmed reductions in GHG footprint, fuel consumption, and operating cost, plus equipment-utilization gains.

Brahma cites survey research (from CPA) showing public sentiment toward automated freight trucking is favorable, and says it is more favorable toward a 'human-guided' model like Locomation's than toward fully driverless competitor models.

Brahma frames Locomation's technology as powertrain-agnostic, sitting on top of whatever powertrain (diesel, electric, or hydrogen fuel cell) becomes dominant, and notes early pilot activity concentrated in Texas/Arizona/New Mexico due to favorable weather, topography, and lower traffic congestion.
data_available: Technical/operational description of Locomation's human-guided ARC platooning system
Summary of a third-party ESG impact study on the technology
Public-sentiment survey findings on automated freight trucking
Discussion of reliability/regulatory barriers to automation

title: Ep. 9: Quin Garcia – Autotech Ventures
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Quin Garcia, managing director of AutoTech Ventures, a Silicon Valley venture capital firm investing exclusively in ground-transportation startups on behalf of large trucking-industry corporate partners. Garcia explains the firm's seed-through-Series-C investment approach using its investment in XStream (maker of the Truck Wings active-aerodynamic tractor-trailer gap-closing device) as a case study, discusses why trucking has become attractive to venture capital and tech giants over the past decade, and lays out a framework for thinking about technology 'hype' as a ratio of buzz to actual productivity. He closes with advice for entrepreneurs (empathize with incumbent customers, partner rather than reinvent) and incumbents (be open to outside innovation).
key_findings: AutoTech Ventures manages roughly $300 million in venture capital funds focused exclusively on ground transportation, investing from seed stage through Series C on behalf of large corporate partners.

The firm's investment in XStream (Truck Wings, an active aerodynamic device sealing the tractor-trailer gap) is described as driven primarily by team quality (founder Daniel Burroughs) and market size (fuel as one of the largest trucking cost categories).

Garcia frames technology hype as a ratio of buzz (numerator) to actual real-world productivity (denominator), citing autonomous vehicles circa 2020 as an example of a very high hype-to-productivity ratio.

He identifies two common startup failure modes in trucking: being too tech-centric and failing to empathize with incumbent customers, or coming from the incumbent world and failing to bring genuine technology innovation.
data_available: Description of AutoTech Ventures' fund structure, investment stage focus, and corporate-partner model
Case study of the XStream/Truck Wings investment and product
Framework for evaluating technology hype versus real-world productivity in the trucking startup space

title: Ep. 6: Kevin Otto and Dave Schaller – NACFE Team
abstract: NACFE team members Dave Schaller (formerly 27 years at Navistar, now NACFE's industry engagement director) and Kevin Otto (formerly 38 years at Cummins, now a NACFE consultant) discuss their engineering careers and how they came to work with NACFE. They describe NACFE's roughly 10-12 person contractor team of industry veterans -- averaging nearly 35 years of industry experience and roughly 1,000 LinkedIn contacts apiece -- and the organization's three work streams: scaling available technologies, guiding emerging technologies, and running Run on Less demonstrations. Both express enthusiasm about the industry's ongoing electrification "messy middle" and Otto's leadership of a new Technology and Maintenance Council (TMC) electrified vehicles task force. They close with advice for people entering the industry: build a broad view across engineering and business disciplines, expect resistance to change, and recognize that new trucking technologies typically take close to a decade for full adoption per NACFE's annual fleet fuel study.
key_findings: NACFE's roughly 10-12 person contractor/subject-matter-expert team averages nearly 35 years of trucking industry experience per person and about 1,000 LinkedIn contacts each, according to an exercise Schaller ran on the team's collective background.
NACFE's annual fleet fuel study shows that virtually no new technology introduced into the trucking industry achieves full adoption in under a decade.

Otto chairs a new Technology and Maintenance Council (TMC) task force on electrified vehicles, tasked with identifying the top standards-development priorities to help the industry adopt electrified and automated vehicles.
Roughly 9% of the total US workforce is involved in the transportation or warehousing industry, per Otto.
data_available: Career backgrounds of two long-tenured NACFE subject matter experts (ex-Navistar, ex-Cummins)
Description of NACFE's team structure, work streams, and technology-adoption timeline findings
Details on a new TMC electrified vehicles task force

title: Ep. 99: Jim Castelaz – Motiv Electric Trucks
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Jim Castelaz, founder and chief technology and revenue officer at Motiv Electric Trucks, about the company's roughly 15-year history as (by his account) the longest-running dedicated electric truck manufacturer, its pivot from powertrain supplier to full vehicle OEM, and why he believes the medium-duty electric truck market has reached an inflection point. Castelaz stresses the importance of clear vocabulary (kilowatts versus kilowatt-hours) in avoiding costly planning mistakes for fleets and utilities, identifies range, reliability, and cost as the three key metrics for electric trucks, and discusses Motiv customer Purolator's participation in NACFE's Run on Less program.
key_findings: Castelaz says Motiv is the longest-running dedicated electric truck manufacturer (roughly 15 years), pivoting about five years ago from a powertrain-only supplier to a full vehicle OEM offering strip chassis, step vans, and cab chassis (including a new Argo cab chassis).
He identifies range, reliability, and cost as the three key metrics for electric trucks, and cites a Motiv fleet customer reporting 50% fuel cost savings after switching to electric.

Castelaz argues confusion between kilowatts (power) and kilowatt-hours (energy), and related concepts like charge dwell time, have led even well-informed utilities to significantly miscalculate power needs for planned truck fleet electrification.

He emphasizes that single-shift, return-to-depot medium-duty operation (as opposed to trucks run up to 20 hours a day) is a key structural advantage making medium-duty electrification easier than long-haul electrification today.

Motiv customer Purolator participated in NACFE's Run on Less program, and Castelaz praises NACFE for providing independent, third-party-validated performance data that fleets rely on to justify large electrification bets.
data_available: Company history and product portfolio evolution for a dedicated medium-duty electric truck OEM
Framework of range/reliability/cost as the three key metrics for evaluating electric trucks
Discussion of power-versus-energy vocabulary confusion and its real-world planning consequences for fleets and utilities

title: Ep. 130: Chris Guerrero – ENGIE Resources
abstract: Chris Guerrero, VP of Marketing at ENGIE Resources (formerly at Shell, where he worked on the Starship fuel-efficiency project and later Shell Energy's power generation business), discusses his career path in the energy industry and the phenomenon of "green hushing" -- companies pulling back from talking publicly about sustainability work out of caution. He describes the "three basic positions" of the energy business (generation, transmission/trading, retail) and warns that US electricity demand is rising faster than at any point in the last 20 years due to data centers, transport electrification, and industrial onshoring, urging fleets to closely track power supply contract terms.
key_findings: Guerrero's earlier Starship project at Shell (with driver Bob Slyva) tested technology and driving/operating practices on existing Class 8 trucks to improve fuel economy, partnering with NACFE for an impartial evaluation -- this collaboration is how he and Mike Roeth first met.
ENGIE Resources is described as the fifth largest supplier of retail energy to B2B businesses in the US, part of ENGIE which operates in 30 countries with roughly 95,000 employees worldwide.

Guerrero advises fleets and facility operators to closely monitor power supply agreement terms because electricity demand is rising faster than at any time in the last 20 years, citing recent cost exposure during Winter Storm Fern in the Northeast.
data_available: Personal career narrative
Qualitative commentary on energy market trends and power supply contracting advice
No quantitative fuel-economy or fleet performance data

title: Ep 73: Seth Clevenger – Transport Topics
