abstract: Seth Clevenger, managing editor at Transport Topics, discusses his path into trucking trade journalism from local Ohio newspapers, Transport Topics' role informing industry decision-makers on breaking news, regulation, and emerging technology, and the publication's shift from a purely print product toward multimedia, including its own Road Signs podcast. He and Roeth discuss why this is a uniquely transformative period for trucking, with battery-electric, hydrogen fuel cell, renewable-fuel, and automated-driving technologies all emerging simultaneously alongside shifting shipper and consumer expectations, and Clevenger closes urging fleets not to be complacent given the pace of change.
key_findings: Clevenger has worked at Transport Topics for almost 12 years (since roughly 2011) and hosts the publication's own podcast, Transport Topics Road Signs

He characterizes the current period as uniquely transformative for trucking because of the simultaneous emergence of battery-electric, hydrogen fuel cell, renewable-fuel, and automated-driving technologies, contrasting it with a decade earlier when natural gas was the primary alternative being studied
data_available: Clevenger's career background moving from local Ohio newspapers into trade journalism
Discussion of how Transport Topics balances print, web, and multimedia/podcast coverage

title: Ep. 131: Chris Hammond – Great Dane
abstract: Chris Hammond, a 39-year Great Dane veteran transitioning from Executive VP of Sales to Executive VP of Industry Affairs and Strategic Accounts, recounts the trailer manufacturer's 126-year history (from the Savannah Blowpipe Company to a major trailer OEM) and its aerodynamics and telematics (FleetPulse) partnerships. He discusses refrigerated trailer technology like ThermaGuard, the emergence of "smart trailers" with onboard data and cameras, drop-and-hook independence and theft-deterrence needs, and reflects on why fleets may be extending trailer trade cycles as durability improves.
key_findings: Great Dane built the industry's first factory-finished refrigerated trailer in the late 1940s, using a small Briggs & Stratton engine to blow air over blocks of ice; a remade 1953 version now tours as the company's mobile museum piece.

Great Dane's ThermaGuard lining product prevents moisture from getting into reefer trailer wall insulation over time, which Hammond says can otherwise add 1,500-2,000 lbs of water weight and degrade a trailer's temperature-holding ability.

Great Dane trailers now ship standard with FleetPulse telematics; Hammond frames smart trailers with sensors and cameras as a prerequisite for eventual trailer-tractor autonomy and for anti-theft protection when trailers are dropped and hooked independently of the tractor.
Roughly 15% of trailers in the US are refrigerated, per Hammond, carrying goods well beyond frozen food, including floral products, shampoo, and pharmaceuticals.
data_available: Company history and product descriptions (ThermaGuard, FleetPulse)
Qualitative discussion of trailer telematics and refrigeration trends
No independent performance data or fleet case studies

title: Ep. 60: Chet Ciesielski – International
abstract: Chet Ciesielski, VP of on-highway truck business at Navistar/International, discusses how the company works with customers on fuel economy and total cost of ownership, and lays out Navistar's BEV-first strategy (having already launched its eMV medium-duty platform and an electric bus) with plans to bring battery-electric to regional-haul tractors around a 150-mile duty cycle, while pursuing hydrogen fuel cells for longer-haul applications. He notes that private fleets in segments like food and wholesale delivery, often running under 200 miles a day, represent the clearest near-term electrification opportunity, and that charging infrastructure -- not vehicle technology -- is the bigger bottleneck.
key_findings: Navistar sees regional-haul operations around 150 miles as the 'prime path' for its first battery-electric Class 8 tractor, with long-haul (1,000+ miles/day) expected to require hydrogen fuel cells
Ciesielski says conversations with fleets increasingly start with zero-emission and carbon footprint questions before circling back to traditional ICE specs -- a reversal from prior years

Early electric truck deployments are showing promising, though still preliminary, uptime and reduced maintenance indications due to fewer moving parts and no aftertreatment system, though the magnitude of savings (30%, 60%, or in between) is not yet established
data_available: Executive commentary on Navistar's electrification roadmap and customer conversations; no quantitative company performance data disclosed

title: Ep. 117: John Walters – Valvoline
abstract: John Walters, vice president and general manager of heavy duty Americas for Valvoline, discusses his path from the Marine Corps (escorting fuel/supply convoys in Iraq) into fuel/lubricant sales and eventually Valvoline's heavy-duty business, after a prior long tenure at Shell. He talks about how Valvoline is positioning itself to compete in heavy-duty lubricants against established players, and why he views the industry's multi-fuel "messy middle" as an opportunity rather than a threat for the lubricants business, since every powertrain type still needs lubrication, coolant, or grease.
key_findings: Valvoline's heavy-duty engine oils are engineered and designed jointly with Cummins, reflecting a 30-year partnership between the two companies.

NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle event referenced in the episode included four fleets running battery-electric trucks, two running hydrogen fuel cell, three running natural gas, and four running diesel.

Walters argues the lubricants business is not fundamentally threatened by the energy transition because internal combustion engines, hydrogen and natural gas vehicles, and even fully battery-electric trucks all still require some form of grease, coolant, or lubrication.
data_available: Interview on Valvoline's heavy-duty lubricants strategy and the Shell-to-Valvoline career transition
A cited breakdown of fuel-type participation (battery, hydrogen, natural gas, diesel) in NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle event
No independent quantitative study data from Valvoline itself

title: Ep. 139: Josh Fisher – Fleet Owner
abstract: Josh Fisher, editor in chief of Fleet Owner and a nearly decade-long friend of NACFE's Mike Roeth, discusses how AI and changing publishing economics have reshaped trade journalism, and grades the trucking industry's adoption of new technology as improving from roughly a "C" to a "B+" over the past decade. He cites NACFE's Run on Less program, including a recent 11.5 mpg diesel truck result and the 2023 Tesla Semi demonstration, and discusses how aerodynamic, fuel-efficient trucks from the 2007-2010 emissions era are now raising national average fuel economy as they filter into the used-truck market.
key_findings: Fisher grades the trucking industry's adoption of new efficiency, electrification, and automation technology as a "B+" today versus roughly a "C" ten years ago, partly crediting the (since-weakened) EPA 2027 rule for pushing OEM collaboration such as joint Volvo/Daimler fuel cell work and shared battery production efforts.

He cites NACFE's Run on Less program, noting a recent diesel truck result of 11.5 mpg hauling real freight on real routes, and recalls Run on Less publicizing the Tesla Semi's range and charging performance in 2023.

Fisher notes national average diesel truck fuel economy is improving significantly in the last five years as post-2007/2010-emissions aerodynamic trucks with efficient powertrains have matured and filtered down into the used-truck and owner-operator market.

Fleet Owner's core readership is fleets with roughly 6 to 1,000 vehicles, which Fisher says often can't afford to pilot new technologies themselves, so the publication relays lessons learned from larger, better-resourced carriers.
data_available: NACFE Run on Less fuel economy figures (11.5 mpg diesel result cited)
Commentary on national average diesel truck fuel economy trend
Qualitative industry technology-adoption assessment; no independent survey data presented

title: Ep. 116: Leia Guccione – RMI
abstract: Leia Guccione, managing director of carbon-free transportation at RMI and a Navy Reserve officer, discusses how two decades of naval leadership and logistics experience inform her civilian energy-transition work, and describes RMI's Carbon-Free Transportation program's approach to trucking electrification, including deployment support for fleets, grid/utility readiness work, and international programs in Indonesia, Nigeria, and Kenya. She also makes the case that electrifying trucks can accelerate grid decarbonization rather than compete with it.
key_findings: RMI's Carbon-Free Transportation team built a tool called GridUp, developed with industry input, intended to bridge the data gap between how utilities do electricity planning and how fleets do logistics planning.

Guccione argues that electrifying trucks can make the broader grid greener by turning truck batteries and managed charging (enabled by real-time data connectivity) into a flexible resource that helps integrate more renewable generation.

RMI's Carbon-Free Transportation work extends beyond the US to markets including Indonesia, Nigeria, and Kenya, framed as "leapfrog" economic development opportunities for newer transportation technologies.
data_available: Interview on RMI's fleet electrification strategy and the GridUp utility-fleet coordination tool
Discussion of RMI's international (Indonesia, Nigeria, Kenya) electrification work
No quantitative report data cited directly in this episode

title: Ep. 59: Anthony Eggert – Climate Works Foundation
abstract: Anthony Eggert, director at ClimateWorks Foundation, describes the Drive Electric Campaign -- a coalition of over 80 partners with goals of 100% zero-emission bus and two/three-wheeler sales by 2030, 100% passenger car sales by 2035, and 100% truck sales of all types by 2040. He discusses California's Advanced Clean Trucks rule and a 15-state MOU on zero-emission trucks, and uses Norway's and Shenzhen's electrification histories as case studies for how sustained policy support combined with tolerance for early-stage technology failure eventually produces rapid market scaling.
key_findings: As of the episode, six states had adopted the Advanced Clean Truck rule (covering roughly 20% of the US market), part of a 15-state collaborative memorandum of understanding on zero-emission truck transition

Shenzhen went from a few hundred electric buses to over 16,000 (100% of its bus fleet) within a few years after roughly seven years of prior trial-and-error with different bus designs and charging protocols; its electric delivery truck fleet grew from over 60,000 (circa 2017-18) to reportedly over 100,000, supported by over 50 different cargo truck manufacturers at one point

Norway's EV sales success (over 80% of passenger vehicle sales electric) traces to policy adopted in the late 1990s that combined with California's Advanced Clean Cars regulation pushing more EV models to market in the late 2000s/early 2010s -- illustrating that technology-neutral policy plus market experimentation, rather than picking a single winner, drove the outcome
data_available: Specific case-study statistics on Norway and Shenzhen EV/bus/truck adoption; policy coverage figures for US state rules; no NACFE-specific data

title: Ep. 80: Ali Javidan – Range Energy
abstract: Ali Javidan, founder and CEO of Range Energy, describes the company's electrified trailer platform, which replaces one bogey axle with an e-axle, adds a battery pack, and adds a sensing 'smart kingpin' so the trailer can sense tractor pulling force and gently propel itself. He explains the technology's claimed fuel-economy and range benefits, why the company focused on Class 8 trucking (including reefers) over other trailer markets, and recounts his earlier career running touring car racing teams before founding Range Energy. Note: this episode's transcript has significant quality issues (heavy repetition/looping flagged by the ingest pipeline), so coverage of the back half of the conversation is limited.
key_findings: Range Energy's electrified trailer system replaces one bogey axle with an e-axle, adds an underbody battery pack, and adds a sensing 'smart kingpin' that measures tractor pulling force so the trailer can gently self-propel and feel weightless to the tractor

The company claims up to roughly 40% better fuel economy when paired with a conventional diesel tractor, and says it can extend a battery-electric Cascadia's range from a typical 120-180 miles up to over 250 miles

Range Energy completed its first pilot with an unnamed large beverage distributor in Southern California, spending three days observing mechanics' existing toolboxes and workflows before finalizing the product design so no new tools would be required
data_available: Founder's account of Range Energy's electrified-trailer product architecture and claimed fuel-economy/range benefits
Founder's career background in professional touring car racing (BMW, Mitsubishi teams) before entering trucking

title: Ep. 85: Scott Perry – Industry Executive and former NACFE board chairman
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Scott Perry, a longtime industry executive (Ryder System asset management and chief technology officer roles, later a household-goods/final-mile logistics company) and NACFE's board chairman from roughly 2013 to 2017. Perry reflects on NACFE's early 'adolescent years' and an internal debate over whether the organization should test only commercially available technology or also weigh in on emerging/unproven technology, describes the risk calculus fleets face committing to a technology for the 5-10 year life of an asset, and shares insights from his time overseeing a household-goods carrier's long-haul driver network and final-mile delivery acquisition. He closes by discussing NACFE's Run on Less program, including a November 2023 event at the White House with climate advisor Ali Zaidi.
key_findings: As NACFE board chairman, Perry recalls an early organizational debate over whether NACFE should evaluate only proven, commercially available technologies versus also assessing emerging/unproven technologies from new entrants.

He describes household-goods (moving) industry drivers as among the last true long-haul truckers, living in their trucks for extended periods (as much as roughly 300 days a year during COVID), in contrast to most freight networks that have shifted toward daily dispatch or shorter out-and-back cycles.
NACFE's Run on Less Electric Depot culminated in a roughly five-hour event at the White House in November 2023 attended by climate advisor Ali Zaidi and other administration-affiliated officials.
data_available: Reflections on NACFE's founding era and governance debates from a former board chairman's perspective
Career narrative spanning Ryder System asset management/CTO roles and a household-goods logistics company
Discussion of asset commitment risk (5-10+ year vehicle life cycles) in technology adoption decisions

title: Ep. 103: Yann Kulp – Driivz
abstract: Yann Kulp, Director of Sales for the United States at Driivz, talks with Mike Roeth about his earlier work running EV suitability analytics for fleets at a startup he co-founded, and his current role at Driivz, a 12-year-old charger management software company. They discuss how fleets should evaluate EV feasibility and why Kulp favors being "tactical" -- taking incremental action -- over waiting for a perfect long-term strategy.
key_findings: Kulp's prior EV-analytics startup ran suitability analytics on more than 350,000 internal-combustion vehicles considering conversion to EV, evaluating operational feasibility (dwell time, power capacity, battery degradation, cold-weather impact), economic impact, sustainability/carbon impact, and charging infrastructure needs.
In one dataset from a large package-delivery fleet client, roughly 95% of daily routes were under 75 miles, illustrating how much of a fleet's operation can already fit within current EV range.

Driivz, the charger management software company Kulp now works for, will have more than 140,000 chargers running on its platform across 38 countries by the end of the year discussed in the episode, working with US clients including EVgo, Green Lane, Circle K, and Volvo Trucks.
data_available: Methodology and scale of a fleet EV-suitability analytics practice (350,000+ vehicles analyzed)
Company facts about Driivz's charger management software platform and client base
Kulp's career path from industrial electrical products (Schneider Electric/Square D) to EV charging software

title: Ep. 88: Henrik Holland – Prologis
abstract: Henrik Holland, Global Head of Prologis Mobility, describes his 18-year career at Shell (including running Shell's global EV charging strategy and acquisitions such as New Motion and Greenlots) before joining Prologis in 2021 to build a charging-as-a-service business across Prologis's warehouse real estate portfolio, which spans more than 5,000 facilities globally (about 3,500 in the US). He discusses Prologis's dual model of customer-led 'behind-the-fence' depot charging versus a newer 'destination charging' public network, a newly built last-mile EV depot in Queens, NY where trucks run under about 80 miles per day, and his role alongside Mike Roeth on the federal Joint Office electric vehicle working group.
key_findings: Holland reports Class 8 EV charging speeds have increased from about 150 kW to 250 kW and vehicle range from roughly 100 miles to 200-250 miles over the prior two to three years, with further gains expected from vehicles like the Tesla Semi.

The Queens, NY depot he describes involves trucks running roughly 80 miles per day or less, which Prologis and NACFE frame as a 'small energy depot' deployment model well suited to early electrification.

Prologis operates a 'behind-the-fence' model (dedicated customer charging, integrated into new-lease site work for cost synergy) alongside an emerging 'destination charging' network open to multiple fleets, and Holland serves alongside Mike Roeth on the federal Joint Office's electric vehicle working group, which drew 300-400 applicants for its seats.
data_available: Holland's career background at Shell (EV strategy, Cleantech venture investing) before founding Prologis Mobility
Description of Prologis's charging-as-a-service business model and its behind-the-fence vs. destination-charging approaches
Discussion of a specific last-mile EV truck depot deployment in Queens, NY

title: Ep. 2: Rob Reich – Schneider
abstract: Rob Reich, Schneider's chief administrative officer (with responsibility for equipment, recruiting, safety, and facilities) and NACFE board chairman, discusses Schneider's scale (roughly 10,000 trucks and 40,000 trailers across truckload, dedicated, and intermodal operations) and walks through NACFE's three core work streams: confidence reports on currently available technology, the Run on Less real-world efficiency demonstrations, and guidance reports on emerging technology like electric and hydrogen trucks. He also discusses Schneider's commitment to continued technology testing despite pandemic-era cost pressure.
key_findings: NACFE's fleet fuel study evaluates roughly 85 technologies, and the organization had published 18 confidence reports as of this recording.
NACFE's first (long-haul) Run on Less demonstration averaged 10.1 mpg and a later regional-haul run averaged 8.7 mpg, compared with a national average of roughly 6.1 mpg for Class 8 tractor-trailers.

Reich describes NACFE's three main work streams as confidence reports (available technology), Run on Less (demonstrating the "art of the possible" in real-world operation), and guidance reports (forward-looking work on electric trucks, hydrogen fuel cells, and automation).
Schneider committed to continuing new-technology testing through the pandemic-driven downturn rather than pausing it, to avoid being unprepared when conditions improved.
data_available: Schneider fleet size figures
NACFE technology/confidence report counts
Run on Less mpg results compared to national average
Qualitative discussion of guidance report methodology

title: Ep. 58: Alison Conway – The City College of New York
abstract: Alison Conway, associate professor at the City College of New York, discusses the challenges dense urban environments pose for goods movement, using New York City as her primary example. She explains how e-commerce eliminated the traditional separation of freight by location and time of day, describes the rise of cargo bikes and box trucks used as 'mobile distribution centers,' and discusses emerging concepts like truck-to-cargo-bike intermodal transfer, containerization for last-mile modality shifts, and 'coopetition' among competing carriers to share delivery infrastructure.
key_findings: In New York City, at least four separate city agencies (Department of Transportation, Department of City Planning, the police department, and the Department of Finance) each play a distinct role in curbside parking and loading policy, making stakeholder coordination for freight solutions especially complex

New York City has an ongoing cargo-bike pilot with several hundred cargo bikes now in operation, commonly used for local grocery deliveries such as by Whole Foods, offering advantages in congestion-bypass and easier parking versus larger delivery vehicles

E-commerce vehicles are difficult to distinguish from passenger cars in traffic data (e.g., a gig driver using a personal vehicle for Amazon Flex deliveries won't register differently on a loop detector or camera), making it much harder to quantify e-commerce's share of urban freight activity than for traditional 5-axle trucks
data_available: Academic/qualitative discussion of urban freight trends and research challenges; no dataset or report figures cited

title: Ep. 89: James Menzies – Today’s Trucking
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with James Menzies, editor of Today's Trucking, about differences between Canadian and U.S. trucking, his 24-year career in trucking journalism (including getting his commercial driver's license to better understand the industry), and how digital publishing has changed trade reporting. The two discuss Canada's long combination vehicles (LCVs, one tractor pulling two 53-foot trailers) as a freight-efficiency example despite poor per-truck fuel economy, Canada's provincially fragmented weight/configuration regulations, and early Canadian findings on cold-weather versus hot-weather battery degradation. They also revisit a January 2024 Today's Trucking article in which Menzies quoted Roeth pushing back on the industry's narrow focus on zero-emission vehicles at the expense of near-term diesel efficiency gains.
key_findings: Canada's long combination vehicles (LCVs) — one tractor pulling two 53-foot trailers — have poor per-truck MPG but are held up as a highly efficient way to move freight overall.
Canadian weight and configuration regulations are set provincially, creating a patchwork of rules rather than a single national standard, unlike U.S. federal/state structure.
Early Canadian fleet experience reportedly found that extreme heat degrades EV batteries more than extreme cold.
A report cited in the conversation estimated it would cost roughly $1 trillion to electrify the entire U.S. truck fleet.

Canadian federal incentives plus provincial incentives in British Columbia and Quebec are driving the earliest EV truck uptake, with private fleets like Loblaw, Tim Hortons, and Bison beginning to deploy electric trucks.
data_available: Comparative discussion of Canadian versus U.S. trucking regulation, vehicle configurations, and infrastructure planning
Early qualitative data on cold-weather versus hot-weather EV battery performance from Canadian fleet experience
Trade-journalism perspective on the evolution of digital versus print trucking media coverage

title: Ep. 39: Jim Sharkey – Pressure Systems International
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Jim Sharkey, Vice President of Global Sales and Marketing at Pressure Systems International (PSI), about the history and maturation of automatic tire inflation systems (ATIS) for trailers. Sharkey traces PSI's origin around a 1993 patent for automatic inflation, the company's early work proving ROI with fleets, and its growth into an industry standard, and discusses PSI's involvement in industry groups like PMC and TMC. He closes with his views on how electrification, autonomy, and hydrogen will affect PSI's tire-focused business and on the technician shortage as a barrier to new-technology adoption.
key_findings: PSI pegs that roughly 70% of new trailers built in North America today come equipped with an automatic tire inflation system.

Sharkey identifies three quantifiable ROI drivers for automatic inflation systems that NACFE's tire inflation confidence report also found: longer tire tread life, improved fuel economy, and avoided emergency roadside breakdowns, with payback often achieved in under a year.

PSI was founded around a patent for automatic inflation acquired in the early 1990s, with the company formally organized in 1993; commercialization took several years of field demonstrations with fleets before wider adoption.
data_available: History of automatic tire inflation system (ATIS) technology development and PSI's role in the trailer ATIS market
Sharkey's personal career background moving from Rockwell International's heavy truck engineering group into PSI sales leadership
PSI's perspective on how electrification, autonomy, and hydrogen intersect with tire technology, and on the technician shortage as an adoption barrier

title: Ep. 23: Paul Stith – Black & Veatch
abstract: Paul Stith, director of global transportation initiatives at Black & Veatch and a NACFE board member, discusses the steep learning curve around electric truck charging infrastructure, drawing on his own experience (his family had driven roughly 300,000 electric miles across nine EVs since around 2010) and Black & Veatch's infrastructure engineering background. He explains why depot-based, return-to-base trucks with long dwell times are the strongest near-term electrification targets, describes lessons from transit bus "opportunity charging," and discusses the scale of grid investment utilities face as truck charging demand concentrates in warehouse districts.
key_findings: A single electric truck may need roughly half a megawatt-hour of energy, so charging even a handful of trucks at one site can approach the power draw of an entire skyscraper.

Stith describes "waves of electrification" (a framing he attributes to CALSTART) in which trucks (Class 3 to Class 8) with smaller battery packs, long dwell times, and return-to-base operation -- such as step vans finishing routes by early-to-mid afternoon -- are the best near-term adoption targets, with long-haul further out.

He points to transit bus electrification as a directly relevant precedent, describing an NYC deployment where buses "opportunity charge" for roughly 5-10 minutes at layover stops along fixed routes to extend range without full depot charging.

Stith raises the idea of adjusting hours-of-service rules (for example, a longer mid-route break) to create natural windows for en-route truck charging, describing this as a speculative but potentially helpful policy lever.

He notes warehouse districts can concentrate enough new electric truck charging demand to become the largest load a local utility has ever served, and says utilities are increasingly engaging on integrated resource planning for this demand through groups like SEPA, where he co-chairs the fleet electrification group.
data_available: Personal EV mileage/ownership figures
Approximate energy-demand figures for truck charging (megawatt-hour per truck)
Transit bus opportunity-charging case example (NYC)
Qualitative discussion of utility funding sources (VW settlement, diesel replacement funds)

title: Ep. 16: Jack Roberts – Senior Trucking Editor and Freight Futurist
abstract: Jack Roberts, a longtime trucking journalist and NACFE's "freight futurist" working on its Perspectives on Autonomy project, reflects on decades of covering trucking technology, including the commercially unsuccessful early-2000s Navistar/Eaton hybrid vocational trucks compared with the surprising success of automated manual transmissions. He and Mike Roeth discuss how autonomous trucking is likely to arrive in evolutionary steps rather than a sudden leap, using driver-assistance features and traffic-jam-assist scenarios as examples, and offer advice for fleets on staying prepared for emerging technology.
key_findings: Roberts covered the debut of Navistar/Eaton's first hybrid vocational (Class 6/7) trucks around 2000, a technology that ultimately "fizzled" commercially, in contrast to automated manual transmissions launched around the same era, which grew from modest ~50% take-rate goals to routine 90%+ take rates today.

He argues autonomous trucking will arrive in manageable, evolutionary steps, citing existing driver-assistance features (active cruise control with braking, anti-rollover systems, steering assist) as the on-ramp toward higher automation levels, much as AMTs became foundational to today's automated driving systems.

His advice to fleets: stay open-minded about immature technology since its capabilities evolve quickly, and designate an internal point person as an informal "technology officer" to track and periodically report on relevant emerging technology.
data_available: Historical account of hybrid vocational truck and AMT adoption trajectories with approximate take-rate figures
Qualitative discussion of autonomous trucking rollout scenarios
No independent quantitative fleet performance data

title: Ep. 8: Jay Lau – TuSimple
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Jay Lau, director of transportation at TuSimple, about the company's path toward SAE Level 4 autonomous class 8 trucking. Lau explains TuSimple's focus on highway and near-highway operation (rather than final-mile or full point-to-point autonomy), describes the newly announced Autonomous Freight Network built with launch partners UPS, U.S. Express, and McLane, and discusses TuSimple's co-development partnership with Navistar to build autonomy into a factory-produced vehicle rather than a retrofit. He also addresses workforce concerns, describing TuSimple's driver-training partnership with Pima Community College and framing the shift as a transition rather than a loss for trucking jobs.
key_findings: TuSimple's Autonomous Freight Network launched with partners UPS, U.S. Express, Penske, and McLane, initially covering the Tucson-Phoenix corridor and expanding as far east as Dallas at the time of the interview.
TuSimple stated it expected a commercially available Level 4 autonomous truck product by 2024, developed via a roughly three-year co-development partnership with Navistar.
Level 4 autonomous trucks will retain a cab for the foreseeable future (not a cabless power unit), in part due to FMCSA regulatory constraints on vehicle definitions.
TuSimple partnered with Pima Community College to offer an 'autonomous operator' certification program to help transition current drivers into the new technology rather than displace them.
data_available: Description of TuSimple's proprietary high-definition mapping approach and its use in the Autonomous Freight Network
Discussion of the technology stack (cameras, LiDAR, radar, onboard compute, self-driving algorithms) underpinning the Level 4 system
First-hand account of the driver workforce transition strategy and partner-fleet rollout plan

title: Ep. 47: Henry Albert – Albert Transport
abstract: Henry Albert, owner-operator and president of Albert Transport and a former championship race car driver, explains how he applied racing-derived driving techniques (focusing effort on flat and downhill stretches rather than climbs, minimizing lateral tire drag) to fuel economy, starting with flatbed load positioning (tucking loads forward and tapering them to reduce aerodynamic drag) in the 1990s. He recounts participating in NACFE's original Run on Less in September 2017, where seven trucks averaged 10.1 mpg, describes his current speed-management strategy on a Laredo-to-Charlotte route to balance fuel savings against hours-of-service and revenue, and discusses Freightliner's Team Run Smart driver program.
key_findings: In the original Run on Less (September 2017), seven participating trucks averaged 10.1 mpg overall, with several trucks, including Albert's, recording individual days above 12 mpg.

Albert says he was achieving close to 8 mpg on flatbed wallboard loads years before Run on Less by positioning loads (tucked forward, tapered toward the rear like a 'raindrop') to reduce aerodynamic drag, versus lower mileage for loads positioned farther back on the trailer.

Albert describes deliberately running near posted speed limits only when it will let him complete an extra 'turn' (round trip) that would otherwise be infeasible, and slowing to 60-62 mph when the extra turn isn't achievable, treating fuel economy and freight throughput as a combined optimization rather than either alone.
On his current Laredo, TX to Charlotte, NC route (1,382 miles), running at posted speed limits, Albert completes the round trip in four driving days, freeing a fifth day for local work or home time.
data_available: Owner-operator's first-person account of aerodynamic and driving-technique fuel-economy practices
Run on Less (2017) results and driver commentary
Description of the Freightliner Team Run Smart driver feedback program

title: Ep. 65: Graham Doorley – Solo Advanced Vehicle Technologies
abstract: Graham Doorley, CEO and founder of Solo Advanced Vehicle Technologies, describes his company's clean-sheet battery-electric heavy truck platform designed to exceed 500 miles of range and to be 'driver agnostic' -- capable of human operation via its first model (the SH1) while being architected for eventual full autonomy (the SD1), in partnership with third-party autonomy providers. Drawing on his prior experience building the Tesla Model S and later working on Waymo's autonomous truck program with Google, he discusses how removing the driver and associated cab systems could improve total cost of ownership by over a dollar per mile and free up weight budget for additional battery capacity.
key_findings: Solo's first truck, the SH1, is a human-drivable battery-electric long-haul platform; the fully autonomous SD1 version removes the driver and associated systems (seats, HVAC, instruments) to add battery range and eliminate hours-of-service driving limits

Doorley estimates that switching from internal combustion to battery-electric alone saves tens of cents per mile, and that removing the human driver and paying for autonomous software instead could save over a dollar per mile in total operating cost

Doorley was surprised that large carriers were far more progressive and eager for electrification and autonomy than traditional truck OEMs (Paccar, Daimler), which he found comparatively resistant to design changes based on his time integrating autonomous sensor systems onto their trucks at Waymo
data_available: Founder commentary on product strategy, TCO estimates, and lessons learned from OEM/carrier conversations; no independent test data

title: Ep. 50: Bill Bliem – NFI Industries
abstract: Bill Bliem, senior VP of fleet services at NFI (a 90-year-old, family-owned, dedicated-contract carrier with about 4,500 trucks, 13,000 trailers/chassis, and roughly 60 million square feet of warehouse space), details a decade-long fuel-economy program that raised fleet MPG by about 1.5 miles per gallon and cut NOx emissions 81.3% through measures like speed governing around 61-63 mph, wide-base tires, five-minute idle shutdown, battery-powered APUs, automated manual transmissions since 2014, and a tight 36-inch trailer gap. He also describes how a 2017 visit to Tesla's early Semi reveal, followed by direct outreach to Daimler, Volvo, and International executives, led NFI into the Daimler Innovation Fleet and its first electric tractor on the road by 2019, with continued growth of its production battery-electric tractor fleet alongside a new heavy-duty charging microgrid.
key_findings: NFI improved its fleet's fuel economy by about 1.5 mpg over roughly a decade while cutting NOx emissions 81.3%, through a bundle of measures: speed reduction/governing around 61-63 mph, wide-base tires with aluminum wheels (removing about 1,200 lbs of tractor weight), five-minute idle shutdown, battery-powered APUs starting in 2010, fleet-wide automated manual transmissions from 2014 onward, and a tight 36-inch (vs. 42-inch) fifth-wheel/trailer gap setting.

A 2017 visit to see Tesla's electric truck program, followed by NFI's CEO directly engaging Daimler, Volvo, and International executives, led NFI into the Daimler Innovation Fleet (alongside Penske) and its first electric tractor on the road in 2019, one of the earliest in the industry.

NFI operated a day-cab drayage electric tractor in NACFE's Run on Less – Electric, and Bliem described plans to grow from 12 pre-production demo units to several dozen production battery-electric tractors by the end of the year, with further growth planned in the following quarter, alongside a new heavy-duty charging facility with an on-site microgrid.
NFI's dedicated freight business runs an average length of haul of about 375 miles, and the company uses slip-seating (two drivers per truck) to run some trucks over 1,000 miles a day.
data_available: Decade-long fuel-economy improvement case study with specific MPG and NOx figures
First-mover account of a fleet's path into electric tractor adoption (Daimler Innovation Fleet)
Run on Less – Electric drayage truck case reference
Fleet composition and operating-model details for a large dedicated/drayage/warehousing carrier

title: Ep. 21: Patrick Molloy – Rocky Mountain Institute
abstract: Patrick Molloy of Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI), who works alongside NACFE's hydrogen and electric truck research team, explains hydrogen's role as a decarbonization pathway across steel manufacturing, aviation, shipping, and trucking, framing it as complementary to -- not competing with -- battery-electric vehicles. He traces why hydrogen struggled to gain traction historically and what has changed, describes his own hydrogen-focused podcast, and advises fleets and manufacturers to move at a measured pace informed by others' deployment experience.
key_findings: The existing US hydrogen market, largely used in oil refining and fertilizer/ammonia production, is roughly 10 million metric tons annually, providing an established industrial base as new decarbonization uses (steel, aviation, shipping, trucking) emerge.

Molloy frames hydrogen and battery-electric trucks as complementary rather than competing: hydrogen fuel cells make sense where weight, refueling-duration, or continuous around-the-clock operation favor a diesel-like refueling model, while a fuel cell vehicle is still fundamentally an electric vehicle.

He attributes hydrogen's renewed momentum, after struggling since 1990s-era advocacy, to cross-learning from battery-electric vehicle advances, improving fuel cell performance and longevity, and substantial cost declines on the electrolyzer side used to produce hydrogen.
He co-hosts a hydrogen-focused podcast that has featured electrolyzer manufacturers Nel and ITM Power, fuel cell maker Ballard Power Systems, Toyota, and aviation hydrogen startup ZeroAvia.
data_available: US hydrogen market size figure
Qualitative comparison of hydrogen fuel cell vs. battery-electric truck fit by use case
No independent truck-level performance or cost data presented

title: Ep. 20: Rick Mihelic – Mihelic Vehicle Consulting & NACFE
abstract: Rick Mihelic, NACFE's director of emerging technology studies (and principal of Mihelic Vehicle Consulting), discusses his path into the organization via a 2013 platooning test with Peloton and CR England on the Utah salt flats, and explains the technology-adoption S-curve and NACFE's adopter-type framework (innovators through laggards) that underlies much of its research. In a rapid-fire segment, he gives quick assessments of connectivity, hybrids, electric trucks, hydrogen fuel cells, full automation, and platooning, and closes with advice on separating technology hype from real-world performance.
key_findings: NACFE's 2013 platooning test with Peloton and CR England, conducted on the Utah salt flats, was one of NACFE's first "collaboration reports" and Mihelic's first substantive exposure to NACFE's work.

Mihelic describes the technology diffusion S-curve and NACFE's adopter classification (innovators, early adopters, early/late majority, laggards), noting NACFE has studied roughly 100 technologies (tires, aerodynamics, and others) through this adoption lens.

His rapid assessments: electric trucks are "becoming the baseline for comparison," especially in zero-emission zones; hydrogen fuel cell trucks are essentially "hybrid electric trucks" suited to different duty cycles than battery electric; and full automation's goal is increasing daily tonnage per truck by enabling additional shifts, with real workforce implications that need to be part of the conversation.

His advice on interpreting new-technology claims: manufacturers can overstate performance by a factor of up to three, while consumers tend to underrate by a similar factor, so claims should be checked against real-world performance data.
data_available: Historical account of the 2013 NACFE/Peloton/CR England platooning test
Technology adoption S-curve framework explanation
Rapid-fire qualitative assessments of multiple emerging technologies

title: Ep. 95: Yunsu Park – NACFE
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Yunsu Park, NACFE's director of engineering, about his career at Navistar and the driver-incentive startup Propel before joining NACFE, and about his work building the real-time data dashboards for NACFE's Run on Less program. Park describes the evolution of the dashboard across four Run on Less events, including an early 2017 feature overlaying live truck locations with weather/wind data during a period when two hurricanes hit simultaneously, and reflects on balancing quantitative ('right-brain') data work with the human, narrative ('left-brain') storytelling NACFE also produces. He closes with an argument, drawn from his time studying behavior change at Propel, that industry adoption of new technology and information succeeds when it is made as easy as possible for people to try.
key_findings: Park built NACFE's Run on Less real-time truck-tracking dashboard, including an early feature overlaying live truck positions with weather/wind data during the 2017 run, when two hurricanes hit the U.S. simultaneously.
The Run on Less dashboard reportedly received over 100,000 webpage views in a single month (September) in the prior year.

Drawing on his time at the driver fuel-efficiency startup Propel, Park argues the top rule of behavior change is to make the desired action as easy as possible to try, using a 'hand someone a cup of coffee' analogy versus a multi-step signup process.
data_available: First-person account of building and evolving the Run on Less data dashboard across four events
Reflections on data/analytics versus narrative storytelling in NACFE's public communications
Behavior-change framework for driving technology adoption, drawn from prior startup experience

title: Ep. 112: Deborah Lockridge – Heavy Duty Trucking
abstract: Deborah Lockridge, editor and associate publisher of Heavy Duty Trucking, discusses her career path into trucking journalism, what makes the trucking industry unusually collaborative and close-knit compared to other industries, and whether today's simultaneous wave of technology change (electrification, automation, connectivity, hydrogen) is genuinely more challenging than past disruptions like 1980 deregulation or 1990s-2000s emissions regulation. She and Roeth also discuss efforts to attract more women into trucking, and Lockridge shares advice on what makes a good trucking story.
key_findings: In NACFE's 2023 Run on Less – Electric Depot, of 122 people interviewed across 10 sites, nearly half (about 60) were women, cited as evidence that new truck technology may be drawing a more diverse workforce.

The US heavy/medium-duty truck market is roughly 300,000 trucks per segment per year, versus roughly 16-17 million light vehicles sold annually, making trucking a much smaller and more collaborative industry than automotive.

Lockridge argues that today's simultaneous layering of multiple major changes (zero-emission mandates, changing demographics, new technology) feels different from prior disruptions mainly because of the pace and number of concurrent changes, not necessarily their individual severity.
data_available: Reflective interview on trucking trade journalism and industry culture
Discussion of women/diversity in trucking, including a cited NACFE Run on Less – Electric Depot interview statistic
No original quantitative research data from Heavy Duty Trucking itself

title: Ep. 56: Kevin Beaty – YUNEV LLC
abstract: Kevin Beaty, principal consultant at YUNEV LLC and one of NACFE's founding members, reflects on NACFE's early history (including advising Mike Roeth to pursue the Carbon War Room partnership) and discusses a YUNEV battery report drawing on 22 years of experience with suppliers, OEMs, and policy. He compares battery sourcing for passenger vehicle OEMs versus commercial truck OEMs, and closes with a frank assessment of electrification's path forward, emphasizing the talent now drawn to the industry.
key_findings: For a regional-haul heavy truck needing roughly 400-600 kWh of battery capacity for a legitimate 200-250 mile daily range, the battery can represent about 80% of the powertrain's bill of materials and roughly 60% of the total truck cost

Commercial truck OEMs (e.g., Freightliner, Navistar, Peterbilt, Kenworth) purchase batteries at roughly 1,000 times lower volume than passenger car/light truck OEMs (Ford, GM, Tesla, BMW, Mercedes), making sourcing a much more diverse and challenging market

Beaty argues the electric powertrain is fundamentally simpler than diesel (despite new high-voltage learning curves), and that trucking is now attracting engineering and business talent it could not recruit a decade earlier
data_available: Figures and conclusions drawn from a YUNEV-authored battery report (referenced, downloadable from yunev.co); no data tables reproduced in the episode itself

title: Ep. 136: Matt Srnec – Thermo King
abstract: Matt Srnec, a principal engineer at Thermo King focused on electrification, discusses the company's long history in transport refrigeration (since 1938) and shore power (since 1962), its E1000 electrified refrigeration unit, and its Heat King heating product line used mainly in beverage transport. He argues infrastructure -- not core refrigeration technology -- is now the main barrier to electrified trailer refrigeration, references NACFE's 2024 decarbonizing truck and trailer refrigeration report, and describes his effort to create a new TMC recommended practice for efficient reefer work practices.
key_findings: Thermo King created a dedicated electrification-focused engineering team in 2018 to research batteries, power electronics, systems safety, and standardization for transport refrigeration.

Thermo King's E1000 is described as a highly efficient, low-range-impact electrified refrigeration system for electric trucks, but adoption has lagged because electric box trucks themselves have grown more slowly than electric semis.

Thermo King's Heat King heating product is used mainly in beverage transport because manufacturers shifted from carbonated to non-carbonated drinks that can freeze in transit; the unit runs off engine heat and now includes solar charging to keep its battery maintained during the off-season.

Srnec says NACFE's 2024 "Decarbonizing Truck and Trailer Refrigeration" report still largely holds up, with connector/standardization harmonization and battery weight remaining key barriers, and electrified reefer adoption currently limited mostly to regional, return-to-base operations.
He is leading a new TMC recommended practice (RP) for efficient work practices in transport refrigeration, noting no such RP currently exists.
data_available: Company/product history (Thermo King, E1000, Heat King)
Reference to NACFE's 2024 decarbonizing truck and trailer refrigeration report
Qualitative discussion of infrastructure barriers; no independent quantitative data presented

title: Ep. 18: Ellen Voie – Women in Trucking
abstract: Ellen Voie, founder, president, and CEO of Women in Trucking, recounts her path from a shop-class background through freight/tariff work, Trucker Buddy International, and a retention-and-recruiting role at Schneider that led her to found Women in Trucking in March 2007, inspired by her involvement with Women in Aviation. She discusses the industry's shifting "dominant norm" (trucks, uniforms, and facilities historically designed for men), the Women in Trucking Index research the organization built to track gender data that fleets previously didn't collect, and the organization's recent succession planning (hiring VP Debbie Sparks in January 2020). She closes with advice on inclusion, noting that roughly 15% of Women in Trucking's own membership is male.
key_findings: Women in Trucking was formed in March 2007, after Voie -- then a retention/recruiting manager at Schneider -- drew on her involvement with Women in Aviation to ask why no equivalent organization existed for trucking.

The organization created the Women in Trucking Index specifically because fleets historically did not track gender-disaggregated data on drivers, boards, or leadership teams; Voie says more fleets are now voluntarily sharing that data with her.
About 15% of Women in Trucking's membership is male, and roughly half its board of directors is male.
Women in Trucking announced a succession plan in early 2020, hiring Debbie Sparks as vice president in January to gradually take on more public-facing responsibility.
data_available: Guest's career history at Schneider and founding of Women in Trucking
Discussion of the Women in Trucking Index and gender-related industry data collection
Succession planning details for Women in Trucking leadership

title: Ep. 82: Ari Kahn – RMI
abstract: Ari Kahn, manager of carbon-free transportation at RMI, discusses the challenge of integrating two historically separate mature systems, the electric grid and freight logistics, as trucking electrifies, drawing on his prior electric-vehicle experience with New York City government and utility Con Edison before roughly a year and a half at RMI. He compares the light end of the medium/heavy-duty spectrum (small vans like a Ford Transit Connect, charging like a passenger car) to the largest electric trucks (drawing power comparable to a skyscraper), and argues that fleets already responsible for their own on-site fueling and running predictable, depot-based routes are best positioned to be early electrification adopters.
key_findings: Kahn argues the fleets most likely to succeed early with electrification are those already responsible for on-site fueling infrastructure (having already considered or implemented natural gas fueling, for example) with predictable, mostly return-to-base routes.
He raises vehicle-to-vehicle charging as an emerging strategic idea, where a large truck's big battery could partially serve as an energy source to top off smaller vehicles at the same site.

Kahn cites a personal example of relatives who went 'all in' on electrification (two EVs plus geothermal heating) and subsequently became newly anxious about grid reliability during outages, illustrating a broader concern he heard from a utility regulator about rising customer sensitivity to blackouts as more household and vehicle energy needs move onto the grid.
He notes that while smaller/lighter electric vehicle costs have dropped to sometimes match or beat diesel upfront cost, heavier-duty electric truck costs have not yet seen comparable declines.
data_available: Kahn's framework comparing light-duty-like small electric vans to heavy trucks that draw power comparable to a skyscraper
Discussion of which fleet operating characteristics (on-site fueling responsibility, predictable routes) make for the best early electrification adopters
His account of a NACFE-organized visit to a Frito-Lay facility as part of Run on Less

title: Ep. 10: James Brown – James Brown Media
abstract: James Brown, editor, producer, and director at James Brown Media, discusses roughly seven years of producing video content for NACFE (dating to a 2014 meeting at ACT Expo in Long Beach), including an estimated 100 NACFE videos, 60-70 of them tied to the 2017 and 2019 Run on Less demonstrations. He describes the logistics of filming geographically dispersed Run on Less fleets and drivers with dedicated crews, highlights driver-shared efficiency tips like Joel Morrow's tennis-ball-under-the-pedal trick and Henry Albert's relocated license plate, and discusses his own Fresh Tracks web series on clean transportation, whose two episodes cover Xos Trucks' electric delivery truck collaboration with UPS and a fully electric airport shuttle program at San Diego Airport with Green Power Motor Company and San Diego Gas & Electric. He closes with advice on what makes an effective short-form video: engagement, natural unscripted interviews, and a clear call to action.
key_findings: Brown estimates he and NACFE have produced close to 100 videos together since 2014, with 60-70 tied to the 2017 and 2019 Run on Less demonstrations.

Brown's Fresh Tracks series produced an episode on Xos Trucks' electric delivery truck collaboration with UPS, and a second episode on a fully electric airport shuttle program at San Diego Airport involving Green Power Motor Company and San Diego Gas & Electric.

Driver-shared efficiency tips captured on camera during Run on Less included Joel Morrow placing a tennis ball under the accelerator pedal to limit pedal pressure, and Henry Albert relocating his truck's rear license plate to reduce aerodynamic resistance.
data_available: History of NACFE's video production partnership and Run on Less video output
Description of the Fresh Tracks web series episodes on electric delivery trucks and airport shuttles
Driver-shared fuel-saving tips documented on camera during Run on Less

title: Ep. 34: Scott Sutarik – Geotab
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Scott Sutarik, Vice President of Commercial Vehicle Solutions at Geotab, about the growth of Geotab's data and analytics capability and its partnership with NACFE on Run on Less. Sutarik, who first crossed paths with Roeth while an application engineer at International/Navistar in Fort Wayne around 2009, describes Geotab's evolution from a small, privately owned, debt-free telematics company with a single data scientist to an organization with over 100 data scientists supporting fleets, utilities, and partners like NACFE at no cost in many cases, and reflects on how large-scale data challenges long-held industry assumptions.
key_findings: Geotab reports roughly 2.4 million vehicles on the road generating over 40 billion data points per day, processed through a big-data system built in partnership with Google.

Geotab grew its data science capability from a single data scientist and a 2016 acquisition of a three-person startup to a team of more than 100 data scientists, which now supports NACFE on Run on Less analysis, often at no cost to the partner.
data_available: Geotab's scale, ownership structure (privately held, employee-owned, debt-free), and growth trajectory in data science staffing
Discussion of how large-scale telematics data can challenge industry veterans' long-held operational assumptions

title: Ep. 57: Jose “Pepe” Gutierrez – NACFE LATAM
abstract: Jose "Pepe" Gutierrez, who leads NACFE's new Latin America chapter (NACFE Latam), discusses similarities and differences between US/Canada and Mexican trucking, including vehicle configurations, road conditions (the Pan American highway, the Mexico City-Laredo corridor, and mountainous routes like Cumbres de Maltrata), and the state of last-mile e-commerce delivery. He describes NACFE Latam's early outreach through the magazine Revista Transporte and industry events, and explains that rising diesel costs -- more than sustainability concerns -- are currently the primary driver of Mexican fleets' interest in efficiency.
key_findings: Mexican trucking rarely uses 44,000-lb axle configurations (only about 3-4% of the fleet), instead standardizing on 46k/14k axle setups because operators want to carry heavy loads

Electric vehicle adoption in Mexico is still nascent and concentrated in last-mile delivery, with examples cited of a bread company operating about 1,200 electric vehicles and a beer company that had just purchased 100

Gutierrez expects electrification to arrive in Mexico first for smaller/last-mile trucks, with long-haul electrification lagging well behind due to limited charging infrastructure, vehicle range, and what he calls the country's lack of a 'culture of electric vehicles'
data_available: Descriptive market comparisons and a couple of named fleet adoption examples; no NACFE report data specific to Mexico

title: Ep. 122: Graham Richard – Advisor to CEOs and Founders
abstract: Recorded during one of their regular walking conversations through downtown Fort Wayne, Mike Roeth talks with Graham Richard, an advisor to CEOs and founders in clean-economy companies and former mayor of Fort Wayne, Indiana, about his career from the Indiana State Senate through business restructuring work and eight years as mayor. Richard describes applying Lean Six Sigma methods to city government operations, including an early remote idle-shutoff system for the city's street department fleet, and recounts the public-private financing effort behind Fort Wayne's downtown ballpark and broader redevelopment. Their prior connection dates to the late 1990s, when Richard was working to help retain manufacturing jobs at International Harvester's design center in Fort Wayne, where Roeth worked at the time.
key_findings: As mayor of Fort Wayne (elected 1999), Richard's Lean Six Sigma team implemented one of the city's first automated technology improvements for its vehicle fleet: a remote automated shutoff for street department vehicles that idled beyond a set time period.

Richard led the public-private financing effort behind downtown Fort Wayne's Parkview Field ballpark (opened 2009), despite initial public polling showing only about 30% approval for moving the team downtown and using public money; the project has since anchored roughly $1.2 billion in additional downtown investment and hosts more than 400 non-baseball events per year.

Earlier in his career, as an Indiana State Senator starting in 1974 (elected at age 26), Richard worked on low-head hydro and co-generation energy projects following the 1970s oil embargo and passage of the federal Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act.
data_available: Richard's career history spanning the Indiana State Senate, private-sector restructuring work, and two terms as mayor of Fort Wayne
Description of Lean Six Sigma process improvements applied to municipal fleet and utility operations
Detailed account of the public financing and community engagement process behind Fort Wayne's downtown ballpark redevelopment

title: Ep. 93: Bruce Stockton – Wilson Logistics
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Bruce Stockton, chief operating officer of Wilson Logistics and a NACFE founder, about his career at CFI and Con-way Truckload and the fuel-economy package (6x2 axles, direct-drive AMT, wide-based tires, down-speeding) Con-way adopted as a self-described 'fast follower' rather than a pure early adopter. Stockton recounts NACFE's November 2009 founding meeting in Chicago, credits data-driven driver benchmarking (idle time, drive MPG, time in cruise/top gear) for guiding Con-way's technology choices, and describes Con-way funding a Canadian trailer-skirt manufacturer's capital needs in exchange for partial ownership under early CARB requirements. He closes discussing the upcoming 2027 engine emissions rules and a customer contract at Wilson Logistics that now makes electric yard hustlers/terminal tractors a mandatory condition of doing business.
key_findings: Stockton, a NACFE founder, recalls the organization's November 2009 'inaugural meeting' in Chicago, where he and Michelin's Don Baldwin proposed hiring Mike Roeth to run it.

Con-way Truckload adopted a bundled fuel-economy technology package (6x2 axles, direct-drive AMT transmissions, wide-based tires, down-speeding, low axle ratio) guided by driver-level fuel-mileage data tracking (idle time, drive MPG, cruise-control usage, time in top gear).
Con-way was among the first fleets to adopt trailer skirts under early CARB requirements and funded the Canadian manufacturer's production capital in exchange for partial ownership in the company.
A Wilson Logistics customer has made converting yard hustlers/terminal tractors to electric a contractual 'table stakes' requirement, or the carrier loses the business.

Stockton describes fleets, including Wilson Logistics, trying to buy diesel trucks young enough to avoid being early field-testers of the incoming 2027 model-year emissions technology, and notes new aerodynamic devices will become mandatory equipment on new trucks starting the following January.
data_available: First-hand account of Con-way Truckload's fuel-economy technology package and the data practices behind it
History of NACFE's founding from a founding board member's perspective
Discussion of electric terminal tractor adoption driven by customer contract requirements, and concerns about the 2027 emissions rule

title: Ep. 5: Ned Harvey – Rocky Mountain Institute
abstract: Ned Harvey, Managing Director at Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI) and a roughly decade-long collaborator with NACFE dating to the organization's founding, discusses RMI's 40-year mission to transform global energy use and its evolving industry engagement work, using the same "two parents" framing (NACFE representing industry insiders, RMI representing outside sustainability expertise) that recurs across several NACFE podcast episodes. He argues that real decarbonization requires businesses to treat climate as a competitiveness and risk-management issue rather than an externally imposed obligation, describes what he means by operating in a "climate-constrained world" bounded by a path to net-zero emissions by 2050, and suggests fleets can find near-term wins that serve both climate goals and their bottom line, such as driver-retention benefits from investment in driver training or new revenue from vehicle-to-grid electricity services. He closes by encouraging engineering students to see trucking and transportation electrification as an exciting career path comparable to aerospace or motorsports.
key_findings: Harvey frames a 'climate-constrained world' as one in which a company's total allowable carbon budget shrinks toward zero by around 2050, and argues every company is implicitly betting on whether climate-related policy, customer, or financial shifts will affect it.

Harvey suggests fleets can pursue actions that create climate benefit alongside direct business value, citing driver training (which can aid both fuel efficiency and driver retention) and potential new revenue from providing vehicle-to-grid electricity services to utilities as examples.

Harvey describes trucking's 10-15 year tractor/trailer replacement cycle as making the sector better positioned for rapid decarbonization than 'hard to abate' industries like shipping, aviation, or buildings with 30-50 year asset lives.
data_available: Guest's career background and role overseeing RMI's industry program
Discussion of RMI's 'climate-constrained world' framing and net-zero-by-2050 logic
Examples of business cases that pair climate benefit with fleet profitability (driver retention, V2G revenue)

title: Ep. 51: Allen Schaeffer – Diesel Technology Forum
abstract: Allen Schaeffer, executive director of the Diesel Technology Forum, discusses the organization's 22-year history as an industry-funded but non-trade-association venue for engaging regulators, media, and environmental stakeholders on diesel technology, and his own path from respiratory therapy and environmental-health research into 13 years at the American Trucking Associations working on emissions policy. He and Mike Roeth recap a public debate on what technology will dominate long-haul trucking by 2030 (Schaeffer argued for continued diesel dominance), and Schaeffer argues the industry underplays a decades-long emissions-reduction success story while flagging that a proposed near-zero NOx rule does little to address the roughly half of the truck fleet still running pre-2010 diesel engines.
key_findings: Schaeffer says diesel engines today are about 98% lower in both NOx and PM emissions than roughly a decade-plus ago, and highway tractor fuel economy has moved from roughly 6 to 8 to 10 miles per gallon over recent decades.

He argues a proposed near-zero NOx rule fails to address the fact that roughly half of the on-road truck fleet still runs pre-2010 diesel engines, and that retiring/upgrading that legacy fleet could deliver larger near-term NOx and greenhouse-gas benefits than squeezing further reductions from already-clean new engines.

Schaeffer participated in a public debate on what powertrain will dominate long-haul trucking by 2030, arguing diesel would remain dominant (over 50% of new purchases) at that date, and said he would feel similarly confident even projecting to 2040.

He notes near-term diesel efficiency technologies entering the market include cylinder deactivation and start-stop systems, brought in partly through supplier consolidation (e.g., Jacobs/Jake Brake becoming part of the Cummins enterprise), plus continued work on waste heat recovery and next-generation SCR systems.
data_available: Organizational history and mission of an industry-funded diesel advocacy/education forum
Executive's recap of a public 2030-technology-dominance debate
Policy critique of a near-zero NOx rule regarding the legacy pre-2010 fleet
Historical diesel emissions/efficiency improvement figures

title: Ep. 125: Adam Klauber – World Energy
abstract: Adam Klauber, Chief Sustainability Officer at World Energy, discusses the company's evolution from biodiesel toward renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and his underlying philosophy of using voluntary market choice to drive emissions reductions. The conversation covers why renewable diesel is a true drop-in fuel for trucking (unlike biodiesel's blend and gelling limitations), feedstock and supply constraints relative to trucking's total diesel demand, and two specific fueling setups used by trucks in NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle.
key_findings: Renewable diesel (RD) can be used at blends up to 99-100% without engine or infrastructure modification, making it a true drop-in fuel, unlike biodiesel, which carries gelling and blend-percentage limitations.

World Energy estimates there is not enough sustainable feedstock supply to cover all, or even the majority, of US trucking's roughly 45 billion gallons per year of diesel demand; the company expects aviation (SAF) to retain durable long-term demand for liquid renewable fuels even as trucking increasingly electrifies.
Renewable diesel can reduce particulate matter emissions by up to 90% compared to petroleum diesel, an air-quality and public-health benefit distinct from its carbon-reduction impact.

In NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle, one truck fueling at Pilot locations in California ran primarily on renewable diesel, while a second truck based in Topeka, Kansas used an Optimus dual-tank system running high-blend biodiesel, flushing the lines with conventional diesel at the start and end of each trip.
data_available: Interview with cited figures on US trucking diesel demand (45 billion gallons/year), renewable diesel particulate matter reduction (up to 90%), and feedstock-linked production tradeoffs between renewable diesel and SAF
Description of two specific truck fueling configurations used in NACFE's Run on Less – Messy Middle

title: Ep. 134: Dakota Semler – Xos Trucks
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Dakota Semler, Chief Amazement Officer at Xos Trucks, about the company's roughly ten-year history, from an early Class 8 electric tractor prototype tour that visited FedEx and Pepsi, to its pivot toward medium-duty trucks after finding heavy-duty charging infrastructure was the biggest customer barrier. Semler describes Xos's strip chassis manufacturing business (built with contract manufacturer FitzGerald), its powertrain-supply business selling electric drive systems to other OEMs including Blue Bird, and the company's participation in NACFE's 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration.
key_findings: Xos originally built a prototype Class 8 electric tractor and toured customers including FedEx (Memphis) and Pepsi (Texas) to gather voice-of-customer feedback, but pivoted to focus on medium-duty trucks (Class 3-6) after concluding that heavy-duty charging infrastructure was the biggest barrier to adoption.
UPS told Xos that if the company built an electric package car, UPS would switch over a significant portion of its fleet, which helped drive Xos's medium-duty strategy.
Xos has built close to 1,000 strip chassis units with contract manufacturer FitzGerald in Tennessee and counts nine of the top ten strip-chassis fleets in the country as customers.
Xos sells its electric powertrain technology to other OEMs, including a multi-year partnership with Blue Bird to electrify school buses.

An Xos truck participated in NACFE's 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration, covering five states over 18 days and charging at public sites including 350-kilowatt Electrify America chargers located at Walmart stores.
data_available: Semler's career background growing up around his family's 200-truck materials-hauling fleet in Southern California
History of Xos's pivot from Class 8 to medium-duty electric trucks and its powertrain-supply business
Xos's participation details in the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration

title: Ep. 32: Gary Gaussoin – Silver Eagle Manufacturing
abstract: Gary Gaussoin, president and chairman of Silver Eagle Manufacturing and a member of NACFE's founding board, recounts how NACFE grew out of a 2009 Rocky Mountain Institute-convened workshop aimed at building industry trust in fuel-efficiency technologies, and traces his family's nearly 90-year history in trucking, from his father's Depression-era petroleum-hauling business in Oregon (founded 1933) to Silver Eagle's converter-dolly and military-trailer manufacturing. He and Mike Roeth discuss the safety and freight-efficiency case for doubles and triples, and Gaussoin describes Silver Eagle's newer commercial electric cargo trike, a last-mile delivery vehicle licensed from a German company.
key_findings: Gaussoin says NACFE was formed in 2009 out of a Rocky Mountain Institute-convened workshop, modeled on becoming a 'Consumer Reports'-like trusted source to speed industry adoption of efficiency technologies.

Citing industry rules of thumb, Gaussoin says doubles have about half the incidents per million miles of a standard 53-foot trailer, and triples about a third, though public perception and past anti-triples political campaigns (e.g., in Oregon, opposed by the railroads) have limited wider adoption.
Silver Eagle developed a specialized trailer for the military HMMWV starting in 1986, ultimately winning a roughly 7,500-unit TACOM solicitation around 1993 after several years of delay.

Silver Eagle's newer product is a commercial electric (or pedal-electric) cargo trike for last-mile urban delivery, licensed from German company Rytle starting in 2019, building on e-bike work the company began in 2015.
data_available: NACFE founding history from a founding board member's perspective
Company/family history in trucking manufacturing (converter dollies, military trailers)
Safety statistics comparisons for doubles/triples vs. standard trailers
Description of an electric cargo trike product for last-mile delivery

title: Ep. 121: Mike McHorse – NACFE
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Mike McHorse, NACFE's Director of Industry Engagement, about his multi-generation family history in trucking and his career at Daimler/Freightliner marketing the Cascadia platform, including its Evolution and next-generation ('P4') launches and early customer demonstrations of collision-mitigation technology. McHorse describes creating Freightliner's Team Run Smart program, which recruited successful owner-operators to share both truck-operation and business-management advice with peers. He closes by discussing what brought him to NACFE after retiring from Daimler and a stint at Penske's Premier Truck Group dealership network, and draws a parallel between early driver resistance to automated transmissions and current driver skepticism toward battery-electric trucks.
key_findings: McHorse led marketing for Freightliner's Cascadia platform at Daimler, overseeing both the Cascadia Evolution and next-generation ('P4') Cascadia launches, and ran customer demonstrations of early collision-mitigation systems -- including 80,000-pound trucks braking to a stop before hitting an inflatable target vehicle -- to help convert skeptical customers.

McHorse created and ran Freightliner's Team Run Smart program, recruiting successful owner-operators (including Henry Albert, Jimmy Nevarez, and Clark Reed) to share both truck-operation and business-management advice with other owner-operators through blogs and trade-show appearances, launched during a period of rising diesel prices when 5-mpg trucks were still common on the road.

McHorse's family has multiple generations in trucking: his great-grandfather was a technician for Consolidated Freightways in the 1920s, his grandfather ran a Mack dealership in Portland, Oregon, his father was director of maintenance for Consolidated Freightways, and his brother was a Daimler engineer who worked on the FLD's aerodynamic devices.
McHorse joined NACFE as Director of Industry Engagement in 2025 after retiring from Daimler and a period working for Roger Penske's Premier Truck Group dealership network.
data_available: McHorse's multi-generation family history in the trucking industry
Detailed account of his Daimler/Freightliner career, including the Cascadia platform launches and Team Run Smart program
Discussion of value-story marketing and total cost of ownership messaging to fleet customers

title: Ep 55: Venkatesan Murali – Merlin Solar
abstract: Venkatesan Murali, founder and CTO of Merlin Solar, describes his path from semiconductors at Intel through founding an optical telecom company and, eventually, Merlin Solar, and how the company applies flexible solar panels to commercial trucks and trailers -- on tractor fairings (like a Freightliner Cascadia), liftgates, and transport refrigeration units on 36-48 ft and 53 ft trailers -- for idle mitigation, battery maintenance, and hoteling power rather than propulsion. He discusses the lesson of needing to speak trucking's language of ROI and hard data rather than sustainability jargon, and frames solar as a bridge technology as fleets transition from diesel to a mix of diesel and electric to all-electric.
key_findings: Merlin Solar claims pilot data from multiple fleets shows about 10 tons of CO2 saved per truck per year from idle-mitigation via solar, converted from diesel gallons saved
Merlin deploys roughly 6.5 kilowatts of solar on top of 53-ft all-electric truck refrigeration units, which can offset load and let the propulsion battery focus on driving the truck
Murali says his early mistake was pitching in Silicon Valley sustainability language before learning to lead with return-on-investment data tailored to trucking's thin margins
data_available: Anecdotal ROI and CO2 figures from company pilots; no published report or dataset referenced

title: Ep. 111: Giorgio Rizzoni – The Ohio State University and the Center for Automotive Research
abstract: Dr. Giorgio Rizzoni, professor and director of Ohio State's Center for Automotive Research (CAR), discusses his career path from electrical engineering into automotive/truck controls research, how university research centers like CAR are funded and structured to work across disciplines and with industry, and his long research relationship with Cummins dating to 1993. He describes a DOE-funded hybrid-electric refuse truck project using supercapacitors, a current DOE/Oak Ridge/Stanford project studying whether Port of Savannah drayage trucks could be electrified, and his view that trucking technology change is best understood as evolution rather than revolution.
key_findings: A DOE-funded hybrid-electric refuse hauling truck project (with Oshkosh Truck) used supercapacitors rather than batteries for energy storage, because batteries at the time were not adequate to recover the payload/power demands of hydraulic accessories like packing and lifting equipment.

A current DOE-funded project with Oak Ridge National Lab and Stanford studies whether drayage trucks operating out of the Port of Savannah, which commonly run 150+ mile routes into North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, and Florida, could be economically and operationally electrified, including modeling how seasonal air density changes affect aerodynamic drag and energy needs.

Rizzoni frames the trucking industry's approach to automation, connectivity, and electrification as necessarily an "evolution" rather than a revolution, given trucking's safety and reliability requirements.
data_available: Interview describing CAR's interdisciplinary funding and research structure
Historical account of a DOE-funded hybrid-electric refuse truck R&D project
Description of an ongoing DOE/Oak Ridge/Stanford drayage electrification feasibility study near the Port of Savannah
No quantitative report data included in the episode itself

title: Ep. 46: Rob Graff – RMI and NACFE
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Rob Graff, a senior advisor to both RMI and NACFE, about lessons from electric transit bus deployment that apply to truck electrification. Graff describes his path through public policy and urban planning graduate work, the Tellus Institute (where he helped develop the Global Reporting Initiative for corporate sustainability reporting), and the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission, where he founded an Office of Energy and Climate Change Initiatives and ran the Interagency Battery Electric Bus Dialogue — a closed-door peer forum among 11 transit agencies operating over 20,000 buses collectively.
