He recounts key lessons from that work: charger-to-vehicle communication failures despite shared standards, the difference between charging at small scale (2-3 vehicles) versus a 200-300 bus depot, and debates over overhead/catenary charging versus plugs and managed overnight charging versus serial fast-charging. Graff argues these systems-level infrastructure challenges, not just vehicle technology, are equally relevant to truck electrification.
key_findings: The Interagency Battery Electric Bus Dialogue that Graff ran involved 11 transit agencies across different climates and time zones operating over 20,000 buses collectively, sharing information in a closed, vendor-free forum specifically because participants did not want to publicly criticize specific charger brands.

Charging infrastructure challenges that work at small scale (2-3 electric buses) often break down at large scale (a depot with 200-300 buses), including cable management, charging cabinet placement, and wireless communication conflicts between chargers and vehicles.
Some transit agencies explored on-route inductive charging at bus stops but largely abandoned it due to the cost and complexity of relocating underground infrastructure.
data_available: First-hand account of the Interagency Battery Electric Bus Dialogue's structure and key findings across 11 transit agencies
Discussion of charging infrastructure scaling challenges (overhead/catenary vs. plug charging, managed vs. serial fast charging) with relevance to truck depot electrification

title: Ep. 49: Sam Spofforth – NREL
abstract: Sam Spofforth, Clean Cities project lead at NREL (and former 20-year executive director of the Clean Fuels Ohio coalition), explains the DOE Clean Cities program's history (dating to the 1992 Energy Policy Act), its network of roughly 75 local coalitions that provide technical assistance and peer connections to fleets exploring alternative fuels and electrification, and its non-prescriptive, locally driven approach. He shares his view that electric vehicle economics are strong for many use cases but urges the industry to first 'max out' what he calls no-brainer near-term applications, terminal tractors/yard hostlers and low-speed medium-duty last-mile delivery, while treating longer-haul, heavier-duty electrification as still an open question relative to hydrogen and other alternatives.
key_findings: The DOE Clean Cities program, about 29 years old and run through NREL's Alternative Fuels Data Center, coordinates roughly 75 local coalitions nationwide that provide fleets technical assistance and peer-to-peer connections on alternative fuels and electrification, distinct from DOE's more R&D-focused work.

Spofforth identifies terminal tractors/yard hostlers and low-speed light-to-medium-duty last-mile delivery as 'no-brainer' electrification use cases that can be scaled immediately anywhere in the country, arguing the industry should prioritize maximizing these before tackling harder segments.

He says he is not yet convinced electrification is the clear winner for medium-to-heavy-duty trucking broadly, viewing hydrogen as a credible competing pathway for that segment, while treating current alternatives like biodiesel and natural gas as useful 'bridge' solutions in the meantime.

Spofforth notes Clean Cities deliberately avoids walking into a fleet conversation with a predetermined technology answer, instead asking about duty cycles and operations first, since a purely electrification-first pitch can backfire in more rural or skeptical communities.
data_available: History and structure of the DOE Clean Cities program
Description of the roughly 75-coalition national network and its services
Practitioner's ranked view of near-term 'no-brainer' electrification use cases

title: Ep. 98: Dave Mullaney – TruCurrent
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Dave Mullaney, chief transformation officer at True Current (which spun out of a commercial/industrial solar and storage developer), about lessons from China's rapid EV transition and the economics of fleet electrification in the U.S. Mullaney, formerly of RMI, describes falling battery cell and pack costs and their implications for truck asset-life assumptions, and explains True Current's two-part business model: modeling the granular economics of fleet electrification (down to individual truck travel patterns) and physically financing/deploying depot-side energy assets like solar, storage, and microgrid controllers. He closes with reflections on staying open to contrarian ideas and practicing self-forgiveness while working through a fast-moving industry transition.
key_findings: Mullaney cites recent battery pricing of roughly $131-132 per kWh at the pack level and about $89 per kWh at the cell level (per Bloomberg New Energy Finance), down from roughly $700-800 per kWh a decade earlier when he started at RMI, though he notes truck-specific realized battery costs are often higher (around $250-300 per kWh).

China reached roughly half of new car sales being electric within about a decade of RMI's China EV program beginning; Mullaney notes the U.S. saw close to 10% of light-duty sales be electric earlier in the year of the interview.

He argues that with improving battery longevity, traditional truck asset-life assumptions (e.g., a roughly 10-12 year vehicle life, declining efficiency/utilization over time) may not hold for electric trucks.

True Current focuses on depot-based fleet electrification (rather than public/opportunity charging) because the value proposition is simpler when vehicle routes, charging patterns, and electricity rates at a given site are all known in advance.
data_available: Battery cost trend data (cell and pack level) and its implications for truck economics and asset-life assumptions
Comparative discussion of China's EV market trajectory versus the U.S.
Description of True Current's fleet-electrification business model, combining economic/data modeling with physical energy-asset deployment (solar, storage, microgrid controllers)

title: Ep. 77: Matt McLelland – Covenant
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Matt McLelland, VP of Sustainability and Innovation at Covenant, a truckload carrier heavy in team driving and long haul. McLelland describes how shippers are increasingly asking carriers about fuel efficiency and emissions, discusses the difficulty of monetizing 'soft' benefits like driver attraction to electric trucks and the 'green premium' shippers say they want but resist paying for, and makes the case for renewable diesel and other near-term bridge technologies (aerodynamic trailer packages, electric APUs) as decarbonization tools available today. He also describes two startup partnerships Covenant has signed: Remora for tailpipe carbon capture and Repower for idle-trailer repositioning/rental.
key_findings: Per an ATA graphic McLelland cites, the average truck on the road today has 98% fewer particulate matter and NOx emissions than the average truck in 1988 (roughly 60 of today's trucks equal one 1988 truck's emissions).
Covenant's average truck age is 2.1 years, versus an industry-wide average of 6.7 years for owner-operators.
Covenant's ROI analysis on electric APUs came out roughly breakeven on hard fuel-savings costs alone, before accounting for emissions/idle-reduction value.
A test combining aerodynamic products on a trailer yielded 8-10% operating efficiency improvement over the prior configuration.
Covenant has signed deals with Remora (direct tailpipe carbon capture) and Repower (a Chattanooga startup that rents and repositions fleets' idle trailers for revenue).
data_available: Discussion of ROI frameworks for sustainability investments, including 'soft' and hard-to-monetize costs/benefits
Covenant fleet age statistics and industry emissions-reduction context
Trailer aerodynamics test results and startup partnership details (Remora, Repower)
Case for renewable diesel as a near-term, similarly-priced, lower-emission bridge fuel

title: Ep. 26: Muffi Ghadiali – Electriphi
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Muffi Ghadiali, co-founder and CEO of Electriphi (which he founded in 2018 after leading enterprise strategy at ChargePoint), about why commercial fleet charging needs diverge sharply from consumer EV charging. Ghadiali explains that fleets care about reliable home-base/depot charging rather than the size of a public charging network, and that utilities — who understand generation, distribution, and rate design but have limited insight into transportation as a new electrical load — need advance, location-specific information about where and how much fleets plan to charge. He frames Electriphi's role as the bridge between the fleet and utility industries, echoing Roeth's 'middle school dance' analogy for how little the two sides currently talk to each other.
key_findings: Ghadiali contrasts consumer EV charging (network-size focused) with commercial fleet charging needs (reliable depot/home-base charging regardless of public network size), arguing a one-size-fits-all consumer charging solution does not work for fleets at scale.

Utilities need advance notice of exactly where and how much load a fleet's electrification will add — Ghadiali's example is a fleet planning to transition 150 vehicles at a single depot, where the local utility may lack sufficient transformer capacity without prior planning.
data_available: Electriphi's founding story (2018) and Ghadiali's prior EV charging industry background at ChargePoint
Explanation of why fleet/commercial EV charging needs differ structurally from consumer EV charging
Discussion of the utility-fleet coordination gap in planning for depot-scale electrification load

title: Ep. 31: Thomas Healy – Hyliion
abstract: Thomas Healy, CEO and co-founder of Hyliion, discusses the company's origin as a Carnegie Mellon grad-school idea to electrify trailer axles, its pivot to a truck-based hybrid solution after realizing trailers sit idle too often, and the 2021 unveiling of the Hypertruck ERX, a series-hybrid (range-extended) powertrain that uses an onboard natural-gas generator to recharge a small battery pack rather than plugging into the grid. He explains the rationale for targeting natural gas/RNG over diesel or hydrogen in the near term, and reflects on lessons learned building a trucking startup, including the importance of passion, incremental proof points, and quick pivots.
key_findings: Hyliion originally built e-axle technology for trailers but pivoted to a truck-based hybrid because fleets own far more trailers than tractors, leaving trailer-mounted technology idle much of the time.

The Hypertruck ERX is a series-hybrid (the same structural concept as a diesel-electric locomotive or hydrogen fuel cell truck): a full electric drive with a small onboard battery recharged by a generator, initially running on natural gas/RNG with a stated roadmap toward hydrogen.

Healy cites natural gas as offering over a 90% reduction in NOx emissions versus diesel and notes there are already 700+ natural gas fueling stations in the US, far more than hydrogen infrastructure at the time.

Renewable natural gas (RNG), captured from landfills, dairy farms, and wastewater treatment plants and injected into the existing pipeline/fueling network via a credits system, can give a vehicle a net carbon-negative emissions profile.

Healy positions battery-electric vehicles as the fit for local/short-haul delivery (roughly under 150-200 miles/day) and Hyliion's range-extended hybrid as the fit for longer daily mileage (200+ miles/day) where battery weight and cost become prohibitive.
data_available: Founder/CEO narrative and company history
Technical description of the Hypertruck ERX series-hybrid architecture
Comparative discussion of natural gas/RNG vs. diesel/hydrogen infrastructure and emissions

title: Ep. 72: Dan Burrows – TruckLabs
abstract: Dan Burrows, founder and CEO of TruckLabs, describes his company's Truck Wings product -- automatically deploying panels that close the aerodynamic gap between tractor and trailer at highway speed and retract for low-speed maneuverability -- and the fuel savings and reliability lessons learned scaling it since founding the company as a Stanford graduate student in 2015. He discusses busting the 'average speed' myth using fleet telematics histograms, the underappreciated role of real-world crosswinds, and two early field failures (wings deploying while being towed backward, and a cellular-reconnection software bug that left wings open during turns) that shaped the product's current design.
key_findings: TruckLabs reports fuel savings of roughly 5-6% for CNG/electric setups, 4-5% for day cabs, and 2-3% for sleeper configurations from Truck Wings, with typical payback around 15 months, based on 650 million cumulative miles across five of the top 10 US fleets

A randomized trial with Ryder (60 trucks run 6 weeks baseline, then 30 randomly fitted with Truck Wings and run 6 more weeks) showed a 4.2% fuel economy increase using Ryder's own telematics and fuel data

A UPS truck with Truck Wings in NACFE's Run on Less – Electric event, running roughly 50-mile round trips, still spent the large majority of its distance at highway speeds (65-70 mph), showing aero benefits accrue even on ostensibly 'regional' routes
data_available: Company-reported fuel savings percentages by configuration; a controlled Ryder fleet trial result; anecdotal engineering failure case studies

title: Ep. 30: Chris Nordh – Workhorse Group, Inc.
abstract: Chris Nordh, vice president of commercial development at Workhorse Group, discusses lessons carried over from his prior role at Ryder into Workhorse's electric stepvan business, the company's history (formerly Navistar-owned, later acquired by AMP Electric), and its C1000 electric stepvan built for e-commerce's growing package density. He describes purpose-built customization needs across industries like linen delivery, an early-adopter fleet running Workhorse stepvans for over five years as part of NACFE's Run on Less Electric, and raises concern that a shortage of certified electricians -- more than grid capacity -- could become the biggest bottleneck to charging infrastructure buildout.
key_findings: Workhorse's C1000 electric stepvan offers roughly 1,000 cubic feet of cargo capacity versus competitors' typical sub-600 cubic foot last-mile vehicles, positioned for the increasing package density of e-commerce delivery routes.

Purpose-built customization varies significantly by industry: for example, linen delivery customers need a wider vehicle body than Workhorse's standard 88-inch width to fit two rows of industry-standard bins with an aisle between them.
Workhorse partnered with EAVX (a division of J.B. Poindexter) to build a broader range of truck body configurations on its existing electric chassis platform to help scale production volume.
One early-adopter Chicago bakery fleet, a Run on Less Electric participant, had run five of Workhorse's electrified stepvans continuously for five to six years as of this recording.

Nordh's biggest concern for the industry's charging infrastructure buildout is not grid generation capacity but a shortage of certified electricians and skilled tradespeople needed to install charging infrastructure and service electric vehicles.
data_available: C1000 cargo capacity specification vs. competitors
Body customization examples (linen industry width requirement)
Chicago bakery fleet case example (Run on Less Electric participant)
Qualitative discussion of electrician/skilled-trades workforce shortage

title: Ep. 91: Rob Swim – Trucking Industry Veteran
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Rob Swim, a 35-year truck industry veteran who worked alongside Roeth launching International's 7000-series vocational work trucks (and the novelty International CXT 'world's largest pickup') and later worked extensively with truck dealerships. Swim discusses the complexity of vocational/severe-service vehicles, what makes a successful truck dealership (service, parts, and customer knowledge over brand loyalty), and his concern that supporting many simultaneous powertrain options (diesel, natural gas, hybrid, battery electric, hydrogen) may strain dealer training, tooling, and parts support. He also reminisces about International's Scout brand, now revived as a battery-electric vehicle under Volkswagen/Traton ownership.
key_findings: Swim expresses concern that supporting multiple simultaneous powertrain options (diesel, natural gas, hybrid, battery electric, hydrogen) at once may overwhelm dealer training, tooling, and parts-support investment, drawing a parallel to International Harvester's historical struggles trying to be 'all things to all people.'
He notes truck dealer consolidation (multi-brand groups or multi-location single-brand groups) has been driven partly by the need to spread technology investment across locations.
The International Scout brand, discontinued in 1980, has been revived as a battery-electric all-wheel-drive vehicle under Volkswagen/Traton's ownership of Navistar.
He cites NACFE's Run on Less Electric Depot statistic that 60 of the 122 people interviewed on-site were women or people of color.
data_available: First-hand account of launching International's 7000-series vocational trucks and the International CXT brand vehicle
Discussion of what distinguishes successful truck dealerships (service/parts/customer focus)
Perspective on the operational and dealer-support challenges of a multi-powertrain future

title: Ep. 19: Steve Ernest – Jacobs Vehicle Systems
abstract: Interview with Steve Ernest, VP of Engineering at Jacobs Vehicle Systems, covering roughly Jacobs' 60-year history of engine retarders (the Jake Brake) and its evolution into variable valve actuation (VVA) and cylinder deactivation technology for diesel engines. Ernest explains why Jacobs shifted its fully-variable VVA work toward large stationary/genset engines rather than on-highway trucks, describes how cylinder deactivation keeps aftertreatment systems hot during low-load cruising to improve fuel economy and emissions, and discusses Jacobs' work with universities (UConn, University of Hartford, WPI) and DOE-affiliated labs (Southwest Research, Argonne, Purdue, West Virginia University) on engine R&D. He also gives his view that diesel engines will remain viable for decades even as electrification grows.
key_findings: Jacobs found its fully variable valve actuation (VVA) technology was worth about 2% fuel economy improvement (5% in certain regions), which wasn't enough to justify putting it on-highway, so the company is instead targeting stationary/genset engines that run 24 hours a day.
A simpler two-position cylinder deactivation/VVA design captures roughly 80% of the benefit of full VVA at about 20% of the cost.
Selectively deactivating cylinders during low-load cruising reduces airflow through the aftertreatment system, keeping it hotter and improving emissions control while also improving fuel economy.
Ernest expects diesel engines to remain on the road for 20+ years even after California's 2035 rule requiring zero-emission sales, since trucks sold in 2034 will still operate for decades.
data_available: Guest's technical background on VVA and cylinder deactivation engineering history at Jacobs Vehicle Systems
Discussion of Jacobs' university and national-lab R&D partnerships (UConn, WPI, Southwest Research, Argonne, Purdue, West Virginia University)

title: Ep. 61: Jigar Shah – United States Department of Energy
abstract: Jigar Shah, senior director of the Loan Programs Office at the US Department of Energy, discusses the LPO's history (established under the 2005 Energy Policy Act, expanded in 2007, funded substantially by the 2009 ARRA stimulus) and its role catalyzing fleet electrification financing. He introduces the concept of a 'valley of inertia' -- distinct from the classic 'valley of death' -- describing fleets and lenders who understand electrification technology works but hesitate to be first movers, and explains why the LPO is often the financing option of choice since commercial banks lack established resale/collateral markets for EV charging infrastructure.
key_findings: The Loan Programs Office has issued about $30 billion in loans since inception with a loss rate under 3.5%, comparable to commercial bank lending, and had roughly $40 billion in additional loan authority remaining with about $79 billion of active loan applications in process at the time of the interview

Shah says LPO is seeing very little interest in Class 6-8 long-haul truck electrification financing, but much stronger interest in construction equipment, farm equipment, school buses, and Class 3-4 last-mile vehicles, where the value proposition and single-site return characteristics are clearer

He cites survey data that 75% of male and 85% of female truck drivers entered the industry because of a friend or family member, and argues that workforce enthusiasm for decarbonization technologies is now one of the biggest (if underappreciated) drivers of adoption
data_available: LPO program-level lending statistics and loss rates; anecdotal workforce recruitment statistics; no company-specific financials

title: Ep. 22: Denise Rondini, Rondini Communications & NACFE
abstract: Denise Rondini, NACFE's longtime communications director and president of Rondini Communications, discusses principles of effective storytelling and press communications drawn from nearly four decades in trucking trade journalism dating to 1982. She covers what separates a worthwhile press event from a wasted one, why company executives should engage with the trucking press rather than cede their narrative to others, and offers her perspective on the industry's progress on gender diversity and its readiness for technology change like electrification and automation.
key_findings: Rondini has worked in trucking trade journalism and communications since 1982 and has run her own firm, Rondini Communications, since 2012, with roughly 90% of clients (including NACFE) in the trucking industry.

Her core communications advice: write to the length a message actually requires rather than a preset word count, avoid jargon and acronyms that assume shared knowledge, and only convene a press event when there is genuinely new news to share rather than minor updates.

On diversity, she says trucking has "come a long way" since 1982, when she recalls being the only woman at some industry events, while noting leadership ranks remain male-dominated; she cites NACFE's high school math modeling challenge, built around an electric truck problem, as successfully drawing interest from young women.
data_available: Personal career narrative in trucking trade journalism
Qualitative communications and media-relations advice
Qualitative reflection on industry diversity progress; no quantitative diversity statistics presented

title: Ep. 35: Taki Darakos – Pitt Ohio
abstract: Taki Darakos, VP of vehicle maintenance and fleet services at LTL carrier Pitt Ohio (about 850 Class 8 tractors, 600 mostly Class 7 straight trucks, and roughly 2,300 trailers running about 9 million miles/year across the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic), describes the company's multi-year apprenticeship pipeline for drivers and technicians, its relatively easy adoption of safety technologies like lane departure and collision mitigation, and its harder-fought sustainability journey, from on-site solar and micro wind turbines to electric forklifts and newly installed 75 kW DC Level 2 truck chargers.
key_findings: Pitt Ohio runs an apprenticeship program that moves new hires from dock work into sprinters/transits, then non-CDL 18-24 foot trucks, and eventually into CDL straight trucks or tractor-trailers, alongside a parallel vo-tech apprenticeship pipeline for maintenance technicians.
The fleet mix has shifted toward roughly a 55/45 split of tractor-trailers to straight trucks as the company plans around freight needs and future workforce availability.

Safety technologies (lane departure, collision mitigation) have been comparatively easy to adopt with strong OEM support, while electrification has been harder even for a company already running solar, micro wind turbines, and electric forklifts.

Pitt Ohio had just installed 75 kW DC Level 2 chargers at its Parma facility (about a week and a half before the interview) as part of its electric truck rollout, alongside two LEED-certified facilities with on-site wind/solar microgrids.
data_available: Fleet composition and operating footprint details for a diversified LTL carrier
Apprenticeship/workforce pipeline program description for drivers and technicians
Comparative account of safety-tech vs. electrification adoption difficulty
On-site renewable energy and charging infrastructure details

title: Ep. 29: Jack Allen – Proterra
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Jack Allen, Chairman and CEO of Proterra and a 33-year Navistar veteran, about his transition from Navistar's COO role into Proterra's board and then CEO seat as the company scaled from a private transit-bus maker into a public tier-one electric-vehicle-technology supplier. Allen recounts hosting a virtual White House tour of Proterra's Greenville, SC facility and speaking at President Biden's climate summit, and the pair debate underappreciated total-cost-of-ownership factors for electric heavy-duty vehicles — particularly driver preference for quiet, smooth electric operation and the revenue impact of reduced vehicle downtime — plus Allen's view that the industry should focus more on charging infrastructure planning than on the vehicles themselves.
key_findings: As of the episode, Proterra reported having built roughly 300 megawatt-hours of battery systems, sold over 1,000 transit buses, installed 45 megawatts of charging capacity, and formed tier-one partnerships with more than eight companies including Daimler and Komatsu.

Allen argues that TCO calculations for electric heavy-duty vehicles typically capture maintenance savings but underweight the revenue value of reduced vehicle downtime versus diesel counterparts that need more frequent service.
Allen and Roeth reference a bill introduced by Senator Schumer around the time of the episode proposing $73 billion in funding to convert the roughly 70,000 transit buses in the US to electric.
data_available: Proterra's stated scale metrics (battery MWh built, buses sold, charging capacity installed, tier-one partner count) as of spring 2021
First-hand account of Proterra's virtual White House tour and participation in the Biden administration's climate summit
Discussion of underappreciated TCO factors (driver preference, downtime/revenue) for electric heavy-duty vehicles

title: Ep 37: Selda Gunsel – Shell Global Solutions
abstract: Selda Gunsel, president of Shell Global Solutions, discusses her path from chemical engineering in Istanbul to leading Shell's technology organization, and Shell's transition from an oil-and-gas company to a broader energy company targeting net-zero emissions by 2050. She describes Shell's parallel investments across low-carbon fuels, its Starship aerodynamic-efficiency demonstration trucks (run with NACFE), a hydrogen refueling pilot with Toyota and Kenworth between the Port of Los Angeles and a warehouse district, expansion of EV charging through Shell Recharge at its retail stations, and a new waste-derived CNG fueling site in Carson, California.
key_findings: Shell has committed to becoming a net-zero-emissions energy business by 2050, pursuing efficiency improvements, low-carbon fuels, and carbon capture/offsets in parallel rather than a single pathway.

Shell is piloting large-capacity hydrogen refueling stations with Toyota and Kenworth between the Port of Los Angeles and a major warehouse district in California, targeting heavy-duty and long-haul medium-duty trucks.

Shell is expanding EV charging (Shell Recharge) across its roughly 45,000 global retail stations for light-duty and short-route medium-duty trucks, and has launched a first waste-derived CNG fueling site at its Carson, California facility.
A Shell/Deloitte study on decarbonization barriers found the major obstacles were infrastructure-replacement complexity, lack of regulatory incentives, and lack of market/customer demand.

Gunsel says Shell has developed Shell E-Fluids, a specialized lubricant/fluid portfolio for electric trucks, alongside continued work on a 'next-generation' Starship project combining low-carbon fuels, energy-efficient lubricants, and powertrain technologies.
data_available: Executive perspective on Shell's multi-pathway energy transition strategy
Description of Shell's hydrogen refueling pilot with Toyota/Kenworth
Summary of a Shell/Deloitte decarbonization-barriers study
Details on Shell Recharge EV charging expansion and a new waste-derived CNG site

title: Ep. 43: Tim Reeser – Lightning eMotors
abstract: Tim Reeser, CEO and co-founder of Lightning eMotors, traces the company's path from a 2008 hybrid-vehicle startup (originally aiming for the Automotive X-Prize) into a fleet hydraulic-hybrid supplier for UPS, DHL, and transit agencies, and its 2017 pivot to all-electric Class 3-6 vans, shuttle buses, and step vans after two major hybrid customers said they would only buy zero-emission vehicles going forward. He discusses dyno-tested efficiency gains, driver-experience benefits that helped overcome adoption resistance seen with earlier hybrid/CNG products, and DHL's phased Manhattan delivery-van deployment that grew from an initial pilot fleet to a 100-vehicle follow-on order.
key_findings: Lightning eMotors pivoted from hydraulic hybrids to all-electric vehicles in 2017 after two major hybrid customers said they would skip hybrids entirely and buy zero-emission vehicles at the same cost as diesel/gasoline.
Dyno testing on a Class 3 vehicle showed the gasoline version averaging about 14 mpg city/highway versus about 66 mpg-equivalent for the electric version on the same dyno run.

DHL piloted nine Lightning eMotors electric vans for over a year at a Manhattan depot (where vehicles are stored on upper floors and driven inside for loading) before placing a follow-on order for about 100 more vehicles.

Reeser says Lightning built out manufacturing capacity early (starting 2017-2018, ahead of confirmed orders) and expected to build about 3,000 electric trucks and buses in 2022, which he frames as material scale for the commercial (not passenger) EV market.

Reeser argues that unlike earlier alternative fuels (CNG, propane, early EVs) where drivers experienced compromises, today's battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell trucks are the first zero-emission options where drivers report a clear net positive experience (smoother, quieter, more power, one-pedal driving).
data_available: Company history and technology pivot narrative (hybrid to full electric)
Dyno-tested efficiency comparison data (mpg-equivalent)
DHL Manhattan delivery van case study with fleet-size figures
Manufacturing capacity figures for 2022

title: Ep. 52: Diane Newton – HNTB
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Diane Newton, associate vice president at engineering and architecture firm HNTB, about intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and NACFE's collaboration with HNTB on freight technology projects for state DOTs. Newton describes HNTB's roughly 200-person ITS and emerging-mobility practice (covering the “ACES” space: automated, connected, electric, shared) and details the I-70 Truck Automation Corridor project, a four-year grant funded through the Federal Highway Administration's Advanced Transportation and Congestion Management Technology Deployment program, jointly pursued by Indiana and Ohio DOTs, that aims to demonstrate truck automation technology with trucking fleets operating in revenue service. She also recounts her prior work on the Smart Columbus program, the $40 million winner of USDOT's Smart City Challenge, which included eight projects spanning connected vehicles, multimodal trip planning, EV charging incentives, and a connected/intelligent freight delivery initiative.
key_findings: The I-70 Truck Automation Corridor project is a four-year effort jointly pursued by the Indiana and Ohio Departments of Transportation, funded through FHWA's Advanced Transportation and Congestion Management Technology Deployment (ATCMTD) grant program; the cooperative agreement was signed in February 2021 with major work beginning in June 2021, and its purpose is to demonstrate truck automation technology with fleets operating in revenue service.

Smart Columbus, the winner of USDOT's Smart City Challenge, was a portfolio of eight projects (narrowed down from an initial fifteen) including a connected-vehicle safety application, a multimodal trip-planning app, an EV/smart-charging incentive program, and a connected intelligent freight delivery project.
data_available: Details of the I-70 Truck Automation Corridor demonstration project structure, funding, and timeline
Overview of the eight-project Smart Columbus Smart City Challenge portfolio and HNTB's role in it

title: Ep. 25: Jules Kortenhorst – RMI
abstract: Jules Kortenhorst, CEO of RMI (formerly Rocky Mountain Institute, whose trucking experts helped conceive NACFE and later merged with the Carbon War Room), explains the climate science behind the 1.5°C warming target and RMI's roughly 2021 strategic rebrand toward near-term, 10-year action. He discusses why trucking electrification has moved from technically implausible to probable as battery cost, weight, and energy density have improved, argues energy efficiency remains essential even as electrification scales, and contrasts trucking's decarbonization prospects favorably against harder-to-abate sectors like ocean shipping.
key_findings: Kortenhorst explains the international 1.5°C warming target (revised down from an earlier 2°C assumption) set following IPCC scientific review, noting the world has already warmed roughly 1.1°C, alongside accompanying goals of net-zero emissions by mid-century and a 50% emissions cut over the following decade.
He describes RMI's rebrand from Rocky Mountain Institute as reflecting a shift in strategic focus toward near-term, 10-year action alongside RMI's existing long-term, mid-century vision work.

He argues that whereas five to eight years earlier long-haul trucking electrification seemed technically implausible given battery weight, continued declines in battery cost and weight and improvements in energy density have made it go from "not possible" to "probable."

He argues trucking is increasingly viewed as less "hard to abate" than sectors like ocean shipping, since rail electrification is already established in Europe and truck electrification is becoming clearly technically feasible, whereas large container ships crossing oceans lack a comparable near-term electric pathway.
data_available: Climate science context (1.5°C target, current ~1.1°C warming, net-zero and 2030 emissions-cut goals)
Qualitative assessment of trucking electrification feasibility shift over time
Comparative framing of trucking vs. shipping decarbonization difficulty

title: Ep. 42: George Miller – BYD
abstract: George Miller, director of sales at BYD, discusses BYD's history as a Chinese battery maker that expanded into electric buses, forklifts, and trucks, its US manufacturing/service footprint (assembly in Lancaster, CA plus regional service centers), and its partnership with Anheuser-Busch, which deployed first- and second-generation BYD electric trucks (including a Run on Less – Electric participant) for California beverage distribution. He explains why beverage/local-distribution duty cycles suit electric trucks (localized routes, moderate payload, long return-to-base dwell time for charging), and discusses bidirectional charging, charging-infrastructure/utility lead times, and battery recycling as the sector scales.
key_findings: Anheuser-Busch's BYD electric trucks in Run on Less – Electric were making roughly 10 stops per route while carrying about 35,000-40,000 lbs of payload and driving between roughly 30 and 100 miles a day, a duty cycle Miller says is well-suited to BEVs.

Miller says BYD's biggest deployment challenge has been charging infrastructure lead time, citing a case where it took three years to get chargers installed, by which point BYD had moved to its next truck generation.

BYD sees bidirectional charging as a still-'embryonic' but significant opportunity for return-to-base distribution fleets to earn revenue by feeding power back to the grid during peak demand periods (roughly 4-7 p.m.), and expects to enable it on its trucks in the first half of 2022.

Miller advocates a progression from electric forklifts to electric yard/terminal tractors to over-the-road electric tractors as a natural fleet electrification sequence, and stresses standardizing on CCS1 charging and planning utility capacity years ahead.
data_available: Company history and US manufacturing/service footprint for an EV OEM
Case study details on the Anheuser-Busch beverage-distribution electric truck deployment
Discussion of bidirectional charging economics and charging infrastructure lead times

title: Ep. 108: Andrew Halonen – Mayflower Consulting
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Andrew Halonen, president of Mayflower Consulting and co-author of NACFE's lightweighting confidence report, about his career as a materials "technology matchmaker" spanning aluminum, brake calipers, and trailer construction. The conversation covers why lightweighting only pencils out economically for a narrow slice of the market (e.g., bulk haulers), a new trailer core-and-skin technology called origami, the role of recycled content and aluminum vs. steel in truck component sustainability, and how AI is being used to help find cost-effective, sustainable materials chemistries.
key_findings: Bull haulers (e.g., fuel or beverage tankers) may pay $8-$12 per pound for lightweighting, far above the roughly $3-5/lb military or ~$1/lb light-automotive rates, because every pound saved adds directly to revenue-generating payload.
A new trailer technology called origami, using a core with skins, can save up to 2,000 pounds on the walls and roof of a trailer.
A lightweighted Class 8 tractor can reach roughly 15,000 lbs, about 2,000 lbs lighter than a standard tractor.

Aluminum truck wheels run roughly 75% recycled content, similar to steel, but recycled content is far lower (near 0%) for aluminum used in demanding aviation/military applications because recycling reintroduces iron that degrades properties.

Some fleets are shifting from 6x4 to 4x2 axle configurations to cut weight and maintenance cost after recognizing only a small share (e.g., ~3%) of their loads actually require the extra weight-carrying capacity.
data_available: Career interview on lightweighting consulting and materials selection for trucks and trailers
Discussion of NACFE's lightweighting confidence report and its follow-up update
Specific cost-per-pound figures for lightweighting across market segments (bull haulers, military, automotive)
Description of the origami trailer core/skin technology and recycled-aluminum tradeoffs

title: Ep. 45: Gina Lopez – Kalmar
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Gina Lopez, a vice president at Kalmar, about the company's terminal (yard) tractor business and its shift toward electrification. Lopez explains that Kalmar Ottawa, the terminal tractor brand invented in Ottawa, Kansas in the 1950s, is now part of Finnish holding company Cargotec (~11,000 employees globally, ~5,600 at Kalmar), alongside sister companies Hiab and MacGregor. She describes Kalmar's participation in NACFE's Run On Less Electric (its first fully battery-electric run), Cargotec's 2019 commitment to electrify its entire Kalmar Mobile terminal tractor portfolio by the end of 2021, and the company's broader pledge to become a 1.5°C-aligned business by cutting emissions in half by 2030. She details Kalmar's second-generation electric terminal tractor, developed in partnership with Cummins on its battery-electric driveline, which offers configurable battery capacity (tailored to a customer's shift schedule), CCS charging, and emerging megawatt charging capability.
key_findings: Cargotec, Kalmar's Finnish parent company (publicly traded on the Helsinki Stock Exchange), committed in 2019 to electrify its full Kalmar Mobile terminal tractor product line by the end of 2021, and separately committed to becoming a 1.5°C-aligned company by cutting emissions in half by 2030.

Kalmar's second-generation electric terminal tractor uses a Cummins battery-electric system and driveline, with configurable battery capacity so customers running one or two shifts are not paying for capacity built for three-shift operations.
The Kalmar Ottawa terminal tractor brand was originally invented in Ottawa in the 1950s and was acquired multiple times, including by Cargotec's predecessor group in the 1980s.
data_available: Kalmar/Cargotec corporate structure, employee counts, and product portfolio (terminal tractors, reach stackers, container handlers, yard cranes)
Timeline and technical details of Kalmar's electric terminal tractor generations and Cummins driveline partnership
Kalmar's participation in Run On Less Electric as its first all-battery-electric demonstration

title: Ep. 75: Cristina Commendatore – Fleet Owner
abstract: Cristina Commendatore, editor-in-chief of Fleet Owner magazine, discusses Fleet Owner's 95-year publishing history (founded 1928) and its evolution from a print magazine into a multi-platform trucking media outlet, her own career path through community journalism and waste/recycling trade press before joining Fleet Owner, and trucking journalism's role as an unbiased, fact-checked counterweight to social media commentary. She praises NACFE's guidance and confidence reports as resources she relies on when covering zero-emission trucking, and discusses progress -- and remaining work -- on attracting young talent and improving diversity and inclusion in the industry.
key_findings: Fleet Owner magazine was first published in 1928 and today is part of Endeavor Business Media's commercial vehicle group
Commendatore says she relies on NACFE's confidence and guidance reports (including an upcoming hydrogen guidance report) when reporting on near-zero-emission long-haul technology

She credits FMCSA's Women of Trucking Advisory Board and grassroots groups like Next Generation in Trucking (co-founded by Lindsey Trent) with driving progress on diversity, inclusion, and career-technical-education outreach in trucking
data_available: Fleet Owner's publication history and current multi-platform (print plus digital/video) structure
Commendatore's career path through local and trade journalism
Discussion of diversity/inclusion and young-talent recruitment initiatives in trucking

title: Ep. 104: Dean Bushey – NACFE
abstract: Dean Bushey, NACFE's Director of Programs, is interviewed by NACFE Communications Director Denise Rondini (filling in for Mike Roeth) about his Air Force career flying C-5 Galaxy transport aircraft and working with early autonomous drone missions, his subsequent roles at Hitachi Energy on microgrids and as SVP of Sustainability at Travel Centers of America, and his current work co-leading the federal EV Working Group's medium- and heavy-duty subcommittee alongside Mike Roeth.
key_findings: Bushey flew C-5 Galaxy long-range transport aircraft out of Dover Air Force Base in the mid-to-late 1990s, work he compares directly to trucking logistics (fuel planning, route planning, cargo loading), and which also exposed him early to autonomous/pre-programmed drone (UAV) missions.

As SVP of Sustainability at Travel Centers of America, he managed both external sustainability reporting to financial institutions and the operational rollout of alternative fuels at truck stops, including low-carbon diesel, renewable diesel, renewable natural gas, and EV charging.

He predicts significant advances in autonomous trucking on non-edge-case highway segments within five years, with broader integration into normal operations over a 10-to-15-year horizon, envisioning human drivers handling first/last-mile legs around ports with autonomous trucks handling the long-haul middle segment.

He served on the federal EV Working Group's medium- and heavy-duty subcommittee alongside Mike Roeth, one of three subgroups (utilities, charger deployment, and medium/heavy duty) formed under the Joint Office/DOT/DOE to identify ways the federal government could ease EV deployment.
data_available: Career background connecting Air Force long-range transport/UAV experience to trucking logistics and sustainability work
Description of alternative-fuel rollout work at Travel Centers of America truck stops
Prediction timeline for autonomous trucking adoption and structure of the federal EV Working Group

title: Ep. 97: Michele Calbi –Team DriveAway
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Michele Calbi, CEO of Team DriveAway, about her prior work leading a major fuel-economy initiative at Swift Transportation during a period of over-$5-per-gallon diesel, and about DriveAway's niche business relocating new and used commercial vehicles from OEM plants to dealers and fleets. Calbi explains DriveAway's single, 'boom,' and 'decked/piggyback' vehicle-transport methods, and describes the company's deliberate 2022 decision to begin moving electric trucks and buses despite early industry hesitance, along with the distinct operational challenges of relocating CNG, LNG, and hydrogen vehicles compared to diesel and electric.
key_findings: At Swift Transportation, Calbi led an initiative that raised the fleet's average fuel economy from 5.26 to 7.2 miles per gallon across a fleet of over 20,000 power units; the team attributed roughly 30% of the improvement to driver behavior (progressive shifting, coasting to stops).

Team DriveAway made a deliberate 'go/no-go' decision in mid-2022 to begin moving electric trucks, despite some competitors declining due to concerns about battery box ground clearance and vehicle cost; it now moves electric trucks and buses (roughly $400,000 each) for at least one OEM through its freight/broker division.

DriveAway distinguishes CNG relocation challenges (inconsistent online fueling-station data, weight limits on decking) and LNG (requiring specially certified drivers) from diesel and electric vehicle moves.
An OEM partner is now performing a 'first fill' of HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil) renewable diesel on newly delivered trucks.
data_available: Case study of a large-fleet fuel-economy improvement program (5.26 to 7.2 MPG) at Swift Transportation, including the driver-behavior share of the gain
Description of vehicle-relocation logistics methods (single, boom, decked/piggyback loads) for new/used commercial vehicles
Comparative operational challenges of relocating diesel, electric, CNG, LNG, and hydrogen vehicles

title: Ep. 1: Joel Morrow – Ploger Transportation
abstract: Joel Morrow, a driver and technology leader at Ploger Transportation, describes the company's expansion to operating in all 48 states hauling primarily food-grade freight, and its continued essential-freight operations through the early COVID-19 shutdown. The bulk of the conversation covers Ploger's extreme downspeeding powertrain strategy, which uses enough gear overlap between the top three transmission gears that a single truck spec can run efficiently in both local pickup-and-delivery (P&D) and long-haul highway duty cycles -- Morrow cites one truck getting 9.7 mpg on local P&D routes and 8.5 mpg on a heavy (70,000 lb GCVW) high-speed dedicated Utah run, and describes ongoing work with OEMs to automate switching between duty-cycle modes. He also shares a controlled comparison from a single round trip: running the loaded outbound leg at roughly 73 mph produced about 8.5 mpg, while running the empty return leg at 55 mph produced 13.5 mpg and cost only about 17-20 minutes of extra time. He closes with skepticism that battery electric trucks can match the fuel efficiency of a well-specced, super-downsped internal combustion powertrain for long-distance freight in the near term.
key_findings: Ploger's extreme downspeeding powertrain strategy, using significant gear overlap between top gears, let a single truck spec achieve 9.7 mpg on local P&D routes and 8.5 mpg on a heavy (70,000 lb GCVW) high-speed dedicated Utah run -- avoiding the cost of maintaining separate local and long-haul truck specs.

In a controlled round-trip comparison hauling paper rolls, running the loaded leg at about 73 mph produced roughly 8.5 mpg, while running the empty return leg at 55 mph produced 13.5 mpg and added only about 17-20 minutes to the trip.

Morrow is skeptical that battery electric trucks can compete with a well-specced, super-downsped internal combustion powertrain (paired with turbo-compounding) for long-distance freight efficiency in the near term.
data_available: Specific fuel economy comparisons across duty cycles and vehicle speeds for a named driver's truck
Description of Ploger Transportation's downspeeding/gear-overlap powertrain spec strategy
Discussion of Ploger's fleet operations and expansion during COVID-19

title: Ep. 11: Steve Slesinski – Dana Commercial Vehicle
abstract: Steve Slesinski, director of global product planning at Dana Commercial Vehicles, discusses Dana's "e-transition" strategy across medium- and heavy-duty electrified propulsion, why medium-duty and return-to-base applications (school buses, package delivery, transit) are the early front-runners for battery electric, and the emerging regional-haul Class 8 opportunity. He also covers Dana's view that hybrid solutions currently make the most sense for unpredictable long-haul duty cycles, an electric yard tractor program requiring 22 hours of daily operation with only 2 hours for fast charging, and how Dana has organizationally adapted its engineering culture to electrification.
key_findings: Dana considers duty cycles under about 200 miles per day the prime candidates for battery-electric solutions, citing buses and school buses as ideally suited applications.
A regional-haul Class 8 electric tractor is described as essentially "a big version of a class six truck," with early offerings targeting roughly 250-mile range.
One customer spec Dana was developing required a yard tractor to operate 22 hours a day with only 2 hours available for fast charging, requiring active battery cooling during charge.

Dana viewed hybrid (not full battery-electric) as the best current solution for on-highway long-haul service in 2020, since it doesn't require new charging infrastructure along every route and can use existing chassis.
Slesinski predicted (in 2020) that fleets would need to start piloting electric trucks by around 2025, with battery-electric becoming a significant, routine part of fleet specs by around 2030.
data_available: Interview on Dana's electrified powertrain product strategy across medium-duty, regional-haul Class 8, and yard tractor segments
Specific yard-tractor duty-cycle/charging-time spec numbers
Qualitative comparison of battery-electric, hybrid, and hydrogen fuel cell suitability by duty cycle
No NACFE report data or fleet case studies referenced

title: Ep. 69: Rob Kelly – Forum Mobility
abstract: Rob Kelly, senior VP at Forum Mobility, traces his career from SolarCity/Tesla through co-founding charging-as-a-service startup Amply Power to his current role building 'truck-as-a-service' charging depots for port drayage electrification. He describes Forum Mobility's first customer deployment -- five electric trucks (three BYD, one Kenworth, one Volvo) at Long Beach-based Height Logistics moving containers from the ports of Long Beach/LA to the Inland Empire -- and a recent $15 million Series A plus a $400 million joint venture with CBRE Investment Management and Homecoming Capital to fund depot development in Southern California and near the Port of Oakland.
key_findings: Forum Mobility's first customer deployment for Height Logistics used three BYD, one Kenworth, and one Volvo electric drayage truck (a fifth Volvo delivered later), charging on 120kW Tritium chargers, moving freight between the ports of Long Beach/LA and the Inland Empire

Kelly cites NACFE and RMI analysis that most California drayage routes run under 200 miles a day, well within the 100-300 mile range of current-generation electric trucks (Volvo, BYD, and Nikola were cited as offering extended-range options around 250-300 miles)

The company raised a $15 million Series A alongside a $400 million joint venture with CBRE Investment Management and Homecoming Capital to build purpose-built charging depots, with charging service contracts running a 36-month minimum (or 60 months for full truck-as-a-service)
data_available: Specific first-customer deployment details (vehicle counts/makes, charger specs, route); company funding figures; drayage duty-cycle range estimates

title: Ep. 118: Dan Priestley – Tesla
abstract: Dan Priestley, director of the Semi program at Tesla, traces the Tesla Semi's history from its 2017 unveil through the December 2022 delivery event to PepsiCo and Frito-Lay, and explains why Tesla deliberately limited its initial truck variants and focused exclusively on the on-highway (rather than vocational) segment, since on-highway trucks consume the most fuel and offer the largest cost-savings opportunity. He also discusses current headwinds (regulatory and tariff uncertainty), what he's learned working directly with fleets, and speculates that electric trucks' greater longevity could eventually lead fleets to extend how long they keep trucks in service.
key_findings: The initial Tesla Semi trucks delivered to PepsiCo and Frito-Lay in December 2022 remain in operation, with some approaching 300,000 miles; the broader Semi fleet has surpassed 10 million cumulative miles.
Tesla demonstrated 500 miles of range fully loaded on a single charge in real-world traffic and terrain testing ahead of the delivery event.
NACFE's 2023 Run on Less validated approximately 410 miles on a single charge and 1,076 miles in 24 hours for a Tesla Semi hauling heavy beverage loads.

Tesla focused the Semi exclusively on on-highway trucking (not vocational/off-highway applications) because on-highway trucks consume the most fuel and therefore offer the greatest cost and environmental savings opportunity.

Priestley speculates that as electric trucks demonstrate greater longevity (via over-the-air updates and fewer wear parts than diesel), fleets may extend their vehicle turnover cycles beyond the schedules historically driven by diesel out-of-warranty reliability decline.
data_available: Interview with concrete Tesla Semi program history and real-world mileage/range figures
NACFE Run on Less-validated range and daily-mileage data for the Tesla Semi
Discussion of Tesla's product-strategy rationale and fleet feedback on adoption

title: Ep. 119: Rachael Nealer – U.S. Joint Office of Energy and Transportation
abstract: NACFE's Mike Roeth interviews Rachael Nealer, former executive director of the U.S. Joint Office of Energy and Transportation (a joint DOE/DOT office), recorded a few months after she left that role. They discuss the Joint Office's origins under the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, its work supporting NEVI and CFI charging-infrastructure grant programs and the Zero Emission Freight Strategy, and what medium- and heavy-duty electrification can learn from the passenger-EV experience -- notably that depot/home charging proved sufficient long before public charging matured. They also touch on the federal EV working group, current policy uncertainty, and Nealer's view that total cost of ownership still favors electrification even as near-term momentum slows.
key_findings: The Joint Office was created under the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to provide strategic technical assistance across the Department of Energy and Department of Transportation for EV programs including NEVI, CFI, and transit/school bus electrification, though it did not directly administer those grant programs (the Federal Highway Administration did).
As of Nealer's departure a few months before this recording, the Joint Office's medium- and heavy-duty work was just beginning to engage with newly awarded CFI grants.

The Joint Office, working with the Vehicle Technologies Office, published the Zero Emission Freight Strategy, a phased national assessment for electrifying and using hydrogen in freight transportation.

Roughly $1.5 billion was, at the time of recording, still available through the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, and new federal guidance made that funding more flexible for states, potentially allowing more discretionary investment in medium- and heavy-duty charging beyond light-duty highway corridors.
data_available: Discussion of the Joint Office of Energy and Transportation's structure, funding role, and 2021-2025 history
Description of the Zero Emission Freight Strategy and the EV working group's medium- and heavy-duty priorities
Nealer's career background in engineering/public policy research and her passenger-EV-to-truck-electrification analogy

title: Ep. 94: Jordan Spradling – Pilot Flying J
abstract: Mike Roeth interviews Jordan Spradling, vice president of transportation and logistics at Pilot Flying J, about the travel-center chain's dual role supplying fuel/amenities to trucking and operating its own large fuel-hauling fleet. Spradling describes Pilot's scale, its 'shaping the future of energy' strategy across passenger-car EV charging and heavy-duty alternative fuels, and walks through detailed math showing why a full transition to EV charging at a single high-volume travel center would require an enormous, difficult-to-provision amount of grid power. He also announces Pilot's imminent deployment of five hydrogen fuel cell tractors in Southern California to be run in the company's demanding slip-seat, dual-shift, 24/7 duty cycle.
key_findings: Pilot Flying J operates over 850 locations across the U.S. and Canada, sells roughly 12 billion gallons of fuel per year (1.3 billion gallons of which is renewable fuel), and became 100% owned by Berkshire Hathaway as of the prior year.
Pilot's own hauling fleet runs 1,500 trucks and 2,500 drivers, slip-seated and dual-shifted 24/7, weighted to 80,000 lbs per load, delivering diesel, gasoline, and renewable products.

Illustrative math from Spradling: converting a single high-volume site (Fontana, CA, roughly 500 100-gallon diesel fills per day) to EV charging would require about 500 one-megawatt charging events daily, equivalent to the power draw of roughly 700 homes per megawatt.
Pilot partnered with GM to build toward 500 travel-center locations with 350-kilowatt EV fast chargers.

Pilot has hauled over 4 million kilograms of hydrogen to date (in both liquid and gas form) and was about to take delivery of five hydrogen fuel cell tractors, plated and grant-funded, to run in Southern California hauling hydrogen in the fleet's normal slip-seat/dual-shift duty cycle.
data_available: Detailed scale statistics for Pilot Flying J's fuel sales, locations, and its own hauling fleet
Quantitative illustration of the grid-power scale challenge in converting a diesel travel center to EV charging
Plans and rationale for Pilot's imminent hydrogen fuel cell tractor deployment

title: Ep. 96: Jason Mathers – Environmental Defense Fund
abstract: Jason Mathers, a Director at the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) who leads the organization's US truck-focused policy and advocacy work, discusses EDF's 50-plus year history (founded by bird watchers and scientists concerned about DDT and Osprey populations), his own path from the Navy into environmental policy, and how EDF prioritizes local air pollution and climate impacts from freight, particularly around ports and warehouses in overburdened communities. He offers practical advice to fleets and industry members on engaging constructively with EPA greenhouse gas rulemakings rather than ceding the conversation to ideologues on either side.
key_findings: Mathers notes heavy-duty charging levels have moved from roughly 180 kW currently toward 360 kW and eventually 500-550 kW, which he frames as evidence that fleets adopting electric trucks today should expect meaningfully better range and charging speed in the near future.

He advises fleets and industry members engaging on EPA's greenhouse gas phase 1/2/3 rulemakings to read the accompanying regulatory impact analysis documents (500-700 pages) rather than only the final rule, and to call EPA staff directly, since agency staff are generally willing to talk with affected fleets.
data_available: Mathers' account of EDF's origin and its current US truck-sector policy priorities (air pollution, climate, environmental justice near ports/warehouses)
His career path from Navy service through the Union of Concerned Scientists to nearly 20 years at EDF
Practical guidance on navigating EPA heavy-duty greenhouse gas rulemaking documents

title: Ep. 74: Melvyn Roeth – father of NACFE Executive Director Mike Roeth
abstract: A personal, non-trucking-industry episode in which Mike Roeth interviews his father, Melvyn Roeth, an Ohio farmer, about the decision to buy the family's 150-acre farm at a young age, equipment-investment decisions over the decades (including trading an open-cab pull-type combine for an enclosed modern one), and Melvyn's long habit of tracking farm financial and production data on early spreadsheet software to guide business decisions. Melvyn also discusses becoming a financial-management instructor for other farmers through a local adult-education program and setting aside part of the farm as conservation and wildlife land.
key_findings: Melvyn Roeth was an early adopter of spreadsheet software to track farm financial and production data (pigs per sow, bushels per acre, price per bushel), which he describes as critical to making sound business decisions
After decades farming his own land, Melvyn spent about 15 years teaching farm financial management to other farmers through an adult-education program at a local JVS (joint vocational school)
data_available: Personal career/life history of Mike Roeth's father, an Ohio farmer, framed as an analogy for the equipment-investment and data-driven decision-making principles Mike Roeth later applied at NACFE

title: Ep. 101: Ben Sharpe – Atlas Public Policy
abstract: Ben Sharpe, senior researcher at Atlas Public Policy, talks with Mike Roeth about his path from oilfield-services engineering in Indonesia into transportation policy research, his roughly 15 years at the International Council on Clean Transportation, and his current focus on the policy design needed to make public heavy-duty truck charging investments financially viable. They also revisit NACFE's first-ever report, which Sharpe co-authored in 2013.
key_findings: Sharpe co-authored NACFE's first-ever report, published in July 2013 on barriers to adoption of fuel economy technologies, which collected roughly 1,800 survey responses from owner-operators and small fleets via a partnership with Kevin Rutherford's trucking radio program -- a dataset scale Sharpe calls unusual for this kind of research -- and which directly seeded NACFE's ongoing annual Fleet Fuel Study.
He was one of the 122 people NACFE interviewed for Run on Less Electric Depot in 2023, visiting the Tesla Semi site at the Sacramento Beverages plant.

At Atlas Public Policy, he is focused on the policy design question of how to make publicly available heavy-truck charging investments financially viable, noting each such charging station can require power on the scale of "a stadium's worth of electricity."
data_available: Origin story and survey methodology of NACFE's first published report (2013) and its roughly 1,800 owner-operator/small-fleet responses
Career path from oilfield services engineering to transportation policy research
Discussion of policy approaches for financing public heavy-duty truck charging investment

title: Ep. 13: Jessie Lund – Rocky Mountain Institute
abstract: Jessie Lund, senior associate at Rocky Mountain Institute, discusses her path from Denver city sustainability work into RMI's trucking program, the value of the NACFE/RMI "two parents" collaborative model, and a Potential Regions report she led identifying the best near-term US regions for regional-haul electric truck deployment beyond California. She also discusses why trucking is well-suited for rapid decarbonization given its relatively short asset life and concentrated fleet ownership, and offers a crawl-walk-run framework for phasing electrification across duty cycles.
key_findings: The RMI/NACFE Potential Regions report used a three-part framework (technology fit, need, and support/incentives) to identify the best near-term US regions for regional-haul electric truck deployment outside California, highlighting Cascadia (Oregon/Washington), the Colorado Front Range, the Texas Triangle, and the New York/Pennsylvania area.

At the time, only about 2,500 US trucking companies owned 100 or more trucks, the group NACFE and RMI identified as driving most new heavy-duty truck purchasing decisions, out of an estimated 400,000-500,000 total fleets.
A memorandum of understanding among 15 states plus Washington, DC committed to achieving 100% zero-emission medium- and heavy-duty vehicle sales by mid-century.

Lund cites a roughly two-week closure of I-70 through Colorado's Glenwood Canyon, linked to wildfire conditions, as an example of climate-driven disruption to a major freight route, used to argue that the cost of climate inaction can exceed the cost of climate action.
data_available: Interview describing the methodology and key regional findings of RMI/NACFE's Potential Regions report for electric truck deployment
General fleet-ownership-concentration statistics (2,500 fleets with 100+ trucks) cited from NACFE/RMI analysis
No granular fleet-level performance data

title: Ep. 128: Blair Hefty – Coyne PR
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Blair Hefty, senior media manager at Coyne PR, about his nearly 21-year run at the agency and his work leading media relations for the Shell Starship fuel-efficiency demonstration truck since around 2016. Hefty traces his career from a teenage fan-club project for 1983 Indy 500 winner Tom Sneva through motorsports PR for BMW and Michelin's sports car program before joining Coyne in 2005. The two discuss how much of the industry's change is evolutionary versus revolutionary, and what makes a successful trucking industry event, using an October 2024 journalist ride-and-drive event with Shell Starship at Barber Motorsports Park as a case study.
key_findings: Hefty has led media relations for the Shell Starship demonstration truck project at Coyne PR since around 2016, including its 2018 public launch event in Louisville and an October 2024 journalist ride-and-drive test event at Barber Motorsports Park.

Hefty's early interest in PR began as a teenager running a fan club for 1983 Indy 500 winner Tom Sneva, later leading to motorsports communications work for BMW and Michelin's sports car program before he joined Coyne PR in 2005.
data_available: Hefty's nearly 21-year career at Coyne PR and prior motorsports PR background
History and event details of the Shell Starship demonstration truck media program
Discussion of what makes an effective trucking industry event

title: Ep. 138: Vinny Riscica – Con Edison
abstract: Vinny Riscica, e-mobility section manager at Con Edison focused on medium- and heavy-duty vehicle electrification, discusses the utility's scale and reliability record, and the unique challenges commercial EV charging poses to the grid -- where a single truck depot's power demand can rival a sports stadium's. He describes Con Edison's faster "site assessment request" tool for fleets evaluating charging sites, New York's proactive grid-planning process that lets the utility invest ahead of anticipated electrification demand, and the grid benefits of off-peak overnight fleet charging.
key_findings: Con Edison serves around 10 million people through roughly 3.7 million customer accounts, with reliability the company states is about 10 times higher than the US utility average.

A charging depot for Class 7 and Class 8 trucks can require energy demand comparable to a sports stadium or hospital, even though the existing electric service at many sites was originally sized for something as small as a shed.

Con Edison's standard load-letter process takes about a month to a month and a half for engineering analysis; the utility created a faster "site assessment request" (a 5-minute form) that gives fleets a 1-2 week estimate of whether upgrades are needed and how long they would take, supporting earlier planning and multi-site comparisons.

New York's Public Service Commission opened a proactive planning proceeding letting Con Edison make substation and feeder investments ahead of anticipated electrification demand (such as mandated school bus fleet conversions) rather than waiting for individual load requests, to reduce future timelines and costs.

Riscica describes overnight, off-peak fleet charging as beneficial to the grid because it uses otherwise low-demand capacity and can create downward rate pressure for all ratepayers, not only EV adopters.
data_available: Utility scale and reliability statistics
Description of load-letter and site-assessment-request processes with approximate timelines
Discussion of NY Public Service Commission proactive planning proceeding

title: Ep. 17: Rustam Kocher – Daimler Trucks NA
abstract: Rustam Kocher, charging infrastructure lead for Daimler Trucks North America's eMobility group, describes DTNA's roughly three-year-old cross-functional "swarm" electrification team (grown from 11 to over 150 people), its Innovation Fleet (30 e-Cascadias with NFI and Penske in Southern California running port drayage routes, with about 500,000 combined electric-truck miles logged) and its Customer Experience (CX) fleet of 6 e-Cascadias and 2 EM2 medium-duty trucks that use a portable, skid-mounted charger so customers can trial a truck without permanent charging infrastructure. He also covers Thomas Built Buses' electric school bus partnership with Proterra and a vehicle-to-grid pilot with Dominion Energy, the Mitsubishi Fuso e-Canter, and his leadership of the CharIN Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standard effort, including testing at NREL. He closes with practical advice for fleets: plan charging infrastructure carefully before "touching the ground" and scale in stages (1 pilot truck, 10 test trucks, 100 for full deployment).
key_findings: DTNA's electrification 'swarm' team grew from an initial 11 people to more than 150 in about three years, and the company's electric trucks had logged close to 500,000 combined miles as of the recording.
The Innovation Fleet -- 30 e-Cascadias run by NFI and Penske in Southern California -- operates on port drayage routes and is DTNA's primary 'gain knowledge' program.

DTNA's CX (Customer Experience) fleet of 6 e-Cascadias and 2 EM2 medium-duty trucks uses a portable, forklift-movable 40 kW charger on a skid so individual customers can trial a truck for a few months without installing permanent charging infrastructure.

Thomas Built Buses partnered with Proterra on electric school bus drivetrains; a program with Dominion Energy has Dominion purchasing and leasing electric buses to school districts specifically to use them for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capacity when not in service.

Kocher leads the CharIN Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standards effort, aimed at charging trucks with roughly 600 kWh battery packs in 15-20 minutes; testing has been conducted at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory in Golden, Colorado.
data_available: Fleet-level mileage and deployment figures for DTNA's Innovation and CX electric truck programs
Description of DTNA's V2G school bus pilot with Dominion Energy
Overview of CharIN Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standard development status

title: Ep. 14: Clark Reed – Nussbaum Transportation
abstract: Clark Reed, a professional driver with Nussbaum Transportation and participant in NACFE's original 2017 Run on Less demonstration, walks through how hours-of-service rules shape his multi-week over-the-road schedule, his daily pre-trip routine of checking wind and traffic apps to plan around conditions, and specific fuel-economy data from his 2018 Freightliner Cascadia (the truck he ran in Run on Less), including its lifetime average of 9.96 mpg over 412,000 miles, a best single-day mark of 14.1 mpg at 40,000 lbs with a tailwind in Utah, and a disappointing roughly 8.5 mpg day fighting rain, wind, and elevation change on a New Hampshire run. He also describes preparing to transition to a new truck with a 6x4 drivetrain configuration (up from 6x2) and his role writing driver-focused articles for Freightliner's Team Run Smart program.
key_findings: Reed's 2018 Freightliner Cascadia, the truck he ran in NACFE's first Run on Less in 2017, had a lifetime average of 9.96 mpg over 412,000 miles as of the interview.

His best single-day fuel economy on that truck was 14.1 mpg, achieved at 40,000 lbs with a tailwind in Utah; a difficult New Hampshire run with rain, wind, and elevation change produced roughly 8.5 mpg.

A stretch of 64 straight hours of idle time during extreme cold weather in the Dakotas permanently dragged the truck's lifetime average down from over 10 mpg, and Reed says he was never able to fully recover from it.
Reed's new truck will move from a 6x2 to a 6x4 axle configuration.
data_available: Specific lifetime and single-day fuel economy figures for a named driver's truck
Driver's description of daily route-planning routine and hours-of-service management
Driver's account of participating in NACFE's 2017 Run on Less demonstration

title: Ep. 124: Matt Schrap – Forum Mobility
abstract: Matt Schrap, chief commercial officer of Forum Mobility, discusses his career across California regulatory policy (California Trucking Association, Harbor Trucking Association) and now heavy-duty charging infrastructure development. He explains Forum Mobility's business model of building and operating charging sites at locations with existing spare electrical capacity, offering truck-as-a-service leasing bundled with charging, and helping drayage fleets navigate California incentive programs like HVIP. The conversation covers the scale of recent HVIP voucher demand for Tesla Semis and how battery electric technology continues to evolve for the drayage segment.
key_findings: Forum Mobility, roughly four years old, targets charging sites with existing spare electrical circuit capacity to avoid long utility interconnection timelines, and also offers truck-as-a-service leasing bundled with charging for fleets.

As of the recording, California's HVIP drayage set-aside had about $59 million remaining out of an original roughly $158 million, with over $100 million already deployed; a recent broader HVIP funding round was fully claimed within 24 hours.
In the most recent HVIP voucher round, about 83% of vouchers issued statewide went toward Tesla Semis; Forum Mobility alone was connected to more than 270 Tesla Semi vouchers.
The South Coast AQMD's InvestClean scrap-and-replace program offers up to $400,000 toward the purchase of a battery-electric truck in exchange for scrapping an older diesel truck.

Tesla Semis in Pepsi/Frito-Lay drayage-adjacent service were cited as hauling roughly 82,000 lbs about 470-500 miles, described as roughly double the range of existing Class 8 battery-electric technology in North America at the time.
data_available: Interview with specific California incentive-program figures (HVIP funding levels, voucher counts) and drayage electrification business model details
Third-party-cited Tesla Semi payload/range figures
No original NACFE dataset presented in this episode

title: Ep. 28: Matt McLelland – Covenant Transport Services
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Matt McLelland, Innovation Strategist at Covenant Transport Services, about his role scanning emerging technology and trends for the long-haul team-driver carrier, founded in 1986 and headquartered in Chattanooga, TN. McLelland explains why Covenant's roughly 900-1,000 team trucks (running up to 22 hours a day) pose a distinct electrification challenge because team operations leave little downtime for charging, argues that fleets should apply new technologies selectively rather than fleet-wide, and describes how shipper customers are increasingly pushing carriers like Covenant toward decarbonization commitments through corporate social responsibility (CSR) and environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting.
key_findings: Covenant runs roughly 900-1,000 team trucks that stay on the road up to 22 hours a day; McLelland argues this leaves minimal downtime for charging, making megawatt-level fast charging closer to a requirement for electrifying that segment versus single-driver trucks that can charge overnight.

McLelland describes a Covenant customer actively investing alongside the carrier in a battery-electric pilot for a mix of long-haul and short-haul duty cycles, reflecting a broader trend of shippers pushing carriers toward decarbonization via CSR/ESG commitments.

McLelland distinguishes CSR (a company's broad stance on people, profit, and planet) from ESG (specific, publicly reported metrics and targets that companies are held accountable to by investors and society).
data_available: Covenant Transport Services company overview: long-haul team operations, 1986 founding, Landair acquisition adding warehouse/full-service capability, and freight brokerage expansion
McLelland's framework distinguishing CSR from ESG and how shipper pressure on carriers is changing
Discussion of team-truck charging constraints as a distinct electrification challenge

title: Ep. 129: Susan Fall – LaunchIt PR
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Susan Fall, owner of LaunchIt PR, whose trucking career began in 1993 in Qualcomm's OmniTracs division during what she calls the pioneering days of telematics, before GPS was a widely understood technology. Fall describes founding LaunchIt PR 25 years ago, her approach to vetting and coaching trucking-tech founders on messaging, and her firm's work representing the Truckload Carriers Association during COVID, when trucking briefly received unusual mainstream media attention. She closes with advice for both tech companies and fleets on staying visible and disciplined through the current freight recession.
key_findings: Fall started her trucking career in 1993 at Qualcomm's OmniTracs division, describing it as the pioneering era of trucking telematics before GPS was well understood outside government and specialist circles.

She founded LaunchIt PR 25 years ago and cites early client relationships with trucking-tech founders including Steve Bryan (Vigillo), Dick Hyatt (Decisive), and Josh Carter, noting a common thread of founders who approached the market with curiosity rather than arrogance.

LaunchIt PR represented the Truckload Carriers Association during COVID, a period when trucking received unusual attention from mainstream outlets including Fox News, Good Morning America, and the Wall Street Journal as supply chain issues became a widely discussed topic.
