Fall argues that marketing and PR budgets are typically the first cut when freight markets slow, which she considers a mistake since a downturn is precisely when companies should be preparing to capture the eventual rebound.
data_available: Fall's career history from the early days of trucking telematics at Qualcomm/OmniTracs through founding LaunchIt PR
Discussion of how LaunchIt PR vets and works with trucking-technology startup founders
Account of representing the Truckload Carriers Association during COVID-era media attention

title: Ep. 81: Dave Beasley – Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company
abstract: Dave Beasley, Vice President of Commercial Tires, North America at Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company, discusses his 40-year Goodyear career, including four years leading the company's blimp/airship operations (overseeing the conversion of Goodyear's three blimps to new semi-rigid airships) before returning to lead the North American truck tire business. He explains why trucking is fundamentally a relationship business balanced against hard cost discipline, how Goodyear differentiates against cheaper competitors through total-cost-of-ownership data, retreading, and service network reach, and how sustainability work (including soybean-oil-based rubber compounds) and rolling resistance (a direct driver of EV range) now shape Goodyear's five- and ten-year product roadmap.
key_findings: Beasley cites that it is not uncommon for a Class 8 tractor to experience a roadside tire issue roughly once a year, often attributable to improper tire pressure for the load rather than tire defects.

Goodyear's commercial tire business spans from Class 8 tractor-trailers down to smaller retreadable fabric tires used on 2B/3 package vans (e.g., FedEx, UPS), while Amazon's home-delivery fleet primarily uses non-retreadable consumer-style tires that fall under Goodyear's separate consumer tire business.

Goodyear is replacing petroleum with soybean oil in some tire compounds as part of its sustainability roadmap, and frames retreading itself as an inherently sustainable practice given its recycling function.
For electric trucks, Beasley describes rolling resistance as directly analogous to fuel economy for diesel trucks, since lower rolling resistance translates directly into greater EV range.
data_available: Beasley's account of leading Goodyear's blimp/airship operations for four years
Discussion of how Goodyear differentiates commercial tires on total cost of ownership, retreadability, and service network versus cheaper competitors
Description of Goodyear's sustainability initiatives (soybean-oil-based compounds, retreading) and rolling resistance's link to EV range

title: Ep. 36: Todd Mouw – Roush CleanTech
abstract: Todd Mouw, president of Roush CleanTech, discusses the company's history as an engineering-services arm of Roush Enterprises and its decade-plus of building propane and natural gas conversion powertrains (including nearly 30,000 propane-powered Blue Bird school buses), the 'ecosystem' of infrastructure, financing, and technician training needed beyond just powertrain technology, and Roush's newer electric Ford F-650 medium-duty truck program, which was featured in NACFE's Run on Less – Electric. He and Mike Roeth discuss how range, payload, and cost trade-offs point toward propane for higher-range/payload applications and battery-electric for shorter-range, lower-payload use cases in the Class 5-7 segment.
key_findings: Roush CleanTech's propane technology is installed in almost 30,000 Blue Bird school buses across every US state and Canadian province, transporting nearly a million kids a day.

Roush unveiled its own-branded electric truck at the 2018 ACT Expo, starting with a Class 6 non-CDL Ford F-650 platform, and by the time of this interview was developing a second-generation version targeted for market around late 2023.

Mouw argues that in Class 5-7 vehicles, fleets asking for roughly 250 miles of range plus full traditional payload in a battery-electric truck are asking for a combination that doesn't work economically, whereas propane can deliver about 350 miles of range with only a couple hundred pounds of weight impact since tanks are liquid, low-pressure, and take the place of the removed gasoline tank.
Mouw expects diesel to struggle in heavy start-stop, heavy-idle Class 5-7 applications as regulations tighten, with propane and EV splitting that segment depending on range/payload needs.
data_available: Company/product history for propane and CNG conversion powertrains
Description of Roush's electric F-650 program and its Run on Less – Electric participation
Qualitative range/payload/cost comparison of diesel, propane, and battery-electric in Class 5-7

title: Ep. 64: Andrew Bremer – DriveOhio
abstract: Andrew Bremer, managing director of DriveOhio (housed within the Ohio Department of Transportation and created by executive order in January 2018), discusses the agency's mission to coordinate connected/automated vehicle, shared mobility, and electrified mobility policy across Ohio state agencies in pursuit of highway safety and efficiency goals. He details Ohio's early leadership in smart mobility -- the US 33 Smart Mobility Corridor, an early automated-truck demonstration with Otto in 2016, and freight electrification studies dating to 2019 -- electric-grid and DC-fast-charging siting challenges, and the I-70 Truck Automation Corridor project developed in partnership with NACFE and HNTB, including its planned RFP process to recruit fleet/technology 'deployment teams.'
key_findings: Ohio recorded 1,244 traffic fatalities on its roadways in calendar year 2021, which Bremer cites as the core problem DriveOhio (created under a January 2018 executive order) was established to address through smart mobility technology

Ohio ran an early automated-truck demonstration on the US 33 Smart Mobility Corridor with the company Otto in 2016, hauling a salt brine tank for the Ohio DOT, around the same time as Otto's more widely publicized automated Budweiser delivery in Colorado

DriveOhio's I-70 Truck Automation Corridor project, developed with NACFE and HNTB, includes roughly $4 million in grant funding to attract technology/fleet 'deployment teams' and a road-audit component using machine-vision-equipped vehicles to assess I-70 infrastructure readiness, with an RFP planned for release in late September 2022 and trucks targeted on the roadway by mid-2023
Ohio is within a day's drive of 60% of the US and Canadian population, ranks 35th in land area but 7th in vehicle miles traveled and 2nd in number of bridges nationally, per Bremer
data_available: DriveOhio's organizational structure and mission under the Ohio Department of Transportation
Details of the I-70 Truck Automation Corridor project (NACFE/HNTB/DriveOhio partnership), including funding, RFP timeline, and road-audit methodology
Ohio-specific freight infrastructure and traffic-safety statistics

title: Ep. 106: Emilia Sibley – Terawatt
abstract: Emilia Sibley, general manager at Terawatt, talks with Mike Roeth about the company's model of building and operating "electric truck stop" charging hubs for Class 8 fleets near ports, intermodal yards, and warehouse districts. They cover Terawatt's phased power buildout, per-kilowatt-hour pricing, real-estate and grid siting constraints, and how fleets use the sites for both overnight base charging and short pop-up top-offs.
key_findings: Terawatt builds and operates "electric truck stop" charging hubs for Class 8 fleets, phasing power delivery in stages of roughly 5-10 megawatts per site, currently installing 350 kilowatt chargers with plans to upgrade to 750 kilowatts and beyond once the Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standard matures.

Sibley describes two distinct charging patterns fleets use at Terawatt sites: overnight/base charging (roughly 90 minutes to fully charge a Class 8 EV) that replaces charging at a fleet's own facility, and 15-minute "pop-up" top-off charging that lets regional-haul EVs extend a route beyond their single-charge range.

She calls the current shift to EVs a "once-in-a-century transition," comparing it to the shift from horse-and-buggy to internal combustion, and notes that unlike diesel fueling, EV charging as a service is billed per-kilowatt-hour rather than as a capital expense.
data_available: Details on Terawatt's phased power buildout (5-10 MW initial pulls, 350kW-to-750kW+ charger roadmap)
Business model description (per-kWh pricing, in-house maintenance technicians, site selection process)
Discussion of base charging versus pop-up top-off charging use patterns for Class 8 EVs

title: Ep. 110: Mike Rowand – Energy and Electric Transportation Consultant
abstract: Mike Rowand, a longtime Duke Energy executive now consulting with EPRI's EVs to Scale initiative, explains the utility industry's perspective on truck electrification. He describes why fleet charging load is fundamentally different from historic electrification (homes, air conditioning, the internet) in terms of speed and energy density, walks through the difference between power and energy sizing for charging infrastructure, and argues that better fleet-to-utility data sharing and coordination is the most urgent need for fleets preparing to electrify.
key_findings: Electrifying 50-60 Class 8 trucks at a single site can create a power load comparable to that of the Empire State Building.

A typical existing truck stop draws roughly 200-300 kW; a fully electrified truck stop serving only electric trucks could require an estimated 20-30 MW, roughly a 100x increase in power density on the same footprint.

Charging infrastructure sizing depends heavily on dwell time: a truck needing 500 kWh has only a 50 kW power requirement if charged over 10 hours overnight, but the same energy delivered in 1 hour (e.g., slip-seat operations) requires 500 kW.

EPRI's e-RoadMap and GridFAST initiatives are described as tools to help fleets share operational data with utilities, giving utility planners and regulators more certainty about incoming truck-charging load.
data_available: Expert interview with illustrative power/energy figures (kW, MW) for depot and truck-stop electrification scenarios
Discussion of EPRI programs (e-RoadMap, GridFAST) aimed at utility-fleet data coordination
No original NACFE report data cited in this episode

title: Ep. 84: Rachel Ellenberger – Green Seed Collective and NACFE
abstract: Mike Roeth talks with Rachel Ellenberger, owner of Green Seed Collective and NACFE's manager of industry engagement, about her career path from a political science degree into clean transportation work at Clean Fuels Ohio (the state's DOE-designated Clean Cities Coalition) and then into NACFE. Ellenberger describes the regional, boots-on-the-ground role Clean Cities coalitions play in connecting fleets, funding, and policymakers, discusses her work organizing NACFE's Run on Less Electric Depot boot camp, and reflects on being a young woman entering the trucking industry. The conversation is largely a career and industry-culture discussion rather than a technical or data-driven one.
key_findings: The national Clean Cities program, run by the U.S. Department of Energy, comprises roughly 75 regional coalitions across the country and celebrated its 30-year anniversary in 2024.
Of the 122 people NACFE interviewed on camera during the Run on Less Electric Depot site visits, 60 were women or people of color.
data_available: First-person career narrative moving from political science and Ohio politics into clean transportation nonprofit work
Description of the DOE Clean Cities Coalition program's structure and regional focus
Reflections on being a young woman in the trucking/freight-efficiency industry and on NACFE's Run on Less Electric Depot boot camp

title: Ep. 107: Elaine Jones – Stillwater Hospice
abstract: Elaine Jones, CFO of Stillwater Hospice and NACFE's contracted accountant since its founding, talks with Mike Roeth about "target costing" -- the product-design discipline she taught him decades earlier while both worked at Navistar -- and about NACFE's all-contractor nonprofit staffing model. She closes by giving Roeth personal career advice.
key_findings: Jones managed Navistar's product costing department in the late 1990s and taught then-colleague Mike Roeth the practice of "target costing" -- setting a vehicle's cost target and margin upfront, before design begins, based on what the market will pay, then cascading target costs down to individual vehicle systems.

She has served as NACFE's contracted accountant since its founding roughly 15 years ago and describes NACFE's operating model as staffed entirely by 1099 contractors rather than full-time employees, which keeps fixed costs low and provides flexibility but depends on contractors' personal passion for the industry to retain them.
data_available: Explanation of "target costing" as a vehicle product-design discipline from a former Navistar product costing manager
Description of NACFE's all-contractor nonprofit staffing/business model since its founding

title: Ep. 126: Zhe Wang – RMI
abstract: Zhe Wang, a principal in RMI's China program, discusses the fast growth of "new energy" (battery electric and hydrogen fuel cell) heavy-duty trucks in China, the policy and shipper-driven forces behind that growth, and RMI's Rush to Zero program, an 8-fleet, 21-truck field trial modeled directly on NACFE's Run on Less. He explains China's freight market structure of many small owner-operators, the concentration of early electric-truck adoption around port-to-warehouse routes near Shenzhen and Shanghai, and preliminary Rush to Zero findings on cost and emissions.
key_findings: China has roughly 25,000 new energy (electric and hydrogen fuel cell) heavy-duty trucks in operation, about 2-3% of total heavy-duty truck stock, with growth accelerating since 2020.
Chinese electric heavy-duty trucks typically use 400-500 kWh batteries for 200-400 km of range; hydrogen fuel cell trucks achieve similar or somewhat longer range, around 500 km.

RMI's Rush to Zero program, modeled on NACFE's Run on Less, tracked 8 fleets and 21 trucks (charging-based battery electric, battery-swapping, and hydrogen fuel cell) over 7 days of operation in 2025, finding roughly 1 kWh per km efficiency for electric trucks and about a 40% emissions reduction compared to diesel trucks over the trial.

Adoption in China is driven primarily by policy (trucks below certain emission/efficiency standards can be restricted from entering industrial parks or manufacturing zones) plus multinational shippers' voluntary decarbonization targets that push carriers toward new energy trucks to win freight contracts.

Port-to-warehouse routes around Shenzhen and Shanghai, with stable daily distances of roughly 200-300 km, were the first movers for Chinese electric trucking due to route predictability and charging access.
data_available: Interview describing China's new-energy heavy-duty truck market structure and adoption drivers
Preliminary results (efficiency and emissions-reduction figures) from the RMI-led Rush to Zero 8-fleet/21-truck field trial
Note that a full bilingual report was still forthcoming (expected January) at the time of recording

title: Ep. 113: Kim Ehrenhaft – NACFE
abstract: Kim Ehrenhaft, NACFE's design director, discusses her career path from trucking trade-magazine journalism into design, and her behind-the-scenes role producing NACFE's graphics, infographics, and Run on Less site visits. The conversation covers what makes an infographic effective (including the creative decision behind NACFE's comic-panel infographic format for Run on Less – Electric Depot), the philosophy that Run on Less uses real trucks on real routes rather than controlled demonstrations, and what a typical multi-day Run on Less fleet visit involves.
key_findings: NACFE's Run on Less – Electric Depot report used a comic-panel infographic format to present multiple findings at once, a creative departure that Ehrenhaft championed and that was later displayed at the White House and ACT Expo.
Run on Less visits involve real trucks, real fleets, real routes, and real cargo rather than demo or test conditions, which Ehrenhaft and Roeth describe as central to the program's credibility.
The (fifth) Run on Less discussed in this episode involved visiting most of 13 participating fleets across the US and Canada.
data_available: Behind-the-scenes interview on NACFE's design, communications, and Run on Less field-visit production process
No technical fleet performance data; the episode is about NACFE's internal creative/operational process

title: Ep. 67: Marc-Andre Page – The Lion Electric
abstract: Marc-Andre Page, VP of commercial operations at Lion Electric, describes the company's history as an all-electric-only manufacturer since 2013 (starting with Type-C school buses), its current product lines (the Lion 6 Class 6 truck and Lion 8 Class 8 vocational/refuse truck, with a Lion 8 tractor upcoming), and its new roughly 900,000-square-foot US manufacturing facility in Joliet, Illinois. He discusses why Lion has vertically integrated into charging infrastructure -- including holding large charger and spare-parts inventories -- because charger deployment can take up to 52 weeks versus days to manufacture a truck, and references Day & Ross's Class 6 box truck participation in Run on Less Electric 2021.
key_findings: Lion Electric's Joliet, Illinois facility is roughly 900,000 square feet, described as likely the largest dedicated electric truck and bus manufacturing site in the US at the time, with a targeted capacity of 20,000 units per year

Lion can currently build up to 18 school buses and 24 trucks per week, but charging infrastructure installation can take up to 52 weeks -- a mismatch that led Lion to build a year's worth of charger inventory and expand into interoperability testing with tier-one charger manufacturers (ABB, ChargePoint, Siemens, BTC)

Page describes deploying charging depots that scale from 10-20 units to 200+ units, at power levels reaching 500 kilowatts to 5 megawatts per site, requiring new best practices around grid management, peak demand, and utility coordination -- previewing NACFE's planned 2023 Run on Less – Electric Depot
data_available: Company facility and production-capacity figures; description of a customer deployment (Day & Ross) in a NACFE Run on Less event; no independent performance data

title: Ep. 68: Ken Marko – US Foods
abstract: Ken Marko, fleet sustainability senior manager at US Foods, discusses his career path from Peterbilt through managing a large fleet electrification program (solar generation, battery storage, and EV/CNG charging) for Frito-Lay in California, to his current role building US Foods' electrification strategy. He explains why US Foods' regional delivery routes (mostly under 200 miles, within the 200-250 mile range of currently available electric trucks) make it an ideal early electrification candidate, describes a 30-vehicle Southern California EV pilot underway, shares impressions of a recent Tesla Semi 500-mile loaded demonstration run, and discusses his role chairing TMC's S11 environmental/sustainability technology committee.
key_findings: US Foods was deploying 30 electric vehicles at a Southern California pilot site within about six months of the interview, with most target routes in the 100-200 mile range to maximize fuel-cost and emissions benefits

Marko and Roeth both attended a Tesla Semi event where the truck completed a fully loaded 500-mile run down to 4% battery charge; Marko notes the ground-up clean-sheet design put significant engineering emphasis on weight reduction

As chair of TMC's S11 committee, Marko notes roughly 15 recommended practices (RPs) on battery-electric vehicles were in development at the time, covering maintenance practices, software, and infrastructure guidance for the industry
data_available: Career/project narrative including specifics of the earlier Frito-Lay California electrification program and current US Foods EV pilot scope; no separate report data
